#141211 15 2006-02-09T07:15:24Z Tsukatu
Peter Bauer, Almighty Emperor of Everything Having To Do With Graphics (Help Desk Director at the National Association of Photoshop Professionals, Adobe-Certified Expert, and member of the Photoshop World Instructor Dream Team), says the following:

Quote
JPG: JPEG, as it's called, is actually a file compression scheme rather than a file format, but that's not important. What is important is that JPEG throws away some of your image data when it saves the file... use JPEG only for copies. When should you use JPEG? When sending images to a photo lab that doen't accept TIFF files and when sending images (perhaps by e-mail or on CD)... When saving JPEGs, the lower the quality setting you choose... the smaller the file but also the more damage to the image.

GIF: GIF is more appropriate for items like Web buttons and banners... that it is for photos. If you save a photo that's more than perhaps 100 pixels x 100 pixels in size, you might see some degradation of the image quality as similar colors become on color. When you save an image as a GIF, it can contain no more than 256 distinct colors. JPEG and the other common file formats can have thousands of different colors.

PNG: PNG comes in two types: PNG-8 (which is a substitute for GIF) and PNG-24 (which is a substitute for JPEG). PNG has a couple of advantages for Web designers, such as support for transparency, but not all Web browsers can display PNG graphics. Generally speaking, it's safer to use JPEG and GIF.

#6772 1 2006-02-10T09:02:11Z Tsukatu
WARNING: Posting links to or pictures of guro in this thread will result in an immediate suspension or ban, as appropriate.

ADDITIONAL WARNING: The content in this thread will in all likelihood shock you. It is highly recommended that anyone who is not a fan of guro not read any further.

If you are an impressionable youth, get the fuck out of this thread right now.

I mean it.

I'll pay special attention to this thread, so any moderators or administrators that do not wish to read on, don't worry; I'll handle it.

---

I just finished a guro binge.
I do that every once in a while, possibly once or twice a month. I have plenty of reasons for it, actually. For one, I find it fascinating the way people think about someone changes when the person is dead or mutilated. I was interested in seeing for myself how much I consider them things based on how fucked up they are (you know, "a human head" vs "it's still Johnny"). Beheadings do it for me especially. One second, there's a blindfolded person speaking to the camera, people begin hurting him, and then he becomes two independent objects. I've tried to figure the moment I stopped considering the victim a person. I think it's right when the knife tears out through the front of the throat.

I don't do this because I'm sadistic, and I most definitely do not "get off" on this stuff. The first time I started looking at guro I actually got pretty nauseated. I didn't throw up; I have a strong stomach. The next few times weren't as bad, and by now I can and have looked at slideshows of third-trimester abortions while eating a ham sandwich.
Well, except for beheadings. My stomach still turns a little when I see a beheading.

My original reason was that there are plenty of bad people out there who can do plenty of nasty things to me or people around me. We hear about bombings and shit like that all the time, but we never consider what it's like to be part of that. Yeah, we hear that a dozen people died... but what about the ones who were only injured and who stayed conscious throughout the event? We never hear how much counseling they need. So my objective was to see if I can desensitize myself to gore so that I'd be much more able to act if I were ever in such a situation.
I mean seriously, if you were in a subway car that was blown to smithereens and you were alive but trapped under a large piece of debris or something. There'd be blood everywhere. How many people in this world would be absolutely paralyzed with fear? How many people would faint? Go into shock? Or what if, in order to free yourself, you needed to actually come into contact with, for lack of a better term, something nasty?
I won't be the queasy guy who failed to get out of the car in time before it collapsed on him because he fainted or couldn't bring himself to lift the debris when it was caked with organs and cerebral fluid.

Ever seen the movie Saw? How 'bout Saw 2?
Saw 2 was pretty stupid. There were plenty of ways to avoid certain death or mutilation in getting the antidotes. More than half of the ones that were found could've been obtained without any pain whatsoever, and I'm including the one in the safe, the ones in the furnace, and the one in the glass box. Oh, and that key beneath the syringes. Why couldn't he take off his shirt, wrap it around his hands, and use that to sift through the syringes? He's wearing shoes, right? And if he's real concerned, why not just use the fucking bat?
Seriously, people don't think well when they're faced with gore.

Some of what I look at is anime, but mostly it's pictures or video of actual events.

Aaaaanyway, now that you probably think I'm a total freak, comments from anyone with enough nerve to actually read through this?
#141760 8 2006-02-10T16:40:25Z Tsukatu
Quote: Teh Dude, 2006-02-10T12:33:15Z
On topic, if you are beheaded your head stays conscious for about 30 seconds. You can even hear people talking to you.
You're making this up. I had to have seen at least a dozen beheadings (usually executions by some extremist Islamic sect), and not one of the heads was moving just after it was removed. One second they're screaming, and the next the head is completely motionless. The only instance in which I've seen movement after a beheading was when I saw a pig beheaded with a chainsaw. The pig's body kept moving as though it was running away (though it was on its side), but the head was definitely perfectly still.
From a more scientific approach, though:
With both jugular veins severed completely, the head would bleed out in a few seconds at most. Your brain can survive for anywhere from 4 to 6 seconds without oxygen before you go comatose and start getting serious brain damage. Talking is just shaping your throat (specifically by moving your vocal chords) and mouth in specific ways while breathing out slowly, and all breathing is controlled by your diaphragm, which is below your lungs. A severed head, even if it is still alive and conscious, has no means of speaking.

I've been half-rambling about this in religious discussions, though I guess I can directly address it here.
I think it's great that people do nice things for each other, whatever their motivation. I don't care if God, Satan, or Epona tells you to be nice to people, so long as you're nice to people. But I divorce benevolence from religion. Most people think the two come hand-in-hand. I can be just as nice as a religious person (and from my experience, I tend to be nicer) without having any motivation other than my own benevolent will. Part of my beef with religion is the extranneous stuff, such as completely irrelevant or contradictory stories or other rulings to do things other than being nice. It's awesome that the Bible tells you to love your neighbor; it isn't that it clarifies that the neighbor must be a white male who doesn't work Sundays, isn't homosexual, doesn't wear clothing made of two different materials, isn't blind, etc. It doesn't matter who the person you're being nice to is - just be nice!
But what if your kindness is abused? Well lemme tell you this:
Recently I joined a Christian youth group. Well, not a youth group per se, because I only go to one of their functions weekly that involves the people actually in the youth group bringing friends, but still. I'm still quite secure in my atheism, and I have to admit that part of my motivation to come is in the form of a girl, but I have learned a bit from the meetings, and I get much more out of it than I thought I would. In particular, everyone in the youth group is very supportive of just about every other member. It hit me in the first meeting - these people have a really nice setup going on. Every individual feels love and support from everyone else in the group, and so is motivated to be nice to people himself. I haven't found that in any atheist community I've been apart of. Sure, they use Christianity as an excuse, but I don't care. Whatever reason they need to be nice, let 'em have it. I even put up with flagrant contradictions (as you should know, the Bible essentially tells you to kill atheists, gays, Jews, retards, and cripples, but this youth group supports 'em all). Anyway, the lesson here is that kindness will eventually win just about anybody over. If someone abuses your kindness, it just means they're insecure or that something is deeply troubling them. Keeping up your kindness toward that person (to a reasonable extent) will eventually make him happy, and people do some very generous things when they're happy.

Before this turns into a rant (probably too late), one more issue:
Consider the person who, after losing his faith in God, doesn't see a point in being nice anymore. This guy is the kind of person who needs constant supervision if you want him to be nice. He won't be nice unless he knows he'll be punished for being bad, and once he knows no one is watching, he'll feel free to be bad. I have no respect for these kinds of people. They deserve the ignorance their religion breeds.

Live for each day. If you do not believe in an afterlife then you make sure that you have as much fun as possible while you are alive.

I am not kidding you.

#151153 59 2006-03-03T17:00:54Z Tsukatu
iangb and Teh Dude:

The Heisenberg Uncertainty Principle has to do with observation and our ability to predict present and future states. Using it to state that interaction of matter is chaotic, that events are unpredictable on a theoretical level, or that free will exists because of it is not a correct application, however.
The fact is that, even though we don't have a practical (or any, for that matter) means of finding out specific present and future states of things, does not mean that an exact, definitive outcome does not exist. In fact, an exact, definitive outcome is assured to exist unless there is something supernatural affecting the natural universe (i.e. God), and in all other cases, every bit and piece of the natural universe will follow a set, unchanging set of laws and will act in one way, and one way only, even if it's not possible to predict it.

The fact that you cannot predict present and future states of matter gives us the illusion of free will.

People also have a tendency to... "humanize" things. It's a perfectly normal thing to do, and it sure helps us in our conventional, everyday lives, but it becomes a terrible burden in discussions of science and philosophy. By "humanizing" things, I don't mean we anthropomorphize things. I mean that we look at ourselves as independent systems in a bigger system, instead of one massive, jumbled mess of matter, which is what we really are.
When I tried to explain what I meant to people in the past, the following example helped:
Imagine your skin. Zoom in until you can see individual skin cells. You're probably imagining looking top-down at your skin cells, so rotate your vision about 90 degrees so that you can see your skin cells in contact with the air. Zoom in even closer until you can see the individual lipids that make up the phospholipid bilayer on your skin cell membrane. Keep zooming in until you can see the atoms that make up the lipids and can see the atoms of the air next to it. Consider that the only thing keeping those lipids, that cell, and the cells that make up your skin, together is the fact that they have a slightly larger electromagnetic attraction to each other than they do to the air (especially N2, which is totally unattractive to just about anything).
Kind of wierd to think about, isn't it? On the atomic level, you're not a person, just a particular chunk of matter that, when looking purely at the atomic structure of one area of the universe, is very hard to distinguish from any other area with an equivalent density of matter (such as the ground, air, or another organism). If you look on that level, you'll pretty much see what's at the top of the attached picture.
Anyway, because of this tendency to think this way, we often take a more spiritual look at philosophy as opposed to a more sensical scientific look. You are not special. You are a clump of atoms, just like the ground, sky, and seas.

Attachment:
Top: what you would look like if you were to look at yourself on an atomic level.
Bottom: the same as the top, but borders are drawn, very roughly, around clumps of matter that are more attracted to themselves than their surroundings.
Attachment (lost): post-29-1141405254.jpg

Who here has seen that new release, UltraViolet?
*raises hand*

So whadya think?
Good action scenes, great soundtrack, excellent scenery... lack of continuity, poor acting (except for Milla Jovovich, who I am very surprised participated in this), incoherent script, and god-awful blood effects (the ones that existed, anyway).
Am I right, or am I right?

I love seeing Milla Jovovich in Resident Evil movies 'n junk, but this was far beneath her. It's almost depressing to see her in something this low of quality.

Plot-wise, the movie was acceptable through the first two-thirds, but after that everything went to Hell. There were a scattered moments that made me practically leap out of my chair (I was restrained by friends) and shout "What!? Where the fuck did that come from?" It was that same feeling when you fall asleep and then snap awake later on in a movie, but didn't realize you fell asleep, to see that in the movie something completely different and irrelevant is going on.

You remember when Violet uses the hologram not to distract whatsisface's security, but instead to test it, sees it's hopeless, and the next fucking thing she's on the playground with the kid? Why... why does this work? What makes the director think it works? "Oh fuck, can't raid the corporation, might as well dick around in the park before you die. Yeah, I'm pretty much giving up on you, kid." How the fuck did she even get to the park when security apparently owns the city and appears on every street corner, recognizing Violet immediately?

And what's with the bullshit lead-in to have a flaming sword fight, which in and of itself was fucking ridiculous. The director wanted it so badly that he sacrificed continuity. I mean, she's a hemophage, so she can see in the dark (as was demonstrated by her old friends when the villain somehow appears within their organization), so the villain can't exactly use that against her as he had intended. It is revealed later that the villain himself has actually been a hemophage for a long time and so can see in the dark, which doesn't explain how he went so long without being detected (as that what his corporation focuses on), why he wasn't dead when he touches the boy (whom he says will kill hemophages on contact), and why he gets so pissed about Violet getting hemophage blood on him. (Not to mention that pathetic sequence that followed - "You got hemophage blood on me." "Yeah, I did." (pause; takes off gloves) "It's on!" (pause about half a minute long) "Yeah - it is." (commence awkward fight sequence))

They had to have improv'd half of the fuckin' movie. The had to have. No script that shitty makes it to the big screen.

Oh, and can we talk about the complete lack of blood? Violet totally destroys dozens of people with bullets and assorted bladed objects, at some points even removing heads and torsos. But have you noticed that the final moments of the fight sequences, when they're showing everybody dead and Violet doing some pose in the center, that there is no blood anywhere? It couldn't be hidden anywhere - in one of the final battles, she's against guys in white radioactive suits in a steel bluish white room, so blood would stand out, and that's the scene where she cut most of the people up with a katana.
The only blood I can actually remember seeing is the blood in the tanks that the hemophage soldiers are trying to get in the very beginning of the movie (speaking of which, Violet appears to have absolutely no dependency on blood; only an ambiguous getting-sick scene in the very beginning of the movie wherein she cures herself by injecting herself with some mystery non-red-colored fluid) and the scene after the above-described fight against people in white radioactive suits. She grabs a katana by the blade several times, and so what they did to show her bloody hands was slash up her gloves and then color her palms red with a sharpie. There was no actual liquid involved. Oh wait, fine, there was that scene directly afterwards that includes Violet's ass for a glorious minute and a half, and while everyone's eyes are diverted to her latex-covered ass she squeezes a ketchup packet. No joke - she squeezes her hand, and a very thick viscous fluid much like ketchup oozes and drips out.

I like how every fight scene involved Violet calmly walking into the center of a bunch of armed men and then kicking all of their asses, posing at the end. This happens, what, six or seven times? I have to say, the scene where she makes the Chinese guys shoot themselves is pretty badass, but I do have serious problems with plot-based things before and after that segment (Vampirism comes up nowhere else but on that rooftop; degrees of vampirism do not come up anywhere; the Chinese guys on the rooftop are never explained; the base of operations for the hemophages is never explained, such as why it exists and why it hasn't been blown to smithereens yet; why didn't the kid get shot; why is the kid suicidal, and if he isn't suicidal he'd have to be a goddamned retard, which he proves wrong by acting and speaking intelligently). Let's also keep in mind that in just about every scene with guns in which Violet kills everybody, no matter the distance between Violet and her opponents, security never fires at her, instead insisting on charging right up to her face, gun likely on safety.

I could keep on going with other total stupidity, such as "Number of guns detected - many!" (Who the fuck would build that kind of sensor? "Durr, if someone comes in with two hundred fucking guns, clearly the main desk will see some humor in this situation!"), the nonsensical Christ/Nazi symbolism, the noseplugs, my God, the noseplugs, the villain turning around as though he was suddenly stricken with amnesia after seeing his entire bodyguard team be slaughtered by hemophages then choosing to explore a side room and conveniently finding some coffee, the demonstration by the villain that even though the hemophages can move fast enough to dodge point-blank bullets that he can pick up his gun and shoot three of them in the head before they move, Violet's admitting that she can't take on 300 soldiers and subsequent accomplishment of this very feat with uninhibited ease, the fucking gravity device on her belt, the nature and questionable intelligence of Garth, Violet's numerous ridiculously easy escapes, Violet knocking other hemophages out by pulling out their fucking hair, and Violet's sudden crippling depression over her condition.

There are plenty more that I'm not thinking of. There's just sooooo much wrong with that movie. So goddamned much.

I highly recommend you don't see it, or at least see it out of morbid curiosity.
Bring a notepad and see how many retarded things you can count. I bet you you won't be able to scribble fast enough.

I will say, though, that it deserves to be in a movie theater, even if it does belong at the bottom of the list of movie theater movies in terms of quality.

In the same way, my jealousy, pride, vanity, lust, greed, etc., all that good stuff, are considered shackles by Christianity?
I happen to side with Satanism on the issue of the Seven Deadly Sins - Christianity tells you to abandon your pride, isolate your own improvement by fighting envy, never reward yourself or improve your morale by banishing thoughts of gluttony, fighting the most natural instinct shared by all animals that is even necessary to maintain emotional balance and further the survival of the species by staving off lust, ignore the glorious potential of anger, forget your ambitions by refusing greed, and denying yourself some R&R by avoiding sloth - Christianity is effectively telling you that you are, in your present state, completely unacceptable. Look at you, you're a total wreck, and all because your loving God made you that way.
Satanism instead accepts you as you are, and even says that the Church is wrong in calling these things limitations. Consider what the world would be without these things - mindless, uniform, unthinking and unfeeling machines. Why did God make everyone so different if He wants them all to be the same? Consider also that if man were incapable of committing the Seven Deadly Sins, he'd never have any fun!
Christianity says, "look at you, you're dispicable. You're so full of yourself. So self-centered. You're constantly wanting congratulations on your accomplishments. You're always wanting more, more, more. And you want this without serious work, you lazy bum! You can't even look at a woman without thinking of her as a sex object. Pathetic. Absolutely pathetic."
Satanism, on the other hand, says, "hey whoah, here's something that sets you apart from the vast majority of Earth's lifeforms - pride! This advantage means that you maintain a high morale, and even have motivation to improve yourself and your condition. You have Anger, too!? Cool! That's very handy for getting out of dangerous situations, y'know, and coupled with pride, it gives you fervor to accomplish the impossible! Hey, no way, you say you have Envy? What that effectively does is create interaction between the accomplishments of your entire cities! Along with that nifty Greed you got there, that gives you the ability to rise above savagery, and give you constant motivation to increase the standard of living, including art, entertainment, and medicine! Well hey, it's great you have Sloth, too, because without it we'd work ourselve to death, huh? We wouldn't enjoy life without being able to indulge in the simple pleasures of a late afternoon nap. Wow, you're pretty frickin' cool. Humans are a pretty nifty species. Wait - Lust! You have Lust!? You mean... the continuation of your species... you find ultimately pleasurable?? Wicked awesome! Man, humans kick ass!"
I realize I may have something of a bias, but 99% of me wants to be a Satanist based on those two outlooks on the Seven Deadly Sins.
And look at some of your "Virtues:" humility, abstinence, chastity. That looks hella masochistic to me.
Ooh, but look at this... your Virtues are made to counter the Sins, eh?
"humility against pride, kindness against envy, abstinence against gluttony, chastity against lust, patience against anger, liberality against greed, and diligence against sloth"
Now... your doctrine is making a number of mistakes there. It equates "envy" with "malevolence," "lust" with "savagely raping everything that has at least one recognizable organic appendage," "anger" with "impatience/impulsiveness," "greed" with "conservatism," and "sloth" with "inconsistent work ethic," all of which give the Sins, which otherwise have advantages and disadvantages, a strictly negative connotation. My question is, what kind of a lying, sneaky bastard would trick people into considering the Sins something wholly undesirable by flagrantly butchering their definitions? (By the way, the Virtue "liberalism" is inconsistent with the Virtue "prudence.")

The natural desires that Christianity tries so much to suppress are not limitations - they're advantages. They open up a world of possibilities for humans, for fun and for improvement. It is because of the Sins that we have such a high standard of living. A species that cannot commit the Sins would be a savage band of monkeys.
"Ooh! I make fire! Now I can cook fish!" "What!? Where do you get off thinking you deserve the extra privelege of a cooked meal? Do you think you're more worthy than everyone else that you want a meal that won't give you salmonella? Oh, I bet you're so goddamned proud of yourself now that you made a shiny thing. Extinguish that thing at once, never build it again, and eat your shit raw like everyone else! Selfish asshole..."

Christianity wants me to drop the capacity to commit the Seven Deadly Sins. The one who gives this up is the quintessential fool.

#155997 16 2006-03-20T03:05:30Z Tsukatu
Quote: Twistkill, 2006-03-19T02:05:16Z
Why does the evolution theory say we evolved from monkeys? If we did, why do monkeys still exist today?
I don't feel this was addressed enough. I'm sure you well know now that humans didn't come from monkeys; I'm not talking about that.

Let's say that A evolved from B. The fact that A and B both exist today is not a valid argument against evolution. Evolution full well permits it.

In the world where only A existed, there was competition, as there always is among organisms, and the ones who had a mutation that made them closer to B were better able to compete, so they survived. (Keep in mind that the mutated version of the species survives only if it can copulate more than the original verson.) However, those B's only have that advantage in the particular environment in which the B-mutation was developed. From here, there are several answers to the question "why do A's still exist":
-A's are still able to survive and copulate. They may not be as good as B's, but they're still competent and can keep reproducing.
-A's may exist in other parts of the world in environments where the B-mutation never developed.
-A's may exist in other parts of the world in environments where the B-mutation was either not an advantage, or was even a disadvantage.
-The B-mutation may have forced the affected portion of the species to migrate, and create an environment composed of B's, leaving the A's in the original environment.

That's all off the top of my head.

Other funny non-arguments are things like "all mutations are disadvantageous" (which I hope is obviously untrue) and "mutations are caused only by destruction of portions of DNA" (also very untrue).

#156786 25 2006-03-22T22:45:57Z Tsukatu
I have a few things regarding sensation (vision, especially):

If we're going the species engineering approach and we're theoretically planning on creating this species (as opposed to wondering how a human could've evolved easier), I'd really appreciate a customizable lens for the eye that could be adjusted with a special tool made for the job. The lens could balance out an irregularly-shaped eye, eliminating the need for eyeglasses, contact lenses, and laser eye surgery. I guess there's a case against that in saying that glasses have a certain sophisticated look or something, but in this case we'd make one kind of lens (nice and flat) and treat glasses like a hat or something.

I also think that the light spectrum we see now limits our perception drastically. Other animals can see into infrared and ultraviolet spectra, so I don't see why we shouldn't be able to. Modifying the eyes themselves to this degree would be a little complicated, so I think the best solution would be to make another few pairs of eyes, either next to the eyes we already have (and we can do with reducing our eye size - they're much too big as it is; we'd have to flatten them up a bit to retain our current vision quality, but it's not like anyone but a surgeon is going to notice that the back of someone's eyes aren't as far back into their skull or anything) or on a different part of our face altogether (I prefer the former).
The case I can see against this would be that a person would be confused by this flood of new senses - to which I say, no, you would be confused at these new senses because you haven't grown up with them. How do you think we handle the five senses we do right now without flinching? (My Psych book actually makes a good argument for a sixth sense that has to do with your spatial orientation, as a combination of the cochlear fluid in your ears and information sent back by your limbs telling you where they are.)
I guess we'd also look kinda freaky having three eyes in each eye socket, but whatever (one for the visible light spectrum, one for ultraviolet and a bit beyond that, and another for infrared).
Keep in mind the benefits of having these extra eyes, though. Ultraviolet light has a much smaller wavelength than visible light, which means that fewer obstacles can get in the way. We'd be better able to see through substances considered impermeable by visible light. As for infrared, that's far more useful than UV light. We'd be able to see people through thin walls, tell how hot a pipe or bowl of soup is just by looking at it, etc. In terms of playing paintball in the woods, using infrared vision would be like using a wallhack.

An eye in the back of your head? I dunno, but we should consider it. How 'bout one on top? It might be making too many sensitive areas on the head, but then again, what kind of environment do we plan this new human to live in?

Either move the light receptors cells in the existing eye closer to the front of the eye, or give me a tapetum (the thing in the back of the eyes of some animals that bounces light back into the receptor cells, giving them a second chance to pick up the light (as it is, 90% of the visible light entering your eye is blocked or otherwise doesn't hit a receptor cell), also giving those animals a creepy glow when you shine a light at them in the dark (cat)). We'd still need a pupil and an iris to limit the amount of light allowed into our eyes, but we should be able to control that consciously.

The way we gauge distance of a sound is by seeing the difference in time that the sound reaches the ears. If it reaches your right ear before your left ear, you know the sound is coming from your left, and the time difference tells you how far away it is in that direction. This means, however, that we can't tell how far away a sound is that is anywhere on the plane running straight through our faces (in front, below, above, or behind our heads). To fix this, most people turn their heads. This might be a trivial point, as some people might not see turning the head as an inconvenience, but putting a muscle to control the position of the ear would spare you the trouble as well as allow you to more rapidly adjust your ear to find the distance of the sound.
That or put a third ear under the eye on the back of your head.

That's all I have time for right now, but I'm very interested in this subject. I'm going to go into Biomedical Engineering in college, which will be more artificial, granted, but considering I'm planning on building a human-like machine...
...more on that later. Maybe.

#7605 1 2006-03-24T05:30:38Z Tsukatu
This has probably come up here before, but I'm starting a new thread for two reasons:
- Any previous thread on the same subject is not in the first page of recent threads, so it's long dead by now.
- This thread has to do with something a little more specific - the existence of free will and simultaneous existence of am omnipotent being. That's quite different from the existence of free will (which I believe cannot be determined at the moment).

For those interested, this will also be posted on my religious discussion forum. I may bring up things people said on that forum.

A brief introduction:

All of reality is nothing more than one gigantic chemical reaction that follows the natural laws of the universe throughout its duration. Because any state of the universe can be predicted theoretically by observing the energy states, positions, etc., of the contents of the universe, this means that in order for there to be an unpredictable event (and therefore a non-binding event; an event that is not forced into happening because that is the outcome of the chemical reactions involved), then there must exist a random event (a random event is defined as one that is not predictable) to steer it off of that predictable course.

So, without further ado:

Free will is entirely contingent upon the existence of random events.

Now, either (A) random events exist, or (B) random events don't exist. (A) is a positive assertion, and (B) is the only other option available in a boolean phrase (true or false) such as this one, which means that (A) and (B) are all-inclusive; it's either (A) or (B). If it's not (A) then it has to be (B), and if it's not (B) then it has to be (A). (C ) is right out. (A) and (B) shall be the letters to be considered, and none else. They are the only two options because they are the only two existing options.

(A) The existence of random events means that there exist events which cannot be predicted. It follows, then, that if there exist events which cannot be predicted, then free will has a chance of existing.
However, (B) the non-existence of random events means that there is no such thing as an unpredictable event. This means that the universe follows along one, theoretically predictable path. This would mean, if you haven't guessed yet, that free will does not exist.

Taking an atheistic stance on this, it is up to you to look into the argument scientists are having over which is true, (A) or (B).

Taking a stance that believes in an omnipotent deity, on the other hand, eliminates one of (A) and (B) from consideration, as you will soon see.
An omnipotent deity is an omniscient deity. An omniscient deity knows everything. This means that the omnipotent deity knows the future! It knows everything that will happen to you and knows every decision and thought that you make. In other words, the omnipotent deity can predict all events (let that soak in for a little bit).
Hey, wait a second! If something can predict all events, then all events are predictable (because something can predict them), which debunks (A) the idea that random (unpredictable) events exist. (A) is debunked because (A) says unpredictable events exist, but we have (hopefully) seen that something (an omnipotent deity) can predict all events, meaning that those unpredictable events can't exist. Someone who believes (A) that unpredictable events exist cannot believe that an omnipotent deity exists, as that omnipotent deity would be able to predict those events.
That means that if you believe in an omnipotent being that you automatically side with (B). If you do not side with (B), then you are arguing against your god's omnipotence.
(B) states that random events don't exist, and therefore neither does free will (because all events are predictable - we've gone over this, remember?).
Quod erat demonstrandum, it is irrational for someone to believe in both an omnipotent being and free will.

EDIT: Christ, I've had to edit this thing six times because of those infernal emoticons.

#162733 57 2006-04-07T03:12:29Z Tsukatu
What helped me get it:
When you pick one of the three doors, you're giving yourself a 1 in 3 chance. That means that there's a 2 in 3 chance that what you're looking for is in the group of doors we can call "the rest of the doors." The host's opening one incorrect door for you doesn't improve your chances as much as it redefines the objective to be "pick a group of doors, and you win the prize if the group of doors you selected contained the prize," and dividing the three into two groups: (1) the door you initially picked and (2) the two others. We've already seen that (1) has a 1 in 3 success rate, and that (2) has a 2 in 3 success rate. It is most logical to switch over.

You can extend this example to 100 doors, with the host eliminating all but two doors, just as he did when you only had 3 doors in total. This means that there are two groups that you can choose from: the group that is 1% likely to include your door, or the group that is 99% likely to include your door.

If you don't get this group business, let's try common sense:
There are four hundred and eight billiondy doors in front of you. One contains a piece of candy, and all of the others contain agonizing death. You pick one at random, since that's the best you can do. The host removes all of the choices except for two: going down the line of doors, he skips over the door you chose and one other particular door. You know that the candy is behind either the door you chose or the door remaining, and he only left your door closed because it's the one you picked. I should hope that you choose to switch.

If you still don't get it and insist on seeing every possible outcome (had to resort to this for one of my friends):
Attachment (lost): post-29-1144379549.jpg

#163807 23 2006-04-11T05:27:59Z Tsukatu
Trogdor007,

But isn't distance proven through depth, shown by the 3rd Dimension?

You technically only need the first dimension to have distance. That's why I said that motion requires the fourth dimension and at least one of the first three.

You can have distance across a single line (e.g. the distance between point A and point B is 5 meters, and a zero-dimensional point travels from point A to point B in 5 seconds, meaning that the motion can be quantified as moving at 5 m/s).

You can have distance across two dimensions, too. Mario makes a running jump, moving from (0,0) to (3,4) (measured in meters), which means he moved a total of 5 meters. Let's say it takes him a second to get from (0,0) to (3,4). This means his motion can be quantified as 5 m/s.

You can also have distance in three dimensions. A baseball player hits a ball into left field. The ball soars up and out, and a wind comes in from the side, accelerating the ball toward center field in its flight. This one's a heck of a lot more complicated to figure out, but you can find the arc length of the ball's path (using some nifty calculus... integral(sqrt((dx/dt)****+(dy/dt)****+(dz/dt)****)dt) anyone? (this assumes we have 3D parametric coordinates for the path of the ball)) and divide that by the amount of time it took to get there, and you have a nice average velocity that you can use to describe motion.

(There are a few other ways of describing motion, but I really don't feel like naming them all.)

#165944 76 2006-04-18T00:39:43Z Tsukatu
Quote: sweep, April 17, 2006 07:58 am
What I don't understand is how the one with the least votes is don't know.

I'm sorry, but it's the only logical option. I can understand votes of yes, some people have a faith, and this a faith they stick by and truly believe in. But otherwise, who are you to say there is or isn't a God? What evidence do you have to prove it either way? Seriously. There is none. Because you can't know what a God would be like, or exactly what degree of control a God would constantly be able to maintain, it's all beyond comprehension, and therefore if you did not vote agnostic then I have to view you as incredibly illogical.

Apart from those with a real faith that there is a God. That is different if, because it's part of a belief that their religion is the correct religion.
Incorrect you are, my good sweep.

First off, agnosticism is not an alternative choice to the question of theism vs atheism. Theism and atheism label your belief, whereas agnosticism professes ignorance of the subject, which has to do with knowledge. Belief and knowledge are distinct. For this reason, agnosticism and theism are two different properties, completely independent of each other. Instead, you can describe yourself one of the following ways:
Theist: you believe X
Atheist: you don't believe X (which is quite different from "you believe that not X"; atheism is negative in its nature; it is denial, NOT assertion to the opposite of theism)
Slap on the term "agnostic" before one of the above two: whatever your theist/atheist leaning, you believe that at least some portion of the question of X is closed to human knowledge.
So you can be one of the following four:
Theist
Atheist
Agnostic Theist
Agnostic Atheist
Saying that you're agnostic is not enough information. It tells what you know, which does now answer the question of what you believe. Theism and Atheism are all-inclusive descriptors. You cannot be neither theist nor atheist. If you are "on the dividing line," it comes down to practice. Do you pray to, worship, or otherwise acknowledge a deity? If so, you are an agnostic theist. If you do no such thing (inaction), then you are an agnostic atheist.

On a scale based entirely on my own opinion, sanity increases moving to the right:
Theism -> Agnostic Theism -> Agnostic Atheism -> Atheism
(additionally, there are generally two kinds of atheist - the "implicit" atheist refuses to believe that X exists; the "explicit" atheist argues vehemently that X cannot exist; I am an explicit atheist)

I'll take the time now to define terms that I will use in the rest of this rant. When I say "god", I mean any being that is at least partially super-natural or transcending of the natural universe. A being that is within the natural universe is not worthy of worship, for obvious reasons that I will get into if you're too tired to think about it, and maybe, like, give me a brownie or something. The agnostic says that this being, because it is supernatural, is inherently unknowable.
From here, we can either (a) attack the idea of a supernatural being, or (b) attack the idea of an unknowable being. Let's start with (a).

(a) Saying that a god is "supernatural" doesn't give us any positive assertions about a god. It tells us what a god isn't - it's not natural. The question remains: what positive characteristics can we ascribe to a god?
On a slight tangent: the notion of a supernatural being is incomprehensible. We're supposed to conceive of a being exempt from natural law - a being that does not fall within the domain of scientific explanation - but no one can explain how we can conceive of existence other than "natural" existence. "Natural existence" is a redundancy; we have no familiarity with "unnatural" existence, or even a vague notion of what such existence would be like. We cannot even begin to claim that we think that there exists a supernatural being - it is completely irrational to do so, as such a claim has no foundation, and therefore no validity.
Natural law is based upon the limited nature of existence. It pertains to the presence of regularity in the universe, and for this reason is referred to as the "uniformity of nature." Entities behave according to specific causal conditions, and we know that an object will act according to a set series of laws; an acorn, given the right conditions, will grow into a tree; it will not grow into an elephant; a dog will not sprout wings and breathe fire; a colony of ants will not burst into a chorus of the National Anthem.
This next sentence is crucial: Every entity has a specific nature, specific characteristics, that determine the capacity of that entity. For example, a plant has a specific nature and specific characteristics that place the capacity for thought out of possibility. Basically, the characteristics of an entity determine what an entity can and cannot do; limitations are an integral part of the natural universe, and they constitute the foundation of natural law. Regularity in nature is the consequence of limitations. No existing thing can randomly do anything at any time under any conditions. This uniformity in nature permits the systematic study of reality (science) and the formulation of general principles of nature ("laws") which are used in predicting future states. While the particular scientific laws will change as man's knowledge increases, the principle of natural law itself is a constant; it persists as a corollary of existence.
That last paragraph is vital to the understanding of the next series of arguments. Please make sure you didn't just skim that last paragraph, and that you actually understand it.
A god, as we have seen, cannot exist within this framework, but theists say it exists nonetheless. This brings up the considerable problem of how anything can exist as a supernatural being. If a supernatural being is exempt from natural law, it does not possess specific, determinate characteristics. These attributes would impose limits, and these limits would restrict the capacities of this supernatural being. Essentially, assigning any characteristics whatsoever to this supernatural being would chain it permanently and completely into the natural universe, and this would disqualify the being as a god. For this reason, a god must be a being that is without a specific nature, a being that is indeterminate - a being, in other words, that is nothing in particular. But these characteristics (or, more precisely, lack of characteristics) are incompatible with the notion of existence itself.
To be is to be something as opposed to nothing, and to be something is to be something specific. A supernatural being, if it is to differ in kind from natural existence, must exist without a limited nature - which amounts to existing without any nature at all.

So far, as an agnostic, you should be nodding your head and saying, "I told you so. I said God is unknowable, didn't I?" Because both a theist and an atheist can agree with the unknowability of a god, but an atheist uses it to reject the idea of a god whereas a theist uses it as evidence that a god falls beyond the scope of human understanding, we need to move on to another argument, one that argues not with metaphysics, but with epistemology. Coincidentally, wasn't that our (b), attacking the idea of an unknowable being?

(b) The belief that god is basically unknowable is the most important element of theistic belief. It is shared by all theists. Their only argument is with regard to what degree god's nature can be known. Remember that theists don't just believe that the nature of a god is unknowable now, but that it is unknowable in principle; Man will never understand a god.
Here's the kicker: if one believes that a god is inexpressible, then one quite literally has nothing to say and should therefore retreat into silence. Talking about it will only lead to all kinds of absurd paradoxes.
If consistently adhered to, an agnostic theist will have the following discussion with an atheist...
Theist: "I believe in the existence of a god."
Atheist: "What is 'god'?"
Theist: "I don't know."
Atheist: "But what is it you believe in?"
Theist: "I don't know that either."
How is the agnostic theist's claim to the existence of a god significant in any respect? How does his "belief" differ from no belief whatsoever?
So here it is: The flaw with agnostic theism (I'll talk about agnostic atheism in a little bit) is that it is not possible to think something exists without some knowledge of what it is that is alleged to exist. In the words of Ludwig Feuerbach (I love this guy): "To deny all the qualities of a being is equivalent to denying the being itself. A being without qualities is one which cannot become an object to the mind, and such a being is non-existent." If a god is unknowable, then the concept of "god" is totally devoid of content, and the word "god" becomes a meaningless sound. To state that "god exists", where "god" represents absolutely nothing, is to say nothing at all. It's the same as saying, "a blark exists." The agnostic, any agnostic, by refusing to state the content of the word "god", exempts himself from reason and serious consideration.
Back to agnostic theism, to posit the existence of something which, by its nature, cannot be known to man is to submerge oneself in hopeless contradictions. In particular, to claim that a thing is unknowable, one must first know that it exists - but then one already has knowledge of it, to that extent; to assert the existence of the unknowable is to claim knowledge of the unknowable, which is a contradiction, as it no longer becomes unknowable.
If you feel like bending your mind into a pretzel, consider the overkill argument that the claim that a being is incomprehensible is itself demonstrative of knowledge of that unknowable thing. To state that a being is incomprehensible is to pronounce knowlege of its nature, in which case we are again involved in a contradiction.
It devolves into two possible situations. You can claim something is unknowable, but be unable to attest to any qualities of this unknowable thing, which equates to saying nothing in the first place, or you can produce knowledge in support of your claim, which results in several contradictions right off the bat that cannot be avoided simply because of the nature of your original asserion.
(On another minor point, again overkill, consider that accurately labeling a thing "unknowable" requires omniscience.)
To claim that god is unintelligible is to confess that one does not know what one is talking about. It is equivalent to saying: "I will explain the concept of a god by pointing out that it cannot be explained."
Atheists like myself contend that the concept of a god is unintelligible, this being a major reason why it cannot be accepted by any rational man. The theist who openly admits this should definitely not expect to be taken seriously. The idea of the unknowable has been reduced to an insult to the intellect, and it renders theism wholly implausible.

By trashing the notion of (b) an unknowable being, we have indirectly destroyed the concept of (a) a supernatural being. If it is irrational to assert the existence of an unknowable being (I should hope that after reading all of that that you understand that it is, in fact, irrational to assert this), it is equally irrational to assert the existence of its metaphysical corollary: the supernatural being. If knowledge of the unknowable is a contradiction (duh), knowledge of the supernatural is a contradiction as well. This has the effect of excluding agnosticism from the sphere of rational consideration, in which case atheism wins by default as the Burden of Proof idea decrees.

From here, a person who still claims to believe can go two ways. He can abandon his defense of a supernatural being altogether, which is a simple surrender to atheism, or he can continue to proclaim the existence of a supernatural being that is knowable to humans.
The second path is usually adopted by the theists (especially Christians, not surprisingly) that like to think they know what they're talking about.
However, as you claim to be an "agnostic," I think my arguments against that position would be in vain, as you have already rejected them. Even if you for some reason don't reject them (the ones that begin defining god, which you can see above doesn't make sense), you should still be well aware that once a being can be described by any characteristic that makes sense in the natural universe, it is irrevocably, permanently, and completely chained within the natural universe. Any description gives it limitations, and any limitations removes any and all possibility that the being exists outside of the natural universe.

If you understand the above argument (the whole thing), you can see that on my sanity chart...
Theism -> Agnostic Theism -> Agnostic Atheism -> Atheism
...the agnostic atheists are no different from the atheists, so they might as well call themselves as such, and the agnostic theists split up into two groups, one that joins the atheists, and the others that retreat to theism. This happens because agnosticism no longer becomes a rational position to take, and it is devoured entirely by atheism.

Congratulations, sweep, you've forced me to put into words that which accounts for 5% of my disbelief in a god.

#167656 4 2006-04-22T03:06:14Z Tsukatu
Get Process Explorer. This nifty little widget will let you take a closer look at processes. Thing is, it might be a specific thread within the process that's causing trouble (as is not uncommon for me if I leave Azureus on overnight).

For example, when my explorer.exe starts going ballistic and eating all of my CPU and memory, it's not the fault of explorer.exe, but rather the thread ntdll.dll!RtAllocateHeap that is within explorer.exe.

So yeah, get Process Explorer and have it boot on startup, and then right-click on the problem process, go Properties -> Threads, and kill the specific thread that is causing the problems.

#168037 37 2006-04-23T06:05:18Z Tsukatu
Bob is a carnival, watching a show. In the third act, a man lifts an elephant with his mind. Bob, upon seeing this, is surprised, for he remembers seeing that same man lift that same elephant earlier in the first act. Bob has experienced deja vu.

Let's make it a given that the man lifts the elephant only in the third act, and that no such feat was performed in the first act.

When Bob asks those around him whether they have already seen this, they tell him no, the man has only lifted the elephant in the third act.

Here is a log, from an objective viewpoint, of what Bob sees:
In the first act, a man juggles a variety of different objects.
The second act is "the Aristocrats" act.
In the third act, the man lifts the elephant.

Here is a log of what Bob has in his memory per act; new events are in bold:
First act: "I am at a show in a carnival."
Second act: "I am at a show in a carnival. In the first act, a man juggled things."
Third act: "I am at a show in a carnival. In the first act, a man juggled things. In the second act, there was a family who came on stage [...] and while they were still soaked with it and naked, they yelled, 'the Aristocrats!'"
End of third act: "I am at a show in a carnival. In the first act, a man juggled things, and then another man came on and lifted an elephant. In the second act, there was a family who came on stage [...] and while they were still soaked with it and naked, they yelled, 'the Aristocrats!' In the third act, that same man lifted that same elephant again.."

If Bob had left sometime before the third act, he never would have had deja vu, and he would not be able to describe the person or the elephant, and he could not say that there was an act involving a man lifting an elephant. However, because he leaves after the third act, he can remember the man lifting the elephant in the first act.

What happened?
Human memory is extremely malleable, and because of this is very unreliable. Every time you remember a memory, you remember it differently (whether the changes are slight or extreme does not matter; keep in mind that future changes can correct past changes). Bob's mind, upon seeing the man lift the elephant, for whatever reason associated it with the first act, and so, looking for a place to put the memory of the elephant, it copies it both into the third act and the first act.

Looking at it as sequential processing (which isn't entirely correct, as the brain uses parallel processing):
:first act viewed
:looking for place to put first act events
:place found for first act events - 7:00 pm
:second act viewed
:looking for place to put second act events
:place found for second act events - 7:30 pm
:woman left of me is asking me what happened in the first act while she was away
:woman was away at 7:10 pm
:memory retrieved from 7:10 pm - man juggled things
:concept sent to Wernicke's area for translation into speech, relayed to motor cortex to relay message to woman
:woman shows recognition, situation has been resolved; returning to task of lower importance - watching show
:third act viewed
:looking for place to put third act events
:place found for third act events - 8:00 pm
:place found for third act events - 7:20 pm
:duplicate memory detected - 7:20 pm and 8:00 pm; bringing this to the attention of prefrontal cortex

...

:wife is asking what happened in first act
:first act determined to be the period between 7:00 pm and 7:30 pm
:events stored in time range 7:00 pm and 7:30 pm are - man juggling; man lifting elephant
:wife is asking what happened in third act
:first act determined to be the period between 8:00 pm and 8:30 pm
:events stored in time range 8:00 pm and 8:30 pm are - man lifting elephant

...and so on.

Since science is dedicated to understanding reality, it rests on the premise that reality can be understood. Theology, on the other hand, is dedicated to the proposition that an important segment of reality (in fact, its ultimate form) is forever unknowable.. There are cross-purposes at work here. Science seeks to make reality coherent; theology seeks to convince us that some aspects of reality are incoherent. To the extent that science succeeds, theology dies of strangulation. (This same principle applies, in a wider sense, between philosophy and theology.)
"The conflicts between science and theology, or between philosophy and theology, are offshots of a more basic conflict, that between reason and theology. Anyone who advocates theism - the belief in the supernatural - simultaneously advocates [religious] irrationalism - the belief in the unknowable. This explains why the issue of god is much more crucial than, for example, the issue of flying saucers. While the existence of flying saucers is of immense scientific importance, this controversy has no particular ramifications for epistemology and the efficacy of man's reason. But the same is not true of theism. The existence of a supernatural realm would have profound implications for human reason, and anyone who believes in a supernatural being must also assume certain beliefs concerning the scope and validity of man's knowledge (whether he is aware of these beliefs or not).
"If we make a new discovery in the field of science, this simply provides us with one more piece of knowledge. If we were to somehow discover the existence of a god, however, this is a discovery for which we would pay a termeendous price. Theism offers us a bit of 'knowledge' which, if true, would destroy the foundation of all present knowlege by obliterating the naturalist context within which we comprehend reality. Theism represents an attack on man's ability to understand the universe - and the advocacy of theism, theology, attempts to reduce man to a state of perpetual ignorance. The concept of god, as Spinoza put it, is an asylum of ignorance."
-Atheism: The Case Against God, by George H. Smith

That bolded statement pretty much says it, actually. (I added the bold; the text was not bold in the original.)

The key idea to keep in mind is that things have a certain working order, and throwing God into the mix, a being that can distort the rigid laws of the universe to his whim, effectively throws a wrench into that monkey. Or whatever. If God ignored the natural laws of the universe when he made Earth, us, etc., we would not be able to study these natural laws because they would not be following anything other than God's whim.
Science does not study God's whim; science studies the natural laws that are applicable within the entirety of our solar system, galaxy, and from what we know of it as of yet, the rest of the universe as well.
In a way, the fact that we can even study science serves to prove that the idea of the Christian God is insanity and ignorance at its finest.
But anyway, that's when we get back to that bolded statement, above.

I don't really know why I posted that, actually. I have next to no faith in your ability to understand it, McP3000.
Oh, well. I hope it offers some intriguing dinner conversations for the rest of you.

What your faith proposes is either a terrifically bad idea or is inherently illogical when investigated thoroughly.

The fact that the physical events in the Bible took place at some point (the Mediterranean Sea flooded) has little to do with it. You believe that the Sea flooded (Noah's Ark); if science supports it, so do I. The difference between yu and me in this instance is that you also for some reason accept a theory created by a bunch of ignorant tribesmen.

You realize the people who made these kinds of justifications for these historic events ("God caused the flood," "God knocked down the walls in the battle of Jericho," "God destroyed Sodom and Gomorrah") have been arbitrarily assigning causes to these events because they were entirely ignorant of what we have discovered over millennia of scientific investigation.

When some shepherd comes out of his cave and sees that it's raining, he has no idea what the hell is going on. Is the sky falling? Did the shepherd do something wrong? He decides to credit this rain to someone who knows better, whether this someone is entirely imaginary or not.
Do you realize that the collective intelligence of most of the contributors to the Bible are well below the intelligence of an average New York City bum? That is seriously an honest, accurate comparison of their powers of reasoning and their knowledge of science.
Given that a bum is smarter than the guy who figured the reason for the Great Flood was God, would you believe a bum if he said on the street, "it's raining because God screwed up and is killing all of his evil creations?" Then why in the nine hells would you believe ignorant shepherd man?

I just don't fucking get it.

Do you realize just how easy it is, in that time period, to make a religion?
For example:
Bob walks out and sees that it's raining. He doesn't know where it came from. To ease his uncertainty and his confusion, he attributes it to dancing purple unicorns. He gets married. His wife doesn't know what the rain is. Bob explains that it's the doing of dancing purple unicorns, and that she shouldn't be worried. He sounds like he knows what he's talking about, and she has no reason not to believe him, so his wife believes it. They then have a kid, and when the kid asks about the rain, his parents tell him that it's dancing purple unicorns. The kid believes his parents, because they're his parents. He goes on to have a wife and kids, and they join with another growing family, explaining to that family that dancing purple unicorns create the rain, and before you know it you have a village. In the village, because everyone believes dancing purple unicorns cause the rain because they don't have any other ideas and the guy who told them seemed to know what he was talking about, every kid believes that dancing purple unicorns cause the rain.
This is pretty much exactly how many of the rationalizations in the Bible came along. Sure, things like the Great Flood could've happened, but you're believing that dancing purple unicorns caused it? Just because on idiot decided that it sounded okay to him?

Anyway, from these roots, your faith became more thoroughly developed by theologians like that asshole Aquinas. See, they had that same irrational mentality that you showed earlier ("I won't change my mind; I'm not that weak willed") and they started making up ways that God actually could exist, despite the skeptics' reasoning.
What people like Aquinas did was essentially the following:
Skeptic: Whoah, what's this stuff?
Aquinas: Falling water.
Skeptic: Where does it come from?
Aquinas: God makes it come.
Skeptic: How does he make it fall?
Aquinas: Uhhh... cuz he can... *thinks a bit* ... control water.
Skeptic: How does he do that?
Aquinas: Er... well, he just... thinks about it. Yeah, there ya go. He thinks about it.
Skeptic: Wow. I don't know anybody who can do that. Can I do that?
Aquinas: Umm... *looks long and hard at Skeptic*... No.
Skeptic: Why not? Can I learn how to?
Aquinas: No, cuz... uhhhh... God can do everything, and he's better than you.
Skeptic: Oh. Can he teach me?
Aquinas is really starting to sweat nervously, because he is forced to make up these answers so rapidly
Aquinas: Uhhhhh... umm... no, cuz... uhhh... he... is very busy.
Skeptic: Oh. Well where does he live? I'll go find him myself.
Aquinas realizes that his shit may very well be ruined.
Aquinas: Ummm... you can't find him.
Skeptic: Why not? How far away does he live?
Aquinas: Cuz uh... he lives very, very far away. Wait, no! He lives up really high. Like, in the air.
Skeptic: How does he live in the air? I keep falling down every time I try to go up in the air.
Aquinas: Yeah, he uh... he lives on those white things? See those white things? Yeah, God's up there.
Skeptic: And what, he throws water down?
Aquinas: I guess. Look, I gotta go... uhm... shave my cat. Nice talkingwithyoukthanksbye!!
Skeptic: Wait! I want to know more about God!

Being a Christian basically involves believing that exchange. I'm quite serious.

#230847 15 2006-09-19T21:42:22Z Tsukatu
Boom!, as a Linux user, I still despise Macs.

Mac OS X uses a UNIX framework, right? So does Linux. That makes the framework identical. The only difference then is between what Macs offer vs what Linux offers, and at what price and convenience.
And that's where it turns into an argument for GPL/OSS software, and that's where the basis of my hatred of Macs lies.

In fact, have a look at an earlier post of mine:
Quote: Tsukatu, 2005-12-30T23:26:59Z
We can look at different operating systems as cars.
A Windows car is a pile of many, many pieces that all build and work off of each other. The result is very shaky, but it somehow manages to work. However, when there is a problem, it's very easy to locate the one problem part and replace it with a very small (if non-existent) fee.
A Mac car is a hermitically-sealed bubble. It's difficult to go on more "freestyle" roads with it, because it was built for efficient work. If something does go wrong with the car, because it's one big piece, the whole sonofabitch has to be replaced.
A Linux car is a tank. I don't mean one of those crappy soviet tanks, I mean something along the lines of a perfectly built (Swiss or German?) hovertank. It's extremely difficult to get it to break down. But what happens when it does break down? Eat three more metaphors:
Getting help with Windows isn't usually that big of a problem. The official Microsoft auto parts dealer is very nice about providing any replacement parts you need, usually at no charge. Sometimes you need to talk to a specialist, who are usually well-trained.
Getting help with a Mac isn't really getting help fixing as much as it is buying a new one.
Now, imagine a world where everybody loves tanks. The guy who invented a tank shared his design openly with the world, and since then an enormous community of tank-lovers and experts emerged, many of them even building their own tanks by fundamentally changing the design of the tank. There are millions of people in the world who know pretty much everything there is to know about a tank. Getting help with Linux is simply going online and finding one of the countless tech help forums that have a "Linux" subforum and asking. Usually anyone there will be able to tell you how to fix it and how to avoid having it happen again, and it's absolutely no cost to you!
We've compared design and repair. Now we'll cover economics.
100 people walk into a massive lot that contains Windows, Mac, and Linux vehicles. 90 of these people are attracted to the shininess and sleek facade of Windows, so they immediately get the impression that Windows is the best designed system. They pay the hefty price of a Windows vehicle, and buy many more Windows applications. 5 of these people are more attracted to Macs, for whatever retarded reason, and they decide to buy a Mac. But only 5 of the initial 100 people decide to walk over to the lot with the massive sign that says "FREE TANKS! GET YOUR TANK HERE! ANY DESIGN YOU WANT, WITH 100% CUSTOMIZABILITY! FREE TECH SUPPORT UNTIL THE END OF TIME! EFFECTIVELY AN UNLIMITED TIME WARRANTY!"

Fuck Macs.
Go Linux.

Mac OS X is an entirely proprietary operating system that is extremely prone to such nastiness as vendor lock-in, which made Microsoft as hated as it is today. You have to pay hundreds of dollars for the Mac, pay hundreds more for the proprietary programs you use, and pay hundreds more for technical support and service.
Linux is completely free, and these days many distributions (such as the legendary Dapper Drake version of Ubuntu) are more straightforward and powerful than Macs. So you're basically getting slightly increased performance out of the machine for free. The most popular graphic design programs, 3D modeling programs, office suite programs, all that useful but expensive stuff, have Open-Source alternatives that are typically just as good or better than the programs you have to pay money for. In addition, those programs are being constantly developed by many more people than Apple can devote to the task. There are greater numbers of more motivated and more skilled programmers working on some obscure Python library than Apple can place on its newest and hottest piece of software or OS X version. And to top it off, help with using Open Source software is seventy fold more accessible, and free as well. Beyond that, if you know what you're doing, you can even customize Open Source programs to your liking and recompile them - I'd love to see a proprietary piece of software try to accomodate that same freedom.
And don't go with that old "but the software on the Mac will be faster" nonsense. They're both built on UNIX, aye? They'll run the same, if not faster on a Linux box.
Mac and Linux also have that "viruses aren't applicable to me" hotness. The issues of concern with Macs and Linux machines are purely security-related, and even then they both do that leagues better than Windows.

What we're reduced to is this: you're given a choice of a sturdy Volvo that you will end up spending several hundred dollars per year on, or you can get a hovertank for free with a comprehensive lifetime warranty and shockingly easy customizability.
Why would any sane person go for the Volvo?

And hey, guess what!? You can do Windows shit on a Linux box as well! See, there's this wonderful pair of programs called WINE and Cedega. They can emulate most Windows applications and games without a hitch, and at no speed decrease. Many Linux gamers (such a thing exists - I'd love to see a solid Mac gamer) even say that playing games like Doom 3 and Halo with Cedega is just like running it natively in Windows.

In terms of my advocacy of operating systems, I'd recommend a Linux machine first because you'd be able to do most everything a person would expect a computer to do for free, then Windows for the serious gamers that play games that Cedega is still working to translate properly. I would never recommend a Mac. They are shitty versions of Linux that are more costly. I don't know why someone would get a Mac. It's beyond me.

Quote: elaxion, September 21, 2006 05:54 pm
For usability reasons, isn't linux difficult? Like running different programs and the like.

Unless you're a very special case, it's just as easy as running a native Windows app in Windows. To run OpenOffice Writer (like Microsoft Word, but free) you go to Start -> OpenOffice -> OpenOffice Writer. To run OpenOffice Writer in Linux, you'd go to Applications (equivalent of Start bar and just as accessible) -> OpenOffice -> OpenOffice Writer.
Even using WINE to run a native Windows application in Linux is very straight-forward and simple. Sometimes there are kinks, but those are usually well explained at winehq.com.

And hey, if you're uneasy about trying Linux, you don't even have to install it to try it out. Linux is the only operating system that offers a LiveCD. You simply boot from the LiveCD instead of booting from your hard drive, and you're running Linux without touching your hard drive at all.
If you're interested in trying it out, go to http://www.ubuntu.com and either download and burn an .iso, or ask them the mail you some CD's (they pay all costs, including shipping).

I know what the first part is... but the rest is beyond me.
It's an animated compilation of cross-sections obtained through an MRI scan. The man is actually a frozen convict (a cadaver), and he is not being cut up in any way. He's lying face down (so his face would be looking toward the bottom of your screen with the top of his head sticking out of the monitor at you) and the scan progresses from his head to his feet.
So the first thing you see is the top of his head, his brain, and then his neck and throat, and then it moves on down to his upper thorax, where you can see the collar bones and his chest (remember that he's facing down), and those two things on the left and right are his arms. When the muscle retracts away from the center, we're viewing his abdomen, and then the scan progresses down through his pelvis, his legs, and eventually down past his feet.

It's science!

#236096 226 2006-10-01T21:03:37Z Tsukatu
Jormungand,

Let me say first of all that I am a staunch supporter of gay rights and gay marriage.

But I do think that people who campaign for gay rights with the platform that gays are normal are delusional.

When I think of "normal" with regards to an object, like a ball, I think of something that closely resembles the object in its intended form, and that closely resembles the quintessential ball. If we include an ellipsoid in the category "ball," it wouldn't be a normal ball. It performs quite differently from a spherical ball, and so it can't be called a good representation of a ball.

When I think of "normal" with regards to organisms, I think of an organism that is able to survive and advance its species. A wolf that is grey, has four legs, claws, teeth, etc., and no diseases or mutations that prevent it from hunting, eating, finding a mate, and reproducing, is normal. A wolf that is born with five legs is not normal. A wolf that is born without a mouth is not normal. A wolf that is born with an inability to produce gametes is not normal. A wolf that thinks it's a walrus is not normal. A wolf that prefers to hunt other wolves and mate with porcupines is not normal.

Homosexuals don't have any obvious physical or mental impairments - they just like their own gender. But because this is contrary to the idea behind any existing lifeform - furthering its own species - homosexuals are not "normal."
Now, keep in mind that this doesn't mean that they're not human. It just means they're an oddity. A bunny rabbit with three ears is still a bunny rabbit. Likewise, a homosexual shouldn't be treated any differently than someone we see born with six fingers, or born with obsessive compulsive disorder. Their deviance from the quintessential human (hard to define, but you'd be a fool to argue that it isn't heterosexual) is not meaningful enough to warrant any persecution or different treatment.

Now, I'm a supporter of aborting children born with seriously debilitating diseases or mutations that would essentially make them a waste of resources to let live, where "resources" includes money, effort, and emotion. For example, I don't think that we should let a child with FAS live. It should be intentionally miscarried or aborted, pretty much to everyone's benefit. However, I'm also very, very conservative when it comes to telling which diseases or mutations deserve death. I would vociferously fight for the right to life of a paralyzed child, a child with AIDS, or an autistic child. They can still contribute something, and they aren't a mockery of a human being.
Similarly, there is absolutely no point in restricting the priveleges we give to a homosexual. They're human, they can think, and can probably even offer us more perspective on critical decisions. Some of the greatest minds in the history of mankind have been gay.

I support gay rights for the very same reason I support the rights of a 12-fingered man. Even though both are obviously not normal, this does not mean that they are "worse" or less capable than a normal human. Their abnormality cannot be called "bad." It certainly isn't normal, but it doesn't disadvantage them. They are just as valuable as a normal human.

But saying that they are normal takes delusion.

Side note I decided to ramble on about for a reason I've forgotten:
I don't believe that the Special Olympics are a good idea. I don't believe we should parade genetic accidents around like a freakshow. I react to it in the same way that I would react to a Silent Hill-esque dementation of a human. An even better comparison would actually be from the movie Resident Evil 2, where a guy's sister is bitten by a zombie and turns into one and is tied to a chair by her brother. She's clearly a zombie and tries to eat him every time he comes near, but he still calls her his sister. He even feeds her human body parts. When a STARS agent comes along, he argues furiously that she's normal and that she has a right to life. When I see a supporter of the Special Olympics, I see that guy.

It's just delusion.
