A-fuckin'-men.
Same shit happened to me, same age. I'm really not trying to trivialize or generalize what you're going through, because I've never felt that anyone else would reach that same level of awareness to feel what I felt, either.

Anyway.
My brother kicks ass at the technical stuff - math, natural sciences, computer science - and to some extent the social stuff. He's only two years older than me, and because I'm smart, too, we were very close for most of our lives. And because we thought similarly and because he was older, I saw him as the future me. I suppose it felt like he was a steady glimpse at myself two years in the future.
And I've done what he's done. Rather, I have an affinity for the same fields. He's better at the technical stuff than I am (he ended up in MIT), but I compensate for that by being more athletic (which bugs him to all hell, but that's a different story entirely).
My brother was also very social. He had his first girlfriend and first kiss in fifth grade. This prompted me to shoot for the same when I was in fifth grade, to no avail. He had a series of girlfriend in middle school, as well, and then continued to have meaningful relationships with girls in high school. And he told me all about them, and I developed a deep passion for being in love. I wanted to know quite badly what that felt like.
I didn't get my first girlfriend until the summer between sophomore and junior year and high school. That didn't make a whole lot of sense to me, because I'm (foregoing the arrogant modesty, as you did) more attractive and personable than my brother. I'm much more of a social butterfly, where my brother is simply more domineering. Where he demands attention, I earn it, and it's generally pretty easy for me. It comes naturally.

When I first saw how my life was differing from my brother's, I began to develop a serious, though amusing in retrospect, identity issue. I didn't understand why I wasn't falling in love as he was. There were some girls in my class that would have complemented my personality very well, and they certainly had their middle-school crushes on me (a series of stories brutally summarized into a self-indulgent but nevertheless accurate statement - 90% of the girls in any academic class I've been in since 3rd grade have been head-over-heels for me at some point in time; this is backed up by countless testimonials, mostly in yearbooks), and I always felt really guilty that I didn't feel anything for them.
So I started trying to.
Those days were some of the most awkward of my life.
I started forcing myself to like these girls because I felt I needed to like someone. It felt very out of place that I was not in love. I did wierd things. Stupid things. I was certainly socially awkward and became distant with a lot of people who were or could have been great friends.

You'd think I'd learn.
Nope. Same shit happened in high school, but worse. It was severely distressing to me that I was unable to fall in love. I blamed everything under the sun, from my natural insensitivity to coincidence, but that didn't stop me from trying to battle my circumstances.
A lot more stupid shit happened, and I started doing irrational things like you've described. I spent hours walking in my backyard in my boxers in the middle of a freezing winter night, I pondered my identity over some lukewarm tea out on a balcony in the rain, and contemplated the nature of love in the fetal position in the back of my closet. I did all sorts of wierd shit like that. My mind was mostly on why I wasn't feeling anything for people, whether I should, who felt what for me... most of it ended up being meaningless.
And, again, I felt that the average Joe would never reach the same level of awareness that I had. I didn't think any normal person would lay in their driveway with some hot cocoa at 3 in the morning and consider whether the small crushes he actually did have for some people was, unbenownst to him, the full extent of romantic love.

So now is the part where I caution you.
I'd been confused about my emotions and I'd been dealing with some truly bizarre identity issues (the full extent of which are irrelevant to this matter), and I got impatient and tried to fix things.
Where did I end up?
Dating a Mormon.
Me.
With a Mormon.
You better believe that's fucked up. It was a sign hitting me in the face that I was doing something against my character, but at least I was doing what I should be doing, if not with the right person. I had already been developing some peculiar identity-fragmenting business (which actually blossomed just before I joined these forums - you may notice that the earliest Tsukatu, which I have inexplicably decided to uphold, was my malice and my arrogance - just a piece of my personality), so I was more or less apathetic.
I thought about it a whole lot by myself, but never got past "what I'm doing is not right, but neither is what would be happening if I didn't do this."

Then again, I'm still not sure what the fuck is wrong with me. I continue to astound my old high school friends with the fact that, as charming and attractive as I am, I have virtually no close friends locally, and I haven't gotten laid. I guarantee you that I have a whole slew of girls interested in me, and I bet you I could point out at least half a dozen with astonishing accuracy, but I have no feelings for them. I'm still working over why the fuck that is, because they're all smart and attractive, and they'd each go along with my personality quite well.

I hope you can get more out of this than I can readily spot, because I totally just spend half a fucking hour rambling about my life and identity.
Heh, and it's 7:00 am for me right now. I stayed up all night. The window's open, the fan's blowing, and it's frigid and raining outside. Music is blasting in my ears, and I can't stop thinking about who I am since the move to college. What does all that tell you? I don't think I've moved past this shit yet, either.

I'm sick of writing about this.
Basically, don't get hasty and end up with a Mormon. I don't know how to work through this, clearly, so I can't really give you much advice beyond that. Sorry.
Just know that you have a sympathetic listener if you need me.

Angels and dragons have always bugged me for exactly that reason. They don't stand up to the same biology that most animals on the planet do, save for bacteria, arachnids, mollusks, and other oddities of evolution. If you look at the internals of any random animal, you should see a human-like anatomy distorted and changed to fit the animal. In whales, you can see two arms with fingers, shaped like fins. You see a spine, a ribcage, even remnants of a pelvis and hind legs which the whales don't even use. Cats follow the same pattern, dogs, birds, monkeys, all share a similar anatomy.

So then where do the extra appendages for wings come from?

[existing animal] + [wings] = [mythical creature]

e.g.
Person + Wings = Angel
Lizard + Wings = Dragon
Horse + Wings = Pegasus

This sometimes worked when [wings] is replaced with [winged thing].
e.g.
Lion + Falcon = Griffin
Horse + Falcon = Hippogriff
Human + Falcon = Harpy

Then again, more commonly, [animal] + [different anima] = [mythical creature].

#253718 8 2006-11-12T22:43:01Z Tsukatu
It's pretty simple stuff. You don't really have to complete everything in a level before going down to the next one.
Eat the things with the dots in 'em to grow big and strong. You'll notice that portions of your body have lit up dots. You'll see them on other creatures you'll find, too. To kill a creature, eat all of its glowing dots (they'll become dull grey and the creature will become pissed off (orange), or will get scared and try to run (blue)). Get the red doodad to go down one level (progress in the game) or the blue doodad to go up (backwards).

You can actually just ignore everything and hunt the red things at each level. You'll face that last boss (a looooong snake with a bunch of glowy dots; eat his, don't let him eat yours; his movement will become slower with each segment of his body lost), who will let out a yellow dot in addition to the normal dots you get for killing a creature. Once you eat the yellow dot, you lose control of your organism and you'll go back to the very beginning with a new, different organism.

Tips I'd give:
Eat every dot you can find floating around. It'll give you plenty of body segments, so you can take a whole lot of hits before you go down. That and it will make you look badass.
For efficiency's sake, at least 75% of your movement should be charging (holding down the left mouse button). Stop charging momentarily to quickly change direction, and then continue charging again. When you're fighting another organism, at least 90% of your movement should be charging.
Before you go into a level that has a bunch of enemies, try to have as few of your segments lit up (from eating) as possible, because you'll take an awful lot of time to digest segments you eat off of other creatures if you come in with a full stomach. You want to be able to eat as frequently as possible.
The revolving organisms you'll find get hostile if they're in bunches, but if you stalk them around a bit and attack one while it's away from the others, it will panic and run away instead of attacking you, making it muuuch easier to kill.
You know those big organisms? Like, the frickin' huge ones that take up the screen? When you eat a bit of one of those guys, they'll release these tiny little sperm-shaped bastards, which will try to eat bits of you. And the thing is, you can't kill them and get that food back, so it's lost forever. The best thing to do when attacking one of those gargantuan organisms is to eat a piece and then run like hell until the little bastards all die behind you. Then come back in for more.
Stay away from the mouth of every creature. I know it sounds obvious, but it's easy to forget that the creature has a mouth. For most of them, it's the circle with the three triangles in it.
After you beat the game as a snake, you'll come back as a circle. You'll notice that your constituent bits rotate when you're charging. Use this when you're fighting. Basically, rotate the dulled portions of your body so that they're facing the enemy, charge right at him, eat a piece of his body, and then rotate your body around again and move off of him. Repeat.
When you beat the boss as the circle, you get another yellow thing and come back as a snake. Then again as a circle. After that, I got bored, so I'm not sure if there's another organism you can be if you're patient enough.

All I can think of now. Too tired to go on.

Actually, a cat can survive something like a twelve-story fall without any serious harm, for the same reason that a field mouse or insect can never die from falling from a high altitude: drag.
When the cat realizes that it's falling, it spreads its limbs and increases its... what is it called again, planar surface area? An average housecat has a high enough planar surface area and low enough density (plus all that hair) that it reduces its acceleration toward the Earth enough to let it fall a greater distance than a human could fall unharmed.

#256383 216 2006-11-18T07:50:47Z Tsukatu
Worst day at work as of yet. Fuck.
All thanks to one asshole.

[rant]
I'm scheduled to cover electronics and furniture for three solid hours until closing all by my lonesome. At any given moment, there are six or seven different customers in electronics and two or three in furniture, and a grand total of 4 or 5 people need help with something, so we usually have other people scheduled. Oh, but not tonight. I naively hope that things will be slow for the rest of the night.
Enter Asshole. Asshole is young, probably in his mid twenties, and is very hamfisted and muscley. Asshole has some shit he wants to return, as well as a laundry list of shit he needs to buy. Asshole is very stupid, extremely inattentive, learns slower than an old dog, and is a horrendous liar. And he's very inattentive (I wanted to stress that some more).
The first thing Asshole does is come up to the service desk and start trying to return his shit. He brings in a very used pocket PC and some toner. Let's keep in mind that Staples has a 14-day return policy. Beyond that, it's not our problem.
Let's talk about that toner first. It's clearly not in the original packaging, but that's not a problem with Staples' lax return policy. We ask if it's been 14 days. He says he's pretty sure it's within that. We give him the benefit of the doubt. But when we start processing the return and put in his Staples Rewards information, it turns out that he bought the toner in fuckin' June. We can't accept it. The next claim is that it's still in the original packaging, so it's still good as new. The "original packaging" it's in is some inky fingerprint-smudged shrink wrap that is poorly wrapped around the toner in a vain attempt to make it look unused. Fuck that shit, we ain't takin' it back. He starts to bitch, and then declares that he'll get back to it in a bit, shifting his focus to the pocket PC.
There's nothing wrong with the pocket PC. It's in satisfactory condition and we'd take it back and everything... except that we notice that he purchased it 15 days ago, so it's outside of the return policy's limit. We weren't about to be nice to Asshole after the shit he already gave us, so we tell him we can't take it back. After he gives us some more bullshit about losing his job (I never understood his explanation as to how failure to return his pocket PC amounts to losing his job), we succumb to the bullshit and decide to get it over with.
Uh-oh! The register won't take his ID, because he's returned too many products without a receipt (yeah, we do that). As a matter of fact, he's returned suspiciously large quantities of expensive items without receipts. Even if we still wanted to, the register wouldn't let us carry out the return.
More arguing ensues, more "I'm gonna lose my job" business. He demands to speak to our General Manager, to his old boss when he, himself, actually worked at Staples, and to a few random Staples departments, like Human Resources. My manager, the only manager on duty, an awesome dude named Chili, gets on the phone. Asshole decides to start his shopping.

This is where I come in. Up until this point, I only caught snippets of what was going on, and was filled in on the above by a coworker who actually works at the service desk.
Just before I help Asshole out, four middle-school girls came in and asked me to get a particular monitor for them. Chili is the only person with the keys to get into the high-ticket room, which is where we keep the monitors. Chili is on the phone, trying to call our General Manager for Asshole. I tell the girls that I'll get it as soon as my manager is off the phone. Just after that, I'm paged to help someone out in furniture. As I'm about to answer it, Chili asks me to help Asshole find the shit he needs to buy.
I haven't dealt with his bullshit yet, so I'm all smiles and niceties. When I ask him what I can help him find, he whips out the pocket PC he was trying to return (I wonder how he would've done his shopping if he had returned it successfully) and listed, "two DVD burners, velcro strips, a planner, and [some other shit]." I say, "right this way," as I usually do, do that "follow me" motion, and start walking toward the computer hardware aisle. He's motionless. I turn back to see what the problem is. He's confused. "Where is all that stuff," he asks. "Right over here, sir. If you'd follow me," and again I do the "follow me" motion and start leading the way. He's still motionless. I look expectantly at him, and he just stares blankly at me. There was absolutely no thought being carried out inside that man's head. After a few seconds, he turns around to face the front of the store, ponders for a few more seconds, slowly starts walking toward the service desk, stops and ponders for half another fucking minute, turns right, notices that that's where we keep the shopping carts, then plods over to get one. It was all very zombie-like. He finally wheels that shopping cart over and gets the idea that he's supposed to follow me. While he was wheeling the cart back, a coworker runs up to me and tells me that there's a lady by the computer hardware aisle who needs my help with something. That's a group of girls, someone in furniture, and someone in the aisle I'm heading to who all need help (and I'm the only person covering that area).
I figure I'll walk Asshole over to the computer hardware and answer that lady's question while Asshole is deliberating something. Just to get the communication flowing as we're walking over, I say, "alright, so we're looking for those DVD burners first." He stops. "What the fuck is it this time," I wonder. He stops moving and whips out his pocket PC. "Two DVD burners, velcro strips..." God fucking dammit, he's listing it all again. "Right, yeah, let's find those DVD burners." His response is to look at me for a few seconds, then list all that shit again. "Right, yeah. Let's do those things one at a time, alright? The first thing you said was DVD burners. They're right over here." I continue leading him to the right section of the aisle.
When we get there, the lady who needed help is waiting impatiently with some video cassette tapes in her hand. I point Asshole over to our cluster of DVD burners and turn to the impatient lady. Suddenly, Asshole is all questions, and I tell the impatient lady that I'll be with her in a moment.
Asshole: "Where's your cheapest DVD burner?"
Me: "That'd be that one right there." I point to one of the four internal DVD burners we have. It's on sale, and so has half the price of the other three, a fact that is advertised prominently by a massive tag.
Asshole: "Where is it?"
Me: "Right here, sir." I pointed directly at the fucking thing last time, how did he miss it? Whatever, I actually poke the box with my finger.
Asshole: "This one here?"
Me: "Yeah, that one there."
Asshole: "It's the cheapest?"
Me: "Right now, yeah."
Asshole: "How 'bout this one?" He points to another DVD burner.
Me: "That's another DVD burner. It does the same trick, it's just more expensive."
Asshole: "Oh. How 'bout this one?" He points to the inexpensive one I've pointed out to him.
Me: "That's the cheap one."
Asshole: "And it's the cheapest?"
Me: "Yeah."
Impatient lady interrupts at this point. Her question about a four-pack of VHS tapes: "it says 6 hours on the front - will each of these tape six hours, or is it all of them that tapes 6 hours combined?" "Each." "Okay, great. Thank you!"
Asshole: "What about this one?" He points to an internal DVD-ROM drive.
Me: "That'll read DVD's, but it won't burn 'em."
Asshole: "But it's cheaper."
Me: "That's cuz it won't burn DVD's." Christ, this guy said he used to work at Staples...
Asshole: "But this one will?" He points back to the cheap DVD burner.
Me: "That's right."
Asshole: "You got anything cheaper than this one?"
Me: "Not right now."
Asshole: "What's 'dual-layer' mean?"
Me: "A dual layer disc has two burnable layers instead of just one. It holds twice the amount. They're more expensive, though."
Asshole: "Alright, I'll take this one here." He takes the cheap one. "There's only one on the shelf. I need two."
Me: "We put out the stock we have recently. It looks like we don't have any more of the cheap burners."
Asshole: "How 'bout I just take this one?" He picks up the DVD-ROM box.
Me: "That one doesn't burn to DVD's. It only reads them."
Asshole: "Oh." He puts the DVD-ROM box where the cheap DVD burner was before he took it. "Well what about this one?" He points to a CD-RW drive.
Me: "That one can't even read DVD's."
Asshole: "Oh. So wait, why don't I just take a second one of these cheap DVD burners?" He grabs the DVD-ROM box he just put in the wrong spot not twelve fuckin' seconds ago.
Me: "Because that's the one that only reads DVD's. You just put it there."
Asshole: "Oh." He's visibly confounded. "That's okay, I'll just go for one right now." He whips out his pocket PC. "Velcro ties. Where do you keep velcro ties?"
The only velcro ties we have in the store are for organizing cables. I walk him three meters down the same aisle and point to all the cable-binding stuff. He doesn't even look where I'm pointing.
Me: "They're right here."
Asshole, as if I didn't just point to them: "You guys got velcro ties here?"
Me: "Yes, we have them right here." I poke the box.
Asshole: "Where do you guys have them?"
This guy can't be fucking serious.
Me: "They're right here. The velcro ties are right here." I poke the box again.
At this point, the customer waiting for me in furniture is fed up and walks over to me personally to ask for help. She's extremely indecisive, and continues to ask how much various chairs cost. I follow her around and read her the index card-sized pricetags we have pinned directly onto the chair backs (it's noticeably uncomfortable when you sit down on top of one). Then she can't even decide if she wants a desk to go with it. Meanwhile, the girls who wanted the monitor are giving me impatient looks. It had been at least ten minutes since they asked me to get the monitor, and they were waiting it out on our office chair displays. I tell them that the manager is still on the phone, and that I'll jump on him the second he gets off.
Suddenly, the alarm system on the digital cameras starts going off. I excuse myself to go check it out. On my way, I notice that Asshole is looking at the section with cable ties.

The problem with the alarm system on the digital cameras is that I need to get into the locked cabinet below the display to turn off the alarm system. To do that, I need to have the right keys, which only Chili has. Chili is busy talking angrily with Asshole's past coworker or something. That means I still can't get into the high-ticket to get the monitor and that I can't turn off the alarm.
The alarm continues to ring. People start getting pissed off at the noise.
Chili takes a break from the phone and runs over to unlock the cabinet below the digital camera displays. As luck would have it, the mechanism to turn off the digital camera alarm is different from every other alarm system we have. I don't know how to turn it off. To get to it, I had to pull out a piece of the display counter itself, so now a second siren starts wailing because it thinks someone's breaking into the cabinet. A bunch of coworkers rush over from the office supply section and start trying to figure out how to turn the alarm off. In the meantime, I manage to snag Chili and get him to open up high-ticket so I can get a monitor. The girl who asked for it notices this and stands outside expectantly.
That monitor's sold out. She'd been waiting something like 20 minutes.
Over the shrieking of the siren, I tell her, "try Best Buy, next door. They probably have their shit together."

My coworkers are failing to shut the alarm system up. I figure there's not much else I can do other than helping out some customers. The other people who have stumbled into electronics needed minimal help, much to my relief. One couple that loved to state the obvious ate up five minutes of my time by the phones, but they were grateful about the help I gave 'em. Impatient lady decides on a chair. She had heard me bitching that I'm alone in covering electronics and furniture and that I'm about to go postal, so she was cautious and nervous when she talked. It was pretty amusing. Anyway, the chair she wanted just happened to be on the third shelf of our stack of chairs in the back room, which is about 7 or 8 meters above the ground. I'd use a ladder, but there are massive stacks of paper conveniently parked in the way. I rely instead on my tallness and my mad ninja one-armed-climbing-while-bracing-a-20-kg-chair-on-one-shoulder skills to get it down, but not before cussing a helluva lot and giving God the finger. I carry the chair out and cut short her line of questions about whether she's allowed to keep her parking space in front of Staples by boring through her skull with my glare. Her eyes remained fixed on the ground and her mouth remained shut for the rest of her time in the building.

Asshole's looking at monitors. Monitors weren't on his list, but he's looking at them. I ask him if he's found other stuff on his list. And would ya know it, he asks me where the fucking velcro ties are. I really, really wish I was kidding. I pointed to his shopping cart, which he had left by the velcro ties. "It's right there where you left your shopping cart." "Where are they?" "Where your shopping cart is. They're in the green box I pointed to. The one you were looking at when I saw you last." "Oh, okay." He continued to examine the monitors. He never onced turned so that his line of sight was within 135 degrees of his shopping cart.
Meanwhile, the alarm is still blasting, though the vandalism alarm stopped. Chili eventually finishes on the phone and turns off the digital camera alarm, which had been raging for at least twenty minutes, more likely half an hour. I go on my first 15-minute break of the day. On the way out I see the girls sitting on some steps nearby. They scored a monitor at Best Buy. "Congrats on the monitor. I hate this fucking place." I gesture behind me. They laugh. Good to know they don't blame me for what happened.

When I come back, Chili's on the phone again, with Asshole in his face. As I pass by the service desk, I hear Asshole say, "...gonna lose my fuckin' job, man." Asshole wants Chili to call everyone under the Sun and says he won't leave until he gets his returns done. I punch back in, straighten some shit out in my departments, help a few people out, and then notice that Asshole gave up and left. When I'm near the service desk, Chili jokes about me being on security detail when Asshole comes back. I ask him what he means. Apparently, Asshole left in a hissy fit and said he'd be back to take $300 worth of merchandise from the store. He didn't come back, though I suppose he could be vandalizing the store as I'm typing this.

Heh, and we had a new guy today. It was his first day, and he was working at the service desk. I bet he had a fun time.

Basically, I really hate that feeling that I have to be everywhere at once, especially when half of those people are total morons, and when there's an alarm going off that I can't do anything to stop. And all of that happened because of Asshole.
[/rant]

And people ask why I'm so misanthropic.

#12339 1 2006-11-18T18:32:43Z Tsukatu
In the UCLA library, some guy was using one of the library's computers. The library monitor came by and asked to see his student ID. The guy refused. The monitor said that the library is for UCLA students' use only, and asked the guy to leave. The guy refused. The monitor called the police. As the police started to come in, the guy got up and started to leave. The police started talking to him, and out of nowhere the guy decides that he's not going to leave. The police can't talk him into getting out of the library, so they tazer him. The guy collapses on the floor and starts shouting about police brutality and how he still refuses to leave.
The police tell him to get up and leave the library, tazer him again, and drag him a little bit more toward the exit. They repeat that sequence several more times. Eventually, they arrest him and force him out of the library.

Caught on a cellphone camera: http://youtube.com/watch?v=4JGlvEcPmug

What do you think about what happened?

---

My opinion:

The guy was in the wrong the moment he came into the library and started using a computer without a student ID. (The fact that he refused to show one instead of claiming it wasn't on him or anything tells me that he was either not a student or was trying to make some retarded stand against authority.) The monitor handled everything just as he was supposed to.
The guy started to leave when he saw that the police were coming. The police stopped him because they wanted to talk to him. I think this might be a point of contention. I don't think that the police were in the wrong for stopping him, because I think it's part of their job to talk to him and see if he was a UCLA student after all, and tell him themselves that he was not allowed to use the university's computers if he wasn't a student.
The guy was not attempting to do the right thing by leaving; he was running away. Then he decides to make the situation worse by declaring out of nowhere that he isn't going to leave. That's another point where he's in the wrong.
(If the police hadn't stopped him, he would've successfully gotten away, so he would still have been in the wrong.)
So the police need to get someone out of the library because he's not supposed to be there in the first place and is making a scene. Talking to him has proven useless, and he just gets louder every time they ask him to leave. He won't even negotiate anymore. What else is there to do? I agree with the police's decision to tazer him.
And here's another spot where the guy is in the wrong: he starts crying about police brutality and abuse of authority to get the sympathy of the students watching. There is absolutely no validity to his claims; he left the police no alternative. He even shouts some funny shit about the Patriot Act, because this clearly has anything to do with terrorism.
The pain from a tazer stops immediately when it's no longer being used, and the guy still has plenty of energy to fight off the officers when they try to drag him, so he's a damned liar for acting like he's too debilitated by the tazer to stand up and leave (and getting more sympathy from onlookers because of it).
The police gave him plenty of opportunities to stand up and leave the library, but the moron keeps on refusing. What the hell does he think is going to happen? They really do give him plenty of opportunity to stand up and leave before they tazer him again. The police are still not in the wrong.

You are kidnapped in the middle of the night, dragged to the top of a cliff, and get thrown off. It just so happens that you accidentally hit an air balloon on the way down in which Edgar Evil is attempting to rape Vicky Victim. #258740 44 2006-11-24T02:52:46Z Tsukatu
*BLAM* *BLAM*
The hapless member fired two more posts behind him frantically and summoned the last of his strength to sprint to the abandoned Meta outpost. He dove into the doorway and kicked the door closed, then scrambled to his feet and moved a nearby crate to block the doorway.
After taking a second to get his bearings, he noticed that only light remaining inside the ruined outpost was coming from a dim lightbulb hanging from the ceiling that flickered every once in a while. He could barely distinguish between the rubble and the turned-over furniture. Moving aside a smashed monitor and the splintered remains of a desk, he made his way to the command console and felt around for the keyboard.
The sudden sound of the handle twitching turned his face pale, and he dove behind an overturned rack of body armor.
The doorknob stopped rattling. A brief silence filled the room before a human-shaped hole splintered its way out of the door as the massive figure walked casually through it, as though it was a cobweb. The figure's orange glowing eyes immediately found the cowering unnamed member across the pitch dark, and it continued its casual lumber toward him.
The member rose to his feet against the wall behind him slowly and aimed his gun at the figure's heart.
*BLAM*
It was like he was firing blanks.
*BLAM* *BLAM* *BLAM*
He could hear the fired posts ricocheting off of the walls.
*BLAM*
The post bounced off of the figure's chest and hit his own arm. He cried out in pain and raised his weapon again.
*click*
He dropped his weapon. The figure hadn't been slowed, and continued to advance. It was less than two meters away.

The member called up whatever courage he had left.
"Even if you kill me," he panted, "the rest of the Meta's will hunt down and kill every one of you Net's."
The figure was unphased. In the dark, he could only tell its expression from its yellow-orange eyes, which looked entirely uncaring.
"I'm not Net."
"What? S-so you're M-Meta then, if you're... if you're not Net?"
He was within the figure's reach.
"H-hey! I'm Meta, t-too! Haha! What luck, right?"
"I'm not Meta."
The figure reached out and grabbed the member by the throat. It lifted him into the air and pinned him against the wall with one hand.
"If... if y-you're not M-Meta," the Meta said between chokes, "and if... i-if you're not N-Net... then w-w-what the h-hell are you?"
"I'm bored."
As that statement soaked in, the figure's eyes turned from their yellow-orange color to a deep red. The sickening crack of the Meta's neck could be heard by the Net outside, who had heard gunfire and come to investigate.
Tsukatu sauntered outside and looked at the Net, who was pointing a gun at his face.
"Declare your allegiance," the Net shouted.
Tsukatu just smiled.

#259685 13 2006-11-25T23:07:54Z Tsukatu
Quote: greenpencil, November 25, 2006 11:00 am
What's the difference between Megabytes and Megabits?
1 bit = a switch that can be 1 or 0
1 byte = 8 bits
1 kilobyte = 1,024 bytes = 8,192 bits (1's and 0's)
1 megabyte = 1,024 kilobytes = 1,048,576 bytes = 8,388,608 bits
1 gigabyte = 1,024 megabytes = 1,048,576 kilobytes = 1,073,741,824 bytes = 8,589,934,592 bits

You can commonly find 500 GB (gigabyte) hard drives for sale, which basically contains 4,294,967,296,000 (4.2 trillion, or 4,200 billion) tiny magnetic switches that can each be a 1 or a 0.
(Except that they usually specify on the back of the box that the terminology they're using is 1 gigabyte = 1,000,000,000 bytes, so if you convert their 500 fake-GB into real-GB, you're actually buying a 465.6 GB hard drive.)

When you're shopping for a wireless router or adapter, you'll notice that Netgear, Linksys, Belkin, etc., don't use bytes because wireless connections aren't restricted to using a physical, 8-bit bus (that and they like to put as big of numbers as they can on the box ). So the standard G speed, 54 megabits per second, is really 6.75 megabytes per second.

Something my roommate brought up when I was talking to him about this:

The transporter works by analyzing the molecular structure of the person at point A, recreating that same structure at point B, and then destroying the original at point A.
The transporter messed up in that it failed to destroy the person at point A.

Here's where we get into all kinds of sticky issues, like the fact that the guy who designed the teleporter knew that it would destroy him, and so was committing suicide.

Then there's the fact that the guy at point A, the original, should be dead. But he isn't. And he flips out and kills the version of himself that's supposed to live on. Isn't that murder?

And going past that, if we don't charge the guy at point A for murder, then he could go back home and continue spawning clones of himself to battle. He'd be killing conscious, living, thinking, feeling beings, and it wouldn't be called murder. That's fucked up.

1. All faith is blind faith
Most definitely not the case. Otherwise, blind faith would be redundant. This is a prime example of the need to define terms. Faith is a belief in something that cannot be proven. Blind faith is belief in something for which there is no evidence. Now, having no evidence for something and disproving something is not the same. For instance, take someone who believes in Santa. They have blind faith because there is no evidence that Santa exists. Now say they found a secret abandoned elf workshop under the north pole. Now the person has faith, because it still cannot be proven, but you cannot say that it is blind faith because there is some evidence supporting the idea.
On a related note, there is no way to prove that there is no Santa. There is always the remotest tiniest portion of a percent chance that he exists. In order to disprove Santas existence, (assuming Santa would be made of matter and/or is visible to the eye) one would have to look simultaneously everywhere in the universe.
1. Jesus was a space alien.
Most definitely not the case. The Jesus we know is an extravagant fairy tale inspired by a much less fantastical madman millennia ago. He was most definitely human, and not a space alien. How very silly of you to think otherwise.
(Oh, and the only way that the statement "there is no way to prove that there is no Santa" is correct is if you assume that what we know about Santa is not completely reliable, and that basically turns Santa into any sort of mystical being for whom we can dream up any characteristics we like so that he continues to exist in our minds. #262606 18 2006-12-01T15:35:01Z Tsukatu
I take Boston's famous T-line to some of my classes. I could really just take a 20-30 minute walk instead of taking a 15-20 minute T-ride, but I ride the T anyway. And the only reason I do this is because the one part of the T's map that goes above ground is right where my university is, and outbound rides on the T from the very first stop that's above the ground is completely free. Going back inbound, though, costs money, so I usually walk back.

Problems with it:
-There are no consistent patterns to any given train's arrival. Sometimes a train comes four minutes after the one before it, and sometimes it takes twenty minutes. And best of all, there's no sign telling you when the next one is coming.
-There are very frequent delays because the above-ground track crosses a whole slew of intersections, and it is obligated to wait for every last car and pedestrian before it starts going again. Each one of these delays is a few minutes long, and it happens a couple of times in each one of my trips.
-The people they hire to drive the cars are a bunch of shit-eating, monkey-fucking motherfuckers. Every single one of 'em. I have not to this day met a polite or patient T-driver. If you're hurrying to get into the car and end up making it so that you even have to wait for the person in front of you to get in, they'll see that you came later than everyone else and close the doors right in front of your face. Then they'll sit there for a minute or two with the doors closed, train motionless, as they wait for traffic to finish flowing (when they could just open the doors for two seconds to let you in). If you come to the front of the car and knock politely, the driver just looks over, smirks, and ignores you. And this happens all the goddamned time. I see it happen every couple of stops to every age group, race, and gender under the sun. The driver usually ignores me when I tell them there's someone outside, too. At any given moment, I have at least five random scraps of paper in various pockets that list reminders, and at least two other schedules (for classes, work1, work2, social events, etc.), and on top of that I try to remember random stuff to do each day.
At first I moved from memory onto the pieces of paper to make my life easier, but it's really annoying scribbling stuff out and writing other stuff down in the white spaces between scribbled out text.
So now I think I could seriously benefit from a very simple, straight-forward PDA.
I absent-mindedly strolled over to the PDA/PocketPC section of the Staples store I work at and started playing around with a Z22. Then I realized that the Z stood for Zire and went to wash my hands seven times, spit over my shoulder, and say two dozen Hail Mary's. So when I got back, I started looking at the Tungsten E2. It looked pretty much like what I wanted, but I didn't think that 32 MB was a whole lot of storage space (because if I get a PDA, I'm also going to have horrific amounts of reference documents on there so I don't have to drag books around with me, and I'd also like a wide selection of awesome games to distract myself when I'm bored).
So then I got to looking at the Tungsten T/X. And I think I want it. I mean, it has four times the space the E2 has, and feckin' wireless. How much more badass can you get? It's a bit higher than I'd be willing to pay, cuz I'd have to save up for a while and I'm very impatient, but a good part of me believes that it's very worth it.

And yes, I saw the PocketPC's, but I'm very disinterested in getting one. They're very expensive and tend to come infested with proprietary Microsoft garbage. I wouldn't buy a Microsoft product for the same reason I'd avoid a Sony product.
Please don't suggest a PocketPC.

So, someone who actually knows about this stuff, what do you say?
I also realize that I've only taken a look at a very limited selection of what's out there - can you suggest something better?

So, God is unprovable, and un-dis-provable. All that is left is the choice. And I, personally, see no need for God. And as I want to discover more about the universe, I do not want to be able to just fall back and say "oh, God did it". That's the easy way out. I feel I can live my life well, following my own moral code, without a metaphorical Father allways keeping His eye on me to make sure I obey, or forcing me through pointless ritual.
Oh, and Pascals wager (the only pro-God argument) does not apply because there are many different mutually exclusive religions. They can't all be true.
My main beef (-sic-, heh) with christianity is that it seperates action from faith. To go to heaven, Jesus proclaims, all you have to do is beleive in Christ. Allthough this implies you have to act in a good way, it never states this, nor does it tell you what a 'good' way is - thanks to our good friend the Old Testament and its outdatedness and openness to misinterpretation. I'm never sure I want to be part of a faith where all that matters is your beleifs, not your deeds.
What's stopping you from believing in the started-the-big-bang-and-then-left-us-to-our-own-devices god of Deism?
He doesn't have any sense of morality that he imposes on us, and he doesn't even care about what we do. He probably didn't even make a Heaven or a Hell, and we just die.
Many people believe in this sort of being to explain the origin of the universe (especially the cause of the Big Bang).
If you fully embrace your agnosticism, there is nothing you can say for or against the existence of this being, clearly. You think this is a perfectly valid, if entirely unprovable (yet un-disprovable) theory, but you're still perfectly comfortable not knowing the details and thinking of this being as a God of the Fundamental Gap, as it were. What if there is such a being, and you're wrong?
Hm... well then I supose there wouldn't really be any consequences unless he decided to act again on the cosmic scale.
So why should you care if there is or isn't such a being? You may as well go on living your life as if he weren't there, because even if he were, he wouldn't have any influence upon your life other than enabling it.
But... don't you want to believe what's true?

#265233 29 2006-12-06T02:09:45Z Tsukatu
About improbability:

You're on a spaceship, cryogenically frozen. The ship's computer will generate a random integer from 1 to 10^40 every second, and will revive you if the number it randomly generated is the number 7. Assume that the ship can navigate it's way around dangerous areas and obstacles in space, that it is fully able to generate its own power indefinitely, and that you will last indefinitely until you are awakened.
You are revived. You have no idea how long you've been frozen. What do you think happened - the computer hit 7, or an extraplanar being entered the ship undetected, didn't set off any alarms, thawed you, and restored you to life, taking as payment the equivalent amount of resources aboard the ship it would take to revive you, and then hacked the computer system onboard the ship to display the number 7 before he left, leaving no trace of his presence? Which one would you guess happened?

Imagine the amount of planets there are in the universe that can support life. That's such a bloated number - there are so many planets that, since the birth of the universe, can support some simple form of life. Now imagine all of those planets, for billions of years (holy shit, that's several billion years... that's a very long time!). Imagine just one of these planets. On this planet, imagine the amount of time it has in its lifespan to generate life. Earth got it right after a painfully long time, and it's hardly past its prime. But still, think of how long it has to generate life somewhere on it. Now expand your view so you take into account all of those life-supporting planets we were talking about. They have so goddamned long to get a series of events down in a certain pattern. And there are so many of them that one's bound to do it eventually.

And even so, you'd love for it to be that improbable, but life didn't come from individual atoms coincidentally falling into place to suddenly create life. The first organisms could hardly even be considered alive as much as lumps of matter that interacted the way they did because of their chemical properties.
When I get to talking about this stuff, I can't help but think that there's another planet seventy galaxies away on which we have things that resemble the organic forms of this planet, but haven't yet grown and gotten complicated enough to be called life, and never get lucky enough to grow out of that stage before their planet is caught in the supernova of its sun.

I lost my train of thought, but the point is that where other people take a look at life and "rationalize" (more like "panic and suspend reason to quell their fears by inventing the idea") that we were all created by something capable of thought, I take a look at life and rationalize that the long, improbable chain of events necessary to create life actually happened.

The previous example I've used when talking about this is a cookie in a box, because I love using examples with cookies in them.
That one was:
There's a closed box with a cookie inside and a button on the top. With each press of the button, there's a 10^-50 percent chance that the box will open to give the button-pusher the cookie. There's a line of people 10^54 people long, and each person in that line gets to press the button once. You're somewhere in the middle. Your turn to press the button comes up. The box opens, giving you the cookie.
People like you would thank God for opening the box, because as we all know the chance that it would open is so small that it's impossible, so it couldn't be anything related to the operation of the box. No, that has to be impossible, doesn't it? God literally forced the box open so you can get the cookie, because He loves you and cares for you and wants you to donate to His followers and slaughter all who oppose Him.
But a rationale person would shrug, think it's nifty that he, of all people, got so lucky, and take the goddamned cookie.

C is simply so much easier to grasp once you get in the swing of things.

Compare:

10 PRINT "Hello, world!"
20 END

vs

[
    uuid(2573F8F4-CFEE-101A-9A9F-00AA00342820)
    ]
    library LHello
    {
	// bring in the master library
	importlib("actimp.tlb");
	importlib("actexp.tlb");

	// bring in my interfaces
	#include "pshlo.idl"

	[
	uuid(2573F8F5-CFEE-101A-9A9F-00AA00342820)
	]
	cotype THello
     {
     interface IHello;
     interface IPersistFile;
     };
    };

    [
    exe,
    uuid(2573F890-CFEE-101A-9A9F-00AA00342820)
    ]
    module CHelloLib
    {

	// some code related header files
	importheader(<windows.h>);
	importheader(<ole2.h>);
	importheader(<except.hxx>);
	importheader("pshlo.h");
	importheader("shlo.hxx");
	importheader("mycls.hxx");

	// needed typelibs
	importlib("actimp.tlb");
	importlib("actexp.tlb");
	importlib("thlo.tlb");

	[
	uuid(2573F891-CFEE-101A-9A9F-00AA00342820),
	aggregatable
	]
	coclass CHello
     {
     cotype THello;
     };
    };

    #include "ipfix.hxx"

    extern HANDLE hEvent;

    class CHello : public CHelloBase
    {
    public:
	IPFIX(CLSID_CHello);

	CHello(IUnknown *pUnk);
	~CHello();

	HRESULT  __stdcall PrintSz(LPWSTR pwszString);

    private:
	static int cObjRef;
    };

    #include <windows.h>
    #include <ole2.h>
    #include <stdio.h>
    #include <stdlib.h>
    #include "thlo.h"
    #include "pshlo.h"
    #include "shlo.hxx"
    #include "mycls.hxx"

    int CHello::cObjRef = 0;

    CHello::CHello(IUnknown *pUnk) : CHelloBase(pUnk)
    {
	cObjRef++;
	return;
    }

    HRESULT  __stdcall  CHello::PrintSz(LPWSTR pwszString)
    {
	printf("%ws\n", pwszString);
	return(ResultFromScode(S_OK));
    }

    CHello::~CHello(void)
    {

    // when the object count goes to zero, stop the server
    cObjRef--;
    if( cObjRef == 0 )
	PulseEvent(hEvent);

    return;
    }

    #include <windows.h>
    #include <ole2.h>
    #include "pshlo.h"
    #include "shlo.hxx"
    #include "mycls.hxx"

    HANDLE hEvent;

     int _cdecl main(
    int argc,
    char * argv[]
    ) {
    ULONG ulRef;
    DWORD dwRegistration;
    CHelloCF *pCF = new CHelloCF();

    hEvent = CreateEvent(NULL, FALSE, FALSE, NULL);

    // Initialize the OLE libraries
    CoInitializeEx(NULL, COINIT_MULTITHREADED);

    CoRegisterClassObject(CLSID_CHello, pCF, CLSCTX_LOCAL_SERVER,
	REGCLS_MULTIPLEUSE, &dwRegistration);

    // wait on an event to stop
    WaitForSingleObject(hEvent, INFINITE);

    // revoke and release the class object
    CoRevokeClassObject(dwRegistration);
    ulRef = pCF->Release();

    // Tell OLE we are going away.
    CoUninitialize();

    return(0); }

    extern CLSID CLSID_CHello;
    extern UUID LIBID_CHelloLib;

    CLSID CLSID_CHello = { /* 2573F891-CFEE-101A-9A9F-00AA00342820 */
	0x2573F891,
	0xCFEE,
	0x101A,
	{ 0x9A, 0x9F, 0x00, 0xAA, 0x00, 0x34, 0x28, 0x20 }
    };

    UUID LIBID_CHelloLib = { /* 2573F890-CFEE-101A-9A9F-00AA00342820 */
	0x2573F890,
	0xCFEE,
	0x101A,
	{ 0x9A, 0x9F, 0x00, 0xAA, 0x00, 0x34, 0x28, 0x20 }
    };

    #include <windows.h>
    #include <ole2.h>
    #include <stdlib.h>
    #include <string.h>
    #include <stdio.h>
    #include "pshlo.h"
    #include "shlo.hxx"
    #include "clsid.h"

    int _cdecl main(
    int argc,
    char * argv[]
    ) {
    HRESULT  hRslt;
    IHello        *pHello;
    ULONG  ulCnt;
    IMoniker * pmk;
    WCHAR  wcsT[_MAX_PATH];
    WCHAR  wcsPath[2 * _MAX_PATH];

    // get object path
    wcsPath[0] = '\0';
    wcsT[0] = '\0';
    if( argc  1) {
	mbstowcs(wcsPath, argv[1], strlen(argv[1]) + 1);
	wcsupr(wcsPath);
	}
    else {
	fprintf(stderr, "Object path must be specified\n");
	return(1);
	}

    // get print string
    if(argc  2)
	mbstowcs(wcsT, argv[2], strlen(argv[2]) + 1);
    else
	wcscpy(wcsT, L"Hello World");

    printf("Linking to object %ws\n", wcsPath);
    printf("Text String %ws\n", wcsT);

    // Initialize the OLE libraries
    hRslt = CoInitializeEx(NULL, COINIT_MULTITHREADED);

    if(SUCCEEDED(hRslt)) {

	hRslt = CreateFileMoniker(wcsPath, &pmk);
	if(SUCCEEDED(hRslt))
     hRslt = BindMoniker(pmk, 0, IID_IHello, (void **)&pHello);

	if(SUCCEEDED(hRslt)) {

     // print a string out
     pHello->PrintSz(wcsT);

     Sleep(2000);
     ulCnt = pHello->Release();
     }
	else
     printf("Failure to connect, status: %lx", hRslt);

	// Tell OLE we are going away.
	CoUninitialize();
	}

    return(0);
    }

See? Simple stuff, here. And the C version flows much more nicely, if you ask me.

#266644 32 2006-12-08T20:30:42Z Tsukatu
XRXRXRX:
One thing I felt needed additional commenting on, because you still seemed unclear.

We define years as Earth years, which is the amount of time it takes for the Earth to make one revolution around the Sun. If there were an Earth II that made a revolution around the Sun twice as fast as Earth I does, then its year would be half of an Earth year.
The important thing to understand is that the concept of "year" is purely language. Just because someone ages a year on Earth II does not mean he ages a year anywhere. If you're thinking of a child going to Earth II and aging to 18 twice as quickly as he would on Earth I, he'd still be a small child, not even beginning purberty, even though we call him 18 Earth II years old, because he's only 9 Earth years old.

And going with what ian said, if the planet was physically travelling faster through space than Earth, then yes, relative to Earth, people from Earth II would have a longer lifespan, but it wouldn't even be noticeable. This is in the same way that Air Force test pilots, who move at ridiculous speeds every day in their line of work, extend their lifespans by a couple of microseconds. It's seriously not going to be noticeable.

What if making other people happy is a sick drug to me?  Like, the ultimate in self-affirming sybaritic pleasures, because it reminds me how potent my actions and decisions really are that I can not only make myself happy, but an entire community of folks whose joy is simply an extention of my own.  What if, by pleasing others, I've only subsidized their ownership of that pleasure and made it partially my own.  That, in the entire (yet tiny) wordlview, they couldn't be happier, but their existence is just a miniscule polyp on the vastness of my own brain, ebbing with joy.

Oh, absolutely. This is one of the most commonly misunderstood things about Satanism.
It's not about self-service at the expense of others.
In the portions of the Satanic Bible where its most basic life philosophy is laid out ("do what makes you happy as long as you don't hurt anyone undeserving in the process;" the Humanist philosophy, shared by such groups as Secular Humanists), after it has discussed a human being's most natural behaviors, needs, and desires, LaVey makes sure to note that one of the things that brings human beings the most happiness is making other people happy. It's a very primal and very powerful, natural human behavior, and you should embrace it.

Being a Satanist doesn't mean you are forced to act like an insensitive asshole.

The point is that free will is a state of being that is far more permanent than life, and not nearly as fragile. To make your statement applicable, you'd have to change it to:
"Are you immortal? Yes, you say? But if someone shot you, you would be dead. Since someone can change that, you aren't really immortal."
And then it just sort of becomes nonsense.

I'm also spotting a popular fallacy...
I think what some of you people are getting at is the idea that God's omniscience can see the result of any choice you make, but the choice is ultimately up to you.
This doesn't fully take God's omniscience into account, because if God knows everything, He will also know which choice you end up going with.
And if omnipotence only applies to what is logically doable, then limiting omniscience, an undoable action, is impossible for God. God can't help but know what you're going to do.

God knows. If it is possible to know what you are going to do (and it is if you believe in an omniscient God), then there is only one path your life can take. It's a bit wierd to say that your life is "decided for you" because of this, but it remains true that your path is set.

Quote: TFM
N v1.4 / Ned v1.1
copyright 2005 by Metanet Software Inc.
Raigan Burns / Mare Sheppard
metanet at harveycartel dot org






N readme  - table of contents

1. Before you Begin
2. Backing up your N progress
3. New in v1.4
4. Tips and Gameplay
5. Custom Levels
6. Updates, News and More Information




-------------------- Section One: Before you Begin ------------------------------


Please read the included license agreement "license.txt". 
N is freeware, and is freely distributable as long as the archive remains intact. 


When you start N for the first time, a Local Storage window may pop up,
requesting permission to store data on your hard drive. 

You must allow this in order to save any progress. 

See section 2 for information on how to back up your N progress.




---------Help with N's Performance

Please set your monitor to 1024x768 resolution;
For optimal performance, close all background tasks.

You will notice a slight improvement in performance if the
mouse cursor is _not_ over the window in which N is playing,
or if you set your display to 16-bit color.



*NEW*

Linux users rejoice!  Many of the problems with N's awful
performance are related to sound, possibly the interaction of
OSS and the Flash player.  Try these fixes suggested
by Linux users on our forum:

1. try playing a song using XMMS or another music player

2. if that doesn't work, try this tip from another Linux user:

------
XMMS did not work for me, and since I am using Fluxbox WM I
cannot easily tag a sound event to N, unlike KDE. But I found
that if I use my browser (for verbosity, Mozilla Firefox 1.01
with Flash plugin installed) to access a Flash page with sound
(such as the menu for homestarrunner.com) I was able to then start
N and play without the lag experienced previously.
------

3. and finally, you might notice some improvement if you set N's
priority to high:

------
start N in console like this:

nice -n 20 ./n_v14
------
(by Jehu)


Also, the above musical/sound fix seems to improve performance
on Mac and PC also -- playing a song in iTunes, Windows Media
Player or WinAmp has been effective in reducing lag for _some_ users. 
Apparently the ninja enjoys listening to music!




---------News/Etc

N was the recipient of the 2005 IGF Audience Choice Award in the Web/
Downloadable category.  We want to take this opportunity to once again
thank everyone who voted for us.  You guys rock!




-------------------- Section Two: Backing up your N progress ------------------------------


When you start N for the first time, a Local Storage window may pop up,
requesting permission to store data on your hard drive.  You must
allow this in order to save any progress.

For a variety of reasons, .sol files sometimes get corrupted or overwritten,
so it's important to keep a copy of your N .sol file just in case. 
For transfer or storage of this backup file, we recommend first zipping,
stuffing, or otherwise compressing it. 

Shared objects are special files created by Flash with the extension .sol.
In order to back up your N progress, you'll first have to search for the file. 
In Windows, search for '*.sol' in system and hidden files and folders, which can
be selected in the advanced search options. 
In Mac OSX, use Find to search for files with extension 'sol' in Home or everywhere.


*** IMPORTANT! ***
Your N .sol file is called 'N_v14b_userdata.sol'.  When you find it, make sure you record the
location of this file, since that is where you'll have to copy your backup file in the event
that your progress is lost.


Copy the .sol file and paste it into a new directory on your hard drive. 
We recommend making a new text file where you can record the directory in which
you found the .sol file. Then compress these two files, and email the archive to yourself
or whatever.


If your progress is corrupted, close N, copy your backup shared object to the
correct directory and restart N.  Your progress should be restored.




-------------------- Section Three: New in v1.4 ------------------------------


-= HIGHSCORES AND TIMETRIALS =-

We made a few changes to N's highscores menu page, notably merging the Time Trials and
Highscore pages so you can more quickly try to beat a highscore when you're watching
a replay.

To play a timetrial level, choose an episode from the [select episode] grid,
then choose a level from the [view scores] menu -- if you've unlocked that level,
a "play level" button will appear. Click on it to begin playing in timetrial mode.


The highscores page now indicates game progress,showing you which episodes and levels
you've unlocked "properly" (by beating previous ones), which you've unlocked via cheating,
and which you've yet to see.  As always, to qualify for highscores and personal bests,
you must play levels you've unlocked properly.


The submit button is now visible permanently. Highscores should be uploaded automatically
as you get them while you play N, but sometimes due to server or connection problems, the
data is sent improperly.  If you see that one of your personal bests should be a highscore but
isn't, just click submit and your score will be added.


Online highscore are accessible outside of the game at:
http://www.harveycartel.org/metanet/n_highscores_e.php

Very shortly these will feature a new Search page! 



-= USER LEVELS MODE =-

You can now play custom levels in N's game mode -- just click on User Levels from N's main menu.  You'll
see a list displaying your current collection of custom levels.  Clicking on entries in the list loads the
level so you can play it immediately.  Click on a column heading ("level name", "author", etc.) to sort levels
by that column.


Included in your N download is a .txt file called userlevels.txt.  This file contains all the user level data
which will be loaded into the game.  We've started it with a sampling of our favourite user maps which didn't
make it into N1.4.  When you add your own levels and levels you've downloaded from NUMA to this text file,
they'll appear on the list you see in User Levels mode. 


*** EXTREMELY IMPORTANT ***
DO NOT DELETE userlevels.txt!!


View the instructions in userlevels.txt for more information on adding and organising user maps.


User Levels mode also features a way for you to save and share replay data. 
After you play a level and return to the user levels menu, the replay will be available in a textbox
on the left side of the screen.  You'll have to manually copy and paste the data to a text file,
but this new feature allows you to swap game mode replays with other N players.

User Levels records personal bests as well -- not for highscores, but to indicate that you've
beaten a user level, and to allow you to replay your best run at any time.  If you've beaten a user
level, a button will appear beside its entry in the list of levels.  Click the button to watch your
personal best replay. As usual, the replay data will be available in the textbox to the left of the list.



-= CONFIGURE MENU =-

New to the Configure menu is the email field.  Entering an address in this field is optional,
but if you want/need your password changed, you'll have to fill in a valid email address
so we can mail you a new password.

Also new to the Configure menu is the Import Progress button.  Your progress from previous versions
of N should have been automatically imported the first time you started N v1.4; however, in the event
that it didn't, or if you've played an older version since then, you can use this button to get 1.4
up to date. 

NOTE:  This button will not clear your current data, but will supplement it.

Also new, the password field has been changed so your password is not visible after you type it in. 
Note however, it may be more difficult to remember your password since you can no longer see it.  If you
do forget your password, enter your email in the email field and then send an email from that address to
metanet at harveycartel.org. 
Include your username and what you'd like your new password to be and we'll reset it for you.


And most excitingly, the flavour selection menu -- as you complete each column of episodes, you will
unlock a new flavour of ninja.  Impress your friends -- collect all 9!




-= IMPROVEMENTS TO NED =-

Ned has been updated from a beta version to official version 1.1.  There are some exciting new changes!

Ned now boasts added feature documentation, viewable gridlines, visually linked door and door trigger
objects, and the ability to copy and paste tiles.  No more tedious duplication of your favourite tiled
shapes or images, now Ned will do all the work!

Note that some of the editor controls have changed as well: holding [ctrl] now allows you to drag
the ragdoll around, and pressing [tab] enters boss mode.


For more information, please read the editor_manual.txt or editor_manual.doc included in your N
download, where everything is thoroughly documented. 





-= PRACTICE MODE =-

We've added a level skip cheat to practice mode -- now you can skip through the levels in
an episode by simply pressing [enter] before you begin a level.  This feature only works if practice
mode is turned on via the Configure menu.

Note that highscores/personal bests cannot be acquired when you're in practice mode, or for any
levels you've only beaten while cheating.



-------------------- Section Four: Tips and Gameplay ----------------------------


---------In General

For information on rules, how to play, etc., view the
In-game Help and Story sections (accessible from the main menu)
Check it out!  There are a lot of different moves to master.



---------Default Key Configuration

You can configure custom keys via the main menu.
The default keys are:

[left and right arrows]: accelerate left/right
[shift]: jump (hold key down for higher jump)

[k]: kill yourself (useful if you get stuck or trapped, or just for fun)
[p]: pause game/quit to main menu

[tab]: boss mode



---------Controlling the Ninja

Learning to control the ninja may take some time, but almost
any maneuver is possible given enough skill. And practice



---------Making Custom Levels

*** Read included files editor_manual.doc or editor_manual.txt to find out
how to make your own levels.




-------------------- Section Five: Custom Levels ------------------------------


Nick Johnson has created NUMA, the N User Map Archive:
http://numa.notdot.net/

You can download maps created by other N users, and upload maps of your own. 

You can also visit our forum for map contests, help and discussion:
http://metanet.forumer.com



-------------------- Section Six: Updates, News and More Information ------------


comments/bug reports/etc:
n at harveycartel dot org


updates and news about N can be found at:
http://www.harveycartel.org/metanet/


and at our forum:
http://metanet.forumer.com



Visit the forum for support with bugs and other issues!




enjoy!

So I've recently stumbled upon the Firefox Myths page, and uh....
...yeah.

That page led to, like, twenty others, where I also started reading tangential essays on why Open Source Software is horrendously insecure. I've done a disgusting amount of reading, and I've decided to switch over to Opera immediately.

I've been reading through sites that support Firefox just as much as those against Firefox, and the main difference is that the claims made by the sites against Firefox are actually substantiated, including by people within Mozilla.

Every chart, table, and graph, as well as countless testimonials, affirm that Opera mops the floor with Internet Explorer and Firefox.
The pro-Firefox sites say, "if you don't want to go with Firefox, at least go with Opera. It's like IE, but coded properly."
And the anti-Firefox sites say, "Go with the stable ol' Internet Explorer, or if you really want to be different, try Opera. It's like Firefox, but coded properly."

Anyway, I have also come out of this with drastically changed views of Microsoft, Linux, and OSS development communities.

Where I have once seen Firefox as the sleek, badass, snazzy, efficient, invaluably useful revolutionary browser, I now see a narcissistic, morbidly obese douchebag hobbling around with excessive amounts of electronic doodads and tools that he himself barely knows how to use, but won't stop showing people.

#269915 9 2006-12-14T06:18:27Z Tsukatu
Another thing to note is that for a static observer (using your spot of ground on the Earth as a frame of reference), looking at a car moving at 100 km/h passing a car moving at 80 km/h, you see that the car in front is moving at 100 km/h. But from the perspective of the car in the back, the car in front of it is moving at 20 km/h, and you're whizzing behind it at 80 km/h.

What happens when we remove the Earth as a reference point?
A spaceship cannot determine its own speed. If you're on a spaceship and you're looking out of a window, and another spaceship shoots by you, you have no way of telling whether the ship is whizzing by you while you're motionless, whether you're shooting by a motionless spaceship, or whether the both of you are shooting past each other.

The stomach is an excellent accelerometer, but a very poor speedometer.

Now, from this standpoint there can be two options. The first, which you have been arguing, is that God uses his omniscience to predict everything, eliminating free will. Alternately, God uses his omnipotence to grant free will. This could make it logically impossible to know the outcome of all decisions with 100% certainty, which gets around the omniscience bit. My first instinct was to respond with "...shut up."
But now that I think about it, what sort of free will does this give us when we can consider what it means for God to know what is knowable?
Things that we fallible humans can determine right now about matter and energy can be used to predict events in the split-second future very accurately. So if we say that it's possible for God to know the exact positions and energy states of fundamental particles as though we had tested found them extremely deliberately to the best of human efforts, and if we also say that God has an infinite memory and can perform instantaneous calculations of horrific amounts of data (and keep in mind that He does not actually make an effort to find this data, but knows it inherently simply because it's possible for us to determine it, even if with serious effort), then God can determine future states of matter and energy with ridiculous accuracy. Sure, it may not be 100% accuracy for all we know, and he may by pure chance miscalculate the action potential of a neuron by 1 electron-Volt every few thousand years.
Sure, this does mean that it may be possible (I'm retreating into agnosticism quite a lot these days ) that God cannot predict all events with 100% accuracy and that free will may therefore exist, but what sort of free will is it? It's a joke. Even if God decided to use his omnipotence to bar future events from being knowable, He still knows enough about the universe that it is entirely inconsequential. Just because He doesn't know the future by definition anymore doesn't mean He's unable to deduce it, especially considering that He allegedly created those natural laws of the universe to begin with.

(If my argument is getting shaky in terms of God's omnipotence how that applies to him interacting with time, it's because I'm extremely dissatisfied with the proposition that existing outside of time, creating universes, and declaring that certain information is forever barred from the realm of what is knowable is logically doable, and that logic even applies to a being outside of time.)

#270402 4 2006-12-15T03:18:30Z Tsukatu
How could it not be relative?

It is a custom in many indigenous tribes to honor their dead ancestors by eating them, in order to help their ancestors spirit live on inside them, and to gain their wisdom and guidance. We think that's horrifying and wrong, and they think it's one of the nicest things they can do for their ancestors, and not only think that it's right, but that there's also absolutely nothing wrong about it.

I like what Sigmund Freud says in Civilization and Its Dicontents.
I'll try to summarize it as best as I can:
The ego is our animalistic nature. If we were to act according to our ego, we'd be insensitive assholes, seeking only to satisfy our own natural needs and desires regardless of what that does to anyone else. We'd be stealing, killing, and raping. But what makes humans so different is that they have this superego, which serves basically as a conscience. It knows what is right and what is wrong, and then denies the ego.
How does the superego gain leverage over the ego? By taunting it with a human being's most desperate need: love. Every time the ego does something that would make it less loved (by an individual, by a community; anything that would make it disliked or lose approval), the superego is right there letting the ego know that, and the ego realizes that it wants acceptance more than it wants that candy bar. After all, it's much easier to associate with someone who doesn't take all of your stuff, right? Better to have a loyal friend than all of his stuff. And the fun part is, the superego can chastise the ego before it even acts - if the ego has the intention of doing something wrong, it is criticized just as severely as though it had actually performed the action.
So right is equated with what gets the person acceptance, and wrong is what makes people dislike him. But if the person has no sense of right and wrong to begin with, how should he be expected to learn it? The answer is the child's parents (or whoever raises the child). When the child is being raised, it needs constant love from its parents. Parents punish the child for doing something wrong by their standards, which conditions the child's superego to understand what would get him love from his parents, and what would lose it. So the parents' sense of right and wrong is more or less imprinted onto the child.
It does vary a little bit, because the child does go through that rebellious phase after the onslaught of hormones begins to mess with their thinking, and there are also minor adjustments made by peer interaction, but ultimately the right and wrong framework that the parents set will be passed to the child (especially because all of those peers the child is hanging out with likely have similar senses of right and wrong as they get from their parents anyway).
In this way, sense of right and wrong follows cultural development. Many cultures clash with regard to what they believe is right and wrong. That doesn't make particular cultures inherently evil.

One of the examples I like the most is geeky: a paladin fights for all that he believes is right; two paladins from two distinct cultures that have never met each other think that the other culture's practices are evil. The paladins Smite Evil each other - does it function?

Quote: Tsukatu, December 17 @  2006 05:16 pm
On this note, has anyone ever watched The Melancholy of Haruhi Suzumiya?
Never heard of it. What's it?
It's an obscure manga and anime about a psychotic high school girl who wants to meet aliens, ESP-ers, and time travelers, make friends with them, and have fun with them (as a child would; her intentions are strictly platonic). She starts up the "SOS Club," which means something in Japanese and is only phonetically translated into SOS, and essentially forces people into it.
She desperately tries to find paranormal stuff, and mysteries to solve, but everything always turns out mundane.
But here's the kicker - all of the "normal" people she forced into her club are just what she's looking for - there's an esper, an ultimately logical extraterrestrial, and an irresistably adorable time-traveler. All are very interested in Haruhi because they believe that she has subconscious godlike abilities, and they want to study her more.
The esper's ESP was awakened three years ago, along with hundreds of others, and they believe Haruhi may have caused something to effect that. The alien who quantifies every aspect of existence with streams of data was sent to observe Haruhi because Haruhi's data signiture is completely screwed up and constantly changing, and stuff changes around her constantly as well. The time traveler was sent to observe Haruhi because it was for some reason impossible to go farther back than three years in the past, before the day the espers were awakened and data streams started getting screwy.
The prevailing theory is that Haruhi created reality three years in the past, additionally creating memories for everyone who was supposed to be older. This theory mostly comes from the fact that time travel was impossible to any point before this alleged creation of reality.
Through the episodes, the characters in the club try to make life interesting for Haruhi, because they suspect that she will simply remake the world subconsciously again if she is insufficiently pleased. There's this whole realm of "closed space" in which massive monsters destroy things when Haruhi is displeased.
Much of it is pretty amusing, and there are copious quantities of fan service (no nudity).

#273302 49 2006-12-19T07:17:36Z Tsukatu
Quote: capt_weasle, December 18, 2006 10:43 pm
Even if it were possible, would be really even use it? With the "messing up time" thing and all. Think about it.

Say you wanted, for whatever reason, to eliminate Person B. So you create a time travel device to destroy him at an early age. You go back in time successfully, and kill him. But there's a problem with that. If you kill Person B, you never meet him while you yourself are living, therefore the motivation to eliminate Person B is non-existent. So if you don't meet B, you don't want to kill B, you don't have any reason to go back in time. So, then what? You don't make a time machine.

There's my two cents.

There's also the intriguing concept of near-instantaneous computer processors and network connections limited only by your processor speed.

Let's say we have a computer that can send information back in time.
You give the machine a calculation, like 1+1.
It notices that those are integers, and instead of going through the calculation process (,>,<[->+<]>. in Brainf*ck) it starts guessing numbers and then evaluates the answer.
Let's say the computer picks the number 1 to evaluate as the answer.
1+1 does not equal 1, so it sends the next number to guess, the number 2, back to itself before it did the calculation to begin with.
So the computer performs as though it started with 2.
The answer is confirmed, because 1+1 does equal 2. Because the answer is correct, the machine doesn't send anything back, and you have your answer.
In other words, as long as you have a machine that is capable of processing information in any amount of time, provided it can also send itself back that derived information over the same amount of time, then you get a computer that instantly generates an answer that is 100% guaranteed to be correct, and it takes almost no time at all, effectively regardless of the operation.
If mice were smart enough to get the time travel thing down, then their machine that figured out the answer to the big question wouldn't have taken so bloody long. Provided it was capable of finding the answer, it would have stated "42" immediately.

Same thing with an internet connection.
Let's say I want to download 25 GB of Christmas-themed Yufie/Tifa yuri, and all I have is a 28.8 Kbps connection. Provided that the download would theoretically remain active for the 85 days it would take me to download that content over such a connection, I will receive that 25 GB of animated girl-on-girl at a rate that is only limited my hard disk's frequency (7200 rpm on most of today's), even though I'm technically downloading it through my horrible connection, and even there is absolutely no traffic on my dial-up line; the only important thing is for the connection to be theoretically able to carry out that download.

Why is it that every time someone brings up time travel that everyone always jumps to killing? How 'bout time travel's effects on the world of computers?
