#277628 65 2006-12-27T08:34:06Z Tsukatu
*shakes head in disappointment*

Whatsisface got the fuse riddle correctly, though.

Troll riddle:
Row outwards in a spiral so that the troll, running to stay on the same side of the shore as you, is opposite of you through the center of the lake when you're 1/4 of the way out from the center. Then beeline to the shore.
You need to move (3/4)r before the troll runs (pi)r.
d = r * t
(3/4)r = x * t --> time it takes to get to the shore is 3(r/4x)
(pi)r = 4x * t --> time it takes to get to you before you get to the shore is (pi)(r/4x).
If you stick those in an inequality: (pi)(r/4x) > 3(r/4x)
The troll takes longer to get to the shore than you do; you can escape.

Manholes are round because other shapes have varying diagonals and can therefore fall easily. I think someone got this one, too, but I'm too lazy to read back in the thread.

Car companies design most locks so that you turn your hand clockwise to unlock the car. They basically assume that most drivers are right-handed (a good assumption to make).
Place your hand out as though you were holding a key and are about to unlock your key. Now turn your hand counter-clockwise and check out your range of motion - it's pretty much 90 degrees. Now turn your hand clockwise - you can easily turn it 180 degrees. Basically, with your right hand, it's easier to rotate a key clockwise than it is to turn it counter-clockwise.
Mindfuck.

Quote: Viridovix, 2007-01-05T14:34:28Z
Start teaching me more than what I know about science, about a religion that makes sense and I'll change my mind. I'd really rather not believe in science at this moment.
I can't teach you anything sensible about religion because religion is inherently unreasonable. Science is about studying the workings of the universe by working with what we can know, but religion loves to take facts far and between and to make these convoluted bridges between them, on top of making shocking amounts of assumptions.
Aquinas knew what he was talking about when he said that Christianity was supplementary to reason and could not actually be called reasonable. His idea that religion "perfects" reason was essentially stating that when we can't find what we want to find through empirical observations, we can always add arbitrary assumptions to it to turn it into religion and satisfy ourselves with the (likely false) knowledge we've attained.

Cookie example describing reasonable vs religious views of reality:
You're in a room with no windows, and only one door that has no handle on your side. The room is entirely sterile and white, and there is an ambient light that has no source. You're sitting in the middle, confused about where you are. The door opens. An elderly chinese man dressed in traditional chinese formal wear bounces happily in and hands you a fortune cookie. Then he bounces back out and seals the door. You weren't able to see anything through the door while it was open.
Let's say you tried thinking reasonably. There really isn't a whole lot to know: you don't know where you are, you think you're the same age and that you're in your right mind, you have all of your limbs, you're wearing the last shirt you remember putting on, there are no blood stains on you, no new bruises, no new tears in you clothing, and no part of your body is more sore than the rest. You can deduce that the chinese man had gained the trust of whoever built and managed this room, or that he was the one who built and managed this room, but you can't say you know anything about where you are or why the room exists. You don't know if the fortune cookie is poisoned or not, but you have little else you can do in this room before you suffocate or die of starvation, and so far eating the fortune cookie and seeing the message is the only course of action that has a chance of changing your current circumstances.
Now let's say you got that far thinking reasonably, but like most humans you're uncomfortable that your presence in the room has no meaning that you can find and that you don't know what's going on behind the scenes or what will happen to you. So we go on to add some aribitrary assumptions. Let's see, which arbitrary assumption would ease your troubled mind most? Oh, I know! Let's arbitrarily assume that the chinese man had been in your place before, now feels sorry for you, and is communicating to you his plans to let you escape from this wicked complex of blood and torture through the contents of the message in the fortune cookie!
See what I did there? I just gave you a purpose, an aribtrarily assigned "good" on your moral compass, and irrational hope that you'll escape from the room as well as the assumed friendship of some power who knows more and is capable of more than you are. There is absolutely no reason you should make that assumption, but you can invent more assumptions of all kinds to prove that that chinese man is looking to help you escape. But it all started with that one ridiculous assumption.
The chinese man bounces in again, this time holding a pair of merchant's scales.
If you were thinking rationally, you'd watch what he does, and try to get around him and out of the room if he does something that makes you significantly more uncomfortable.
If you were thinking religiously, you'd rise to your feet, grab the chinese man's shoulder, and proclaim, "I thank you, mysterious chinese man, for aiding me in my escape."
Maybe the chinese man is about to free you, maybe he's about to torture you, and maybe he's just insane, or otherwise doesn't have any intentions. But if you think religiously you've already blinded yourself to the other possibilities. If it turns out later on that the chinese man is setting himself in a good position to double-cross you and that there's an english gent who actually wants to help you get out, you'd stick by the chinese man and repel the english gent, all because you've made a ridiculous assumption, convinced yourself that it was true, and are not stubbornly sticking with it.

So if you want to be rational, stick with hard science. Watch out for this religious science nonsense, because they like to pack on additional assumptions that haven't actually been established in the scientific community.
If you were to watch What the Bleep Do We Know with some scientist's commentary, you'd hear things like:
WTBDWK: "Our current view of matter is very lacking and fails to explain many phenomena we witness in our lives."
Scientist: "That doesn't make our current view of matter entirely wrong. That just means we're still fine-tuning it."
WTBDWK: "So we propose a new view of matter."
Scientist: "I'm looking forward to seeing which journals he cites."
WTBDWK: "We propose that matter is shaped entirely by the consciousness."
Scientist: "There is no scientific basis for that proposal. You're going beyond what science currently knows about matter."
WTBDWK: "So when you exert your conscious influence upon matter, it changes to your whim."
Scientist: "This has never been documented in any scientific journal anywhere, ever. It has even, as a matter of fact, been denied through countless experiments over the years. Google 'James Randi.'"
WTBDWK: "In this way, we establish that we can all shape the universe, that we are all chained gods."
Scientist: "Are you ser- Is this guy serious? He just took the plain ol' assumption that matter is defined by our consciousness and totally ran with it. All this shows is that when you make a stupid assumption that you can make a whole lot of other nonsense seem true as well."

So it comes down to this: why is it important to act rationally?
The nihilistic side of me wants to say that it isn't important because it won't matter anyway.
But the LaVeyan Satanist in me, which doesn't care why we're here but is focused on making the most of the time we are here, says that acting rationally is the key to enjoying oneself the most in the pithy amount of time he has to exist. And I believe that, because that seems rational to me.

So my advice to you, Viridovix, oh, so obsessed with the reason of science, is to look critically at these "scientific" texts you're reading and start off doubting everything. If you're interested in some revolutionary idea stated, demand proof and don't stop searching for it until it is explicitly proven. This vibration/soul crap is entirely assumption. These people should have won $1 million from James Randi years ago.

#286319 14 2007-01-16T04:52:06Z Tsukatu
Quote: Obby, January 15, 2007 07:20 pm
Quote: Teedle, January 15, 2007 11:09 pm
Quote: Wiki
It teaches that self-control, fortitude and detachment from distracting emotions, sometimes interpreted as an indifference to pleasure or pain, allows one to become a clear thinker, level-headed and unbiased.
That doesn't mean to stifle ALL emotions and never let them exist. Detach yourself from the harmful ones and control the others.

Look critically at what you're saying - by "controlling" emotions, you're undoubtedly talking about ignoring them or otherwise acting as though they weren't there.
If a hobo yells an insult at you and you get angry, but "control" the emotion, what you're doing is ignoring it.
In the example Twistkill gave, "controlling" your emotions would be equivalent to laying down and dying. Suddenly this emotional fortitude means being a coward. And sure, it takes a lot of willpower to force yourself to live like a coward... in the same way that it takes a lot of willpower to walk around in the snow naked - why the hell would you do either?

You can try to rationalize it any way you want - you can call it control over your emotions or whatever - but it gives you the same benefits as pure & simple cowardice, and I doubt many observers would see it otherwise.

Stoicism means reducing yourself. You're combatting your most natural instincts and urges, and that has never been a good recipe for a happy and psychologically healthy life.

I do of course agree that the ability to control one's emotions is a good thing; being brash or overconfident can certainly get you in a good deal of trouble. But Stoicism is the pursuit of ultimate detachment from emotions. If it was something as mundane as being able to keep your head some of the time it wouldn't be a proper noun. Stoics are the sort who waste their lives in monasteries, pursuing some childish notion of what is "wise." Like that zen crap. Don't even get me started on zen.

So, again, I agree that the abillity to regulate your emotions is a good thing, but Stoicism takes it too far.

Quote: iangb, January 18, 2007 03:26 am
just as a thought... imagine you have an object with positive mass (m1), and an (impossible) object with an equal but negative mass (m2). The force between the two objects would be equal and opposite on each, as usual:
f = g(m1m2)/(r)
if m1 = -m2
f = -g(m1)/(r)

So the force on both m1 and m2 is negative. Now, imagine the effect which that force will have. f=ma so a=f/m, so...

for m1 (+ve mass)
a=f/m1 = -g(m1)/(r)

for m2 (-ve mass, = -m1)
a=f/m2 = -f/m1 = +g(m1)/(r)

So m1 will accelerate away from m2, but m2 will accelerate with equal magnitude towards m1. Wham, perpetual motion, energy from nothing, breaking ALL THE RULES. It makes my head hurt thinking about it.

EDIT: technically that situation isn't rule-breaking (possibly, it's a bit dodgy) because the sum of the system has zero mass, so the system has no centre of mass (or the system's centre of mass is simultaniously every point in the universe), so it isn't really moving, as such.
On the other hand, I'd hate to think about a situation where |m1|>|m2|.

theoretical physics ftw enjoy ur job waiting tables

#289258 83 2007-01-23T20:54:44Z Tsukatu
Quote: Bloodbath, January 23, 2007 12:03 pm
How do you make quotes look like everyone elses? (Name and date in brackets)

If you press the "Quote" button above someone's post, you will be taken to an Add Reply page with an extra textbox, which will contain the post you've quoted. All text in that second textbox will be formatted with the quoted user's name and the time his post was made. You can edit the text in that second textbox. Anything remaining in that second textbox when you click "Add Reply" to post your post will be at the top of your post.



If you want to do it manually:
[quote=name, time]Text being quoted.[/quote]
Just replace "name" and "time" with the name and time directly. The first comma character will be turned into a whitespace followed by '@'. So that text that I have above will look something like this:
Quote: name @ time
Text being quoted.

Quote: exuberance, January 25, 2007 04:08 pm
No, no no.

It's not binary logic. If you can't prove something false, it doesn't mean it's true- it means it could be either.

Whether something is true or false does not depend on whether you think it is true or not.

Right, but if you don't have any support for a statement that makes it false by default.
No sense letting it hang in the air.

This is, of course, only relevant to knowledge. You can still feel free to have faith that a particular statement is correct, such as the ever-popular "the God of the Bible exists." But because that has no evidence that we can link to Him, that statement is false by default - we cannot know that God exists. And most theists, because they are agnostic theists and believe that God cannot be known anyway, and that faith in Him is one of the strongest ties to Him, completely agree with this.
But that's venturing into belief without knowledge ("faith," it's called). When we're talking about an argument being false by default, we're just saying that we don't have enough information to know one way or the other.

#290359 59 2007-01-26T23:50:49Z Tsukatu
Quote: Trogdor007, January 26, 2007 01:35 pm
I believe he's using the term "Furry" to refer to a person's sexual preference of people in animal suits, and animal anim porn.  It's pretty synanimous with other forms of perversion.
Er... wow, no. That's a misconception.

A furry is a slang term (some might even consider it derogatory) that refers to someone who believes he has a strong connection with a particular animal. Some believe that they were that particular animal in a past life, some believe they have such an animal guardian, some believe they have a soul that is at least part that animal... the explanations for it are many, though all confoundingly arbitrary.
Furries feel most natural taking on personality quirks of that particular animal and like to think of their interactions with people in terms that such an animal, though intelligent, would think. Most furries also think of themselves as unique in this world of humans, and that the rest of humankind doesn't understand their connection with their animal.
(It's the same sort of desperation that would otherwise steer someone to religion, if you ask me.)
But furries are so well known because of the outspoken furries who write erotic fiction about animals. There are also plenty of artists who draw "furry porn," which depicts anthropomorphic animals. When referring to furries in artwork, furries are represented as these anthropomorphic animals.
Most furries are harmless and are very much content thinking to themselves that they have this special connection with an animal. But the more vocal and assertive ones are the ones who made furries infamous, what with their furry porn.

(On 4chan, posting furry porn anywhere outside /b/ is a bannable offense. Every Friday on /b/ is "Furry Friday," in which the furries like to spam the channel with furry porn. On an April Fool's Day a few years back, 4chan created the /fur/ channel, let users post what they would for that day, and on April 2nd they banned every IP that posted an image in /fur/. Furries refer to this day as "the Fursecution," and everyone else thinks it's hilarious.)

I have a natural hate for furries, which is of the same kind and intensity as the hate I naturally have for Scientologists and people who think they're vampires. But I have much less of a problem with furries in general because they're usually a more timid sort of people.

To be truly benevolent, you should act to help people in the most efficient manner possible as well as, and this is important, anonymously.
Here's the best way you could have handled the situation:
You see granny struggling with her groceries. The benevolent thing to do here is to help her get those groceries into the car to save her the work, and to do it quickly. So what you should have done was get out of the car and sprint up behind her. Make sure you try to run as quietly as possible, though without compromising your speed, so that she doesn't hear you and doesn't turn around to acknowledge you. This makes you anonymous. Now, were you in granny's shoes, you'd be mighty suspicious of some punk who sprinted up to you to help you with your groceries because most people aren't so benevolent. You ought to spare her the worry and the possible emotional stress to her poor old heart, and you also want to make sure she has no idea who you are (anonymity), so the benevolent thing to do in this case is to, just as you come sprinting up behind her, give her a powerful elbow smash to her occipital to knock her out cold. She'd probably be uncomfortable laying on the pavement until she wakes up, so you should get her into the driver's seat of her car. But wait, there's that kid in the back seat, and he might get a look at you so he can track you down and credit you for your benevolent actions! Can't have that! Before you move past the backseat window, grab a hard object and smash the glass, not hard enough to break it but definitely hard enough to make a sizeable crack through which it's impossible to distinguish your features. Put granny in the driver's seat, give her enough money to cover repairs on the car, close her door, load up her groceries, and head back to your car.

There! You've successfully helped an old lady load her groceries into her car, and done so anonymously! You've also given granny a well-deserved period of rest and zero net emotional stress and monetary worth.

I do this kind of stuff on a daily basis.
The next time you're in a similar situation, just ask yourself, "what would Tsukatu do?"

#294876 4 2007-02-07T23:20:48Z Tsukatu
Life has no meaning.
You guys aren't even answering the right question anyway; you're answering the question, "what is the best ideal life should pursue if it exists?"

I've said this in every "meaning/purpose of life" thread so far, and I'll say it again:
There is a tremendous difference between a purpose and a good idea.
"Procreate enough to maintain the existence of the species" is not a purpose, but a good idea.
"To show compassion to all other life" is not a purpose, but a good idea.
In order for there to be a purpose, there has to be something that set life into motion in order to accomplish a particular goal. So imagine a lifeless universe: this universe must have some sort of problem that some lifeless albeit thinking entity needed to solve, and so put created life in order to solve this problem or fulfill a particular purpose. Any purpose given to life that reflects back onto itself ("to treat all other life with respect") is not a valid purpose, for the same reason that an automaton that was created so that it could repair itself has no valid purpose - why make the automaton in the first place?

So if you're going to reply, I ask that you consider a purpose, and not something that's merely a good idea.

#295655 6 2007-02-10T03:35:22Z Tsukatu
Without an ultimate authority to dictate it, morality will come from social interaction.
In fact, all you need to develop morality is two people with a conflict of interests and some patience. If you bring together a cluster of people, you don't need to have word delivered from on high to develop "Grok no hit Thok if Thok no hit Grok."
In just about any "immoral" situation, at least one party comes away hurt and thinking that things need to be a little different. If the people acting immorally can see that and care that they don't get placed in a similar unfair situation, they'll treat people how they themselves want to be treated. Hey... that's the Golden Rule!
The Golden Rule is entirely instinctual to anything with even rudimentary emotion. Morality will come from interaction, and the only circumstance in which threat of eternal torture as a deterrent is necessary is when the parents are too afraid to hit their kid when the little bastard is out of line.

Naturally, different cultures will develop different specifics of their morality based on the intelligence and emotional sensitivity of the community's members, which God knows allows for some serious variation in those cultures' outlooks on morality, but they will all have the same foundation - the Golden Rule.

If you're thinking of an atheistic society, imagine a typical indigenous culture that has never been exposed to any mainstream religion and has only thought of tree spirits and animal spirits in passing. How many of those men, do you think, can bring themselves to just take a woman from that community and rape her, or to kill another member of that tribe for whatever reason?
And even the tribes with their own collection of ancestors and beliefs about nature spirits - they invented them, right? Was there a messiah who came down and had to tell them to be nice to each other? Their animism wouldn't exist if they hadn't stayed together and did their part for their community, and neither would they. They got together at some point, and they stayed alive because the Golden Rule is instinctual.

I feel like I'm rambling. Am I rambling?

Quote: macaddict, 2007-02-15T21:39:29Z
Then how is an atheist different from an agnostic?

A person either believes in God or does not. If they do, they are not an atheist. Of those who do not believe, there are those who are convinced that there is no God, and those who are not sure or too young to understand. The former you'd call an "Antitheist", and the latter an "Agnostic". Where does "Atheist" fit in? I still think it better to throw out the term "Antitheist" and replace with "Atheist" even if the word roots don't technically fit with it.

Could you name me one person who is an Atheist who isn't either an Agnostic or an Antitheist?
WOW.
Have you seriously never read my multiple rants about this? If there was ever evidence that you plumb ignore content in people's posts, this has to be it.

Concise version of the rant:

Agnosticism deals with what you know.
Atheism deals with what you believe.

(I'm going to refer to the opposite of agnosticism as gnosticism for practicality. Note that I am not refering to the Christian sect when I say "gnostic," and am merely refering to someone who claims to have knowledge of the divine.)

Atheism and agnosticism have little to nothing in common. They're two different descriptors. In the same way that a ball can be both blue and bouncy, someone can be both agnostic and an atheist.

The full set of possible claims:
You can believe because you know (gnostic theism).
You can believe even though you don't know; you can have faith, which is belief despite lack of knowledge (agnostic theism).
You can disbelieve because you don't know enough (agnostic atheism).
You can refuse to believe because you know better (gnostic atheism).

Most Christians are agnostic theists, in that they don't claim to have any knowledge or proof of God's existence, but they also don't need it; they have faith. This category also includes Deists.
Other Christians are typically gnostic theists. These are the people who claim to have been spoken to or otherwise influenced by God directly, or think that God's existence can be proven.
Most atheists are agnostic atheists; they deny the theist's claim because of insufficient proof. They don't claim to know that God doesn't exist, only that it hasn't been or can't be proven. This category includes iangb and Atilla.
Other atheists are gnostic atheists, also known as antitheists, who refuse to believe the theist's claim because he rationalizes that anything supernatural is a bunch of baloney, and thereby denounces and derides all claims to the existence of divine things. This category describes me.

Agnostic atheists and gnostic atheists are also called implicit atheists and explicit atheists, respectively. I prefer these two terms because I happen to like Kablizzy's version of antitheism, which is essentially the belief that there may be something out there but that no one has it right so far (so it's a form of agnostic atheism).

There is no "dividing line" or "other" category. You are either an atheist or a theist; you are either an agnostic or a gnostic. If you are ignorant of the subject entirely, you're an agnostic atheist. If you have no idea where you stand (read: if you're retarded), then it comes down to practice: do you actively acknowledge or worship anything divine? If so, you're a theist; if not, you're an atheist. If you sometimes believe and sometimes don't, you're just an idiot plain and simple and don't have the mental capacity to understand the question, which makes you an agnostic atheist by default.
(A stone is also an agnostic atheist, for reference.)

When you ask someone if he is religious and he tells you he is an agnostic, he's not actually answering the right question.
("What is your name?" "May 2nd, 1988.")
It's a correct answer, but not the answer you were looking for. Then again, when most people say they're agnostic they really mean they're agnostic atheists. But that's a human error entirely, and not a problem with the terminology.

$5 says macaddict ignores this outright and continues asking the question or professing inexcusable ignorance on the matter.

For example, I was at work about to leave for the day when one of my coworkers at the customer service desk pointed to a lady and asked if I could help her out before I leave because she had been waiting there for a while. So I go around the desk and ask if I could help her. The first thing she says is that I'm very nice but that my coworker working behind the service desk made her want to cry when she said "can you help that lady." She talked about being mistreated and what she would do were she the manager for about ten minutes as I nodded politely and feigned interest in her monologue. When I finally found a spot to tactfully ask why she came to the store, she presented a fax machine that had a missing cartridge. Then she went on to talk about this car accident she was in, her resulting coma, the doctors' attitudes, the deaths of every member of her family, her trouble in buying the car in which she had the accident, the attitudes in general of people driving winnebagos, spiritual "energy balance crap," her time in medical school, her time spent with patients as a psychiatrist... the lady would not stop talking for another 45 minutes. She was sensitive enough a person that I needed a particularly appropriate spot to bring up the reason she was there, so I spent the whole time with a plastic smile, feigned interest, and feigned sympathy. Quote: Tsukatu
Theism means, basically, "belief, with or without warranted reason, in a supernatural and/or transcendent being."
Atheism means, basically, "anything that's not theism."
Theism is religion; atheism is not a religion, but is the lack thereof.

Atheism is not the assertion to the opposite of theism.
That is, the atheist's claim is, "I do not believe X."
And the atheist's claim is not, "I believe that not X."
The atheist is not carrying out any belief. His atheism does not give him any positive assertions. It merely says that he denies a popular assertion, though not that he believes it to be false.
Another way of putting it: atheists are not convinced that theism is true, but atheism does not say of someone that he believes theism to be false.
This is a crucial distinction.

This makes atheism an "other" category. Some atheists leave it at that and say that they won't believe until they see enough evidence, some atheists develop their own silly notion of universal balance and principles, and some atheists positively assert that the theist's claim is false. The latter is by no means descriptive of all atheists; the only thing atheists have in common is that they are not theists, and that's it. They're free to differ radically from each other in every other aspect.

"Calling atheism a religion is like calling 'bald' a hair color." -Don Hirschberg

#299476 57 2007-02-21T04:50:50Z Tsukatu
Oh, wow, I haven't made the finale post yet?

I finished off my pack two days ago. I had three cigarettes left in the pack, two of which were crumbled enough that they only had half of the normal amount of tobacco in them, so I smoked them all in one last go.

As I progressed through the pack, I developed a stronger desire to just throw the pack away and call it quits, but I forced myself to go through the whole pack... for the experience, goddamnit! (Consequently, I did level up.) The more I did it, the more I hated the thought, the action, and the feeling of sucking that carcinogen-laden carbon monoxide down my esophagus. Sometime in the middle of the pack, I was forgetting entirely that I was doing irreparable harm to my lungs and heart, and my mind was focused on whether or not I thought I could get used to the habit and how the hell people managed to smoke an entire pack a day.
On the day I smoked the last few, I realized I hadn't smoked at all for the last few days and that I should probably finish off. I was staring up at the isolated fire escape stairs I would climb to have a smoke and I was saying to myself, "I don't want to do this. I really, really don't want to do this." I eventually figured that I might as well sprint to the finish and get it all over with.

It just wasn't rewarding. The first nicotine high was pretty fun, I guess, but it was very short-lived and made me feel uncoordinated and dizzy besides. The con's were innumerable. I hated the thought, I hated the feeling of breathing in that thick smoke, and of exhaling it, I hated the taste it left in my mouth, I hated the strong smell it burned into my clothing, I hated having to avoid people who knew me on the way back to my dorm... combine all of those with a generally nauseous feeling every time I lit up, regardless of how many I ended up smoking, and a restless/unfocused mental state I couldn't help after I came back to my dorm.

There were way too many downsides to smoking that would convince me that it's hella not worth it, even if I found any pleasure from the "benefits" it gives.

Though I'm now mildly interested in trying a menthol cigarette, chain smoking, and smoking a cigar, there is no fucking way I'm buying another entire pack or smoking an entire cigar. If I do end up trying either, it'll probably be at a party where someone already has either. And after I know what that's like, I sincerely doubt I'll put that stuff in my body ever again.

So all in all, for me, smoking has been very much like punching myself in the face: intentionally harming myself for absolutely no good reason.
If you don't smoke, don't start.
If you do smoke, well, I just don't get you.

So I spotted some windshield wiper fluid at Staples on clearance for $2.90, and couldn't resist. The label said it was very flammable and that breathing it in could blind or kill you. This was too much potential fun to resist. So I bought a gallon of the stuff as well as a package of matchbooks.

I purchased a preposterous amount of energy drinks, downed four, and proceeded to wander about looking for a shallow spot to ford my ox a dark, isolated area where I could feel free to light several fires without been noticed, at 2:00 AM.

It turned out that the windshield wiper fluid really wasn't that flammable at all. I actually wasn't very surprised, just hoping to be pleasantly surprised. I did manage to get a few very small alcohol fires going, but they were very short lived, and the pictures I have of them are blurry. It wasn't very exciting.

So I decided to go buy some lighter fluid.

After toying with ideas as to what designs I could make out of the matchbooks, I ended up going with this:
[Picture]
[Picture]
[Picture]
...if you still can't tell what that is, here's a better view.

It actually looked kinda nifty as it was dying down.

It was only after I had charred a pentagram onto the pavement that I realized how totally sketchy my surroundings were. I was inspired to take pictures:
[Perspective 1] / [Perspective 1 with comments]
[Perspective 2] / [Perspective 2 with comments]

(Oh, and consequently, I haven't slept for more than thirty hours, and I feel absolutely fine. This stuff is like crystal meth, but without the psychotic episodes and nerve damage.)
#14297 1 2007-03-05T08:14:35Z Tsukatu
Here's a letter I just sent to my College of Engineering advisors:

I don't think Biomed is my thing. I don't think Pre-Med is my thing.
My decision to major in Biomedical Engineering and to declare myself Pre-Medical feels more and more like a decision I forced upon myself because I like the thought of being a doctor. Who am I kidding, I just want the title without having to go through the work. I don't have any interest in biology or helping people, and my interest in artificially improving the human body is borderline fantasy. Even if I did force myself to work at a field that doesn't interest me, I'd only be doing it for the money, and that simply wouldn't be fulfilling.
Despite my constant efforts to delude myself otherwise, or give myself excuses to keep me focused on biomedical engineering, my behaviour throughout my first year at BU speaks volumes of undeniable truth:
I routinely skip Chemistry and Physics lectures, making myself promises that I'll go to subsequent ones to make up for it, and I know that I'll never keep these promises. I've been slacking off like crazy on Chemistry and Physics homework, saying to myself on each assignment that it's only one assignment out of many, and that one 0 on a homework isn't going to matter. I keep telling myself that I'll study before tests, and never end up doing it, getting by with high 60's and low 70's purely on my raw analytical talent. I'm genuinely worried that I will fail both this semester, and even more worried that I can't bring myself to do anything to ensure that doesn't happen. I don't think about Chemistry, Physics, or Biology in my spare time, and I'm not interested in reading news about advances in either. I'm not even amused by related humor.
Now let's talk about EK 127. [Metanet: This is the class on how to use MATLAB. It's basically a programming class.]
I've been to pretty much every lecture class, and am very disappointed with myself when I accidentally sleep through my alarm and miss one. I've never doodled in class or zoned out because my focus has always been on creative ways I can implement new functions that are taught. I'm enthusiastic about showing off what I know, and I'm driven to be at the top of that class. I finish homework far ahead of time and finish the projects in a flash, and continue to rewrite and redo the project to boast my understanding of the subject matter. Where I'm bored by my CH102 classmates' inability to understand units, I feel truly on top of the world every time I effortlessly implement a newly taught concept in a matter of minutes and see my classmates struggle for days to understand it.
I feel like a prodigy. I truly feel that I'm in my element.
But even more importantly, I do computer science related stuff in my spare time, and even instead of doing anything that relates to other sciences. I take breaks from learning about acid/base and redox reactions by learning some more PERL, or by getting lost in some Wikibook about networking protocol. Every other online bookmark I've made has to do with programming humor, Linux development, news about PC hardware manufacturers, and operating system exploits.
But I stick with the Biomed and the Pre-Med because I'm used to dominating at whatever I do, and because it's obvious that Biomedical Engineering is going to be way of the future. So I see my current major as the clearest path toward being a powerful, useful figure in the future. My pipe dream is to start my own biotech company. I don't even know why I still consider that motivation to stick with Biomed; it's never going to happen. With my study habits and complete lack of interest, I'd crash and burn a year or two into medical school, assuming that I receive the divine intervention I'd require to even get in.
I realize that I've been shrinking from Computer Science because the only future I could see for it was being a nameless codemonkey for a huge software company. In other words, the only product I saw of such a major was the life of a total loser, a failure. But I don't know, I've come to see things differently. My partially nihilistic outlook on life tells me that living what pointless life I do have by working my ass off and not enjoying it isn't nearly as worth it as adopting a more modest profession and actually enjoying life. I don't have to be the CEO of the most powerful biotech company in the world to be happy. That title sounds very impressive, but it also sounds like a hell of a lot of work that I am plainly disinterested in doing. Yeah, it'd benefit humanity, but I don't think humanity deserves what I could do for it if I devoted my life to those ends. I tend to simply hate people, in general.
Haha. I wonder how all of this would do as an admissions essay. Please don't boot me out of BU because of this. Haha.
And I'm sorry if I'm not making much sense; I have about six bottles of concentrated energy drink in me and haven't slept for three days.
And y'know what's also bugging me? The crowds I meet through my major. My classmates annoy me. I've met loads of people already, but I'm not interested in being their friend. They like to drink and party, and that's simply not the sort of person I am, and not the sort of person I like being around. To fill that portion of my life, I've only branched further into the online communities I'm a part of. As a result, I'm friends with a bunch of total nerds, and I wouldn't have it any other way. I just can't seem to find that sort of culture with the people in my classes and study groups. Every time I bring up the sort of thing that interests me, I observe how quickly the subject gets changed, and then see how long I can tolerate the mindless chatter before I explain that no, thanks, I don't want to come with you guys and smoke some weed, but thanks for the invitation and I'll see you guys around... and then I pack up my stuff and leave. But I'm confident that I'll find the sort of crowd I'm looking for with a Computer Science or Computer Systems Engineering major.
Now that I think about it... of every meal I've eaten in the dining hall (and I eat twice a day on my plan), I think about three of them actually had another human being sitting at my table with me. I've met loads of people... I just can't connect with any of them. And I've tried. I guess I don't know that it isn't something wrong with me, though. But still, I had loads of close friendships in high school and a very active social life. I am of strong character, I'm charismatic... I can be a social butterfly when I care to be, and I'm very, very pretty... so what the hell? I just want to meet someone I can relate to.
I don't know. Maybe I just need therapy, or Ritalin or something. It just feels like I've discovered that I'm on the wrong road in life, like something is just... wrong, and I can see what is right for me but for some reason push myself away from it.
I intended this email to be a declaration that I want to switch my major, but I think I should think about it a bit more before I do anything like that. Either way, I would really, really appreciate any input you could provide. I'm sure you've seen cases like mine fairly often.
And now I need to finish up a Chem lab in the next five hours. Sleep is for the weak.

Sorry for writing you a novel.
And thanks for reading. It means a lot to me.

-[my name]
[My BU ID]

#303290 12 2007-03-07T19:33:46Z Tsukatu
macaddict,

You are very, very mistaken.
You attribute to atheists beliefs that you have seen in atheists you have argued with. Not surprisingly, these atheists appear to have believed firmly in science. But this does not mean that you should consider these beliefs to be part of their atheism.

This is the wrong way to look at an atheist:
"He is an atheist. Therefore, he does not believe what is suggested by the theists, and he believes in science."
This is the right way to look at an atheist:
"He is an atheist. Therefore, he does not believe what is suggested by the theists."

Again, the term "atheism" is entirely negative in its nature. It does nothing but say that it is not theism. This means that it does not say a thing about science. Many atheists are free to believe in science, and they are just as free to disbelieve it.
Atheism is not a positive assertion; it is denial; it cannot possibly even imply that the atheist believes in anything.

When determining whether "atheist" is the proper term, you should be asking the question, "does it believe in the divine?" There are no other qualifying conditions for something to be an atheist!!
When you look at me and ask, "does Tsukatu believe in the divine," the answer you get is "no," and therefore I'm an atheist.
When you look at a cat and ask, "does this cat believe in the divine," the answer you get is "no," and therefore the cat is an atheist.
When you look at a boulder and ask, "does this boulder believe in the divine," the answer you get is "no," and therefore the boulder is an atheist.
When you look at the color purple and ask, "does purple believe in the divine," the answer you get is "no," and therefore the color purple is an atheist.

Many atheists believe in science.
Many atheists also don't believe in science.
Many atheists simply don't care, and ignore science.
Many atheists are not capable of intelligent thought.

Saying that someone doesn't have belief doesn't mean they have to have a belief in something else.
So just because I don't believe in your Intelligent Design theory, does not mean I have to believe any other theory. I could sit back and think every attempt at explaining our origins is a miserable failure. I could believe in my own, unscientific, convoluted origins story. I am free to do all of these things because atheism does not carry any positive beliefs about anything divine or anything having to do with matters of ultimate concern, such as the origin or meaning of life.

Quote: macaddict, 2007-03-07T15:45:22Z
The only origins story that fits an atheistic worldview is evolution
No, what you're saying is that the only reasonable origins story that fits an atheistic worldview is evolution. In case you weren't aware, people are free to believe their own silly, irrational things.

All you've said is that the most rational thing an atheist can believe is evolution, but this does not make it part of atheism at all.
I can say that the most rational thing to do for an adolescent blonde girl growing up in America is to dye her hair black, and I may be absolutely correct in that, but that does not mean that every blonde girl wants to dye her hair black or that all are planning on it.
Do you see how we can say that something is the most rational consequence, but still have that consequence be independent entirely from the initial thing?

Continuing the blonde girl example:
By including belief in science in the definition of an atheist, you're effectively defining a blonde girl as "someone with a light natural hair color who has dyed her hair black, or is planning to." This is not a blonde! #303297 7 2007-03-07T20:32:59Z Tsukatu
I hate to start off another post in your thread with "I feel exactly the same way" because that often serves to devalue the issue, but...
I feel exactly the same way.

I'm finishing up my first year in college right now, in a friggin' huge school (Boston University), and I don't really have anybody I can call a friend. Of the times I've eaten in the dining hall (twice a day, throughout the entire year), no more than three of those meals actually had someone else sitting at the table. The only person I really talk to is my roommate, and that's only the case because he's there when I'm visibly agitated or amused; if we were to meet in any other circumstance, I highly doubt that we would hit it off well.
And I'm not antisocial. I'm pretty strongly extroverted, I'm clever, I'm funny, I'm attractive, I'm charismatic... If I'm having a simple chat with someone, there is next to no chance that I come off as anything short of charming, delightful, and generally awesome.
That said, why am I so alone?
In classes and such, when I'm within hearing and speaking distance but not involved in an open conversation, I'm usually pretty good at joining it and leaving a good impression. People have very much enjoyed talking with me... but they tend to be isolated incidents, and I hardly ever get invited to anywhere. (In fact, the only times I have been invited somewhere were by less-than-desirable girls who liked me because I'm pretty, and who knew little more about me. I don't take well to that.)

I think, actually, that this is a result of my preference to surprise people. I love blowing people away. I find that makes for some more powerful first impressions. So when I'm new somewhere, I like to stay in the background and then completely take the spotlight from out-of-fucking-nowhere. I don't talk that much in class, and end up coming up with most or all of the brightest ideas when the class is broken into groups for discussion. I hold back during practices when I'm fencing, and when we actually start having official bouts with the rest of the class watching... the first time it happened, I skunked the guy everyone else in the class was afraid of, 5-0, and then beat the next guy, 5-2, before I was cycled out again.
So I think my problem is that I have this fantasy of being "discovered" by the right people, and I turn out to completely surprise them, and that makes for an excellent friendship. And it isn't working because it's a much larger population, and people don't so readily notice the quiet guy and wonder why they haven't talked to him yet. I need to find some way of being more intrinsically interesting.

So anyway, it looks like you're just not branching out fully, just like I'm not. Sure, we do make the effort to join conversations here and there or make small talk with people at school or work, but that's not really giving it your all, is it?
We're also both kind of weird. I won't challenge you for the title, but I do have a very convoluted sense of humor and odd demeanor that tends to clash with common folk after they get to know me. And that holds me back from branching out so much because I hate disappointing people - the goal is to be a pleasant surprise, after all. I like to think that I'm generally good at reading people when I talk to them face-to-face... heck, I'm very good at telling someone's demeanor, how that someone will talk, their intelligence, and how easy it will be to get along with him, all by observing a simple exchange of words they have with someone else... and it's a lot easier if I'm the one they're exchanging words with... so I can pretty much tell after meeting someone whether or not we'd get along. Unfortunately, that turns to be most people. I can still get along with them well if I stifle my quirkiness, but I hate having to do that.

And my roommate is a douchebag, so I have to leave it at this for now.

#304471 16 2007-03-11T19:11:07Z Tsukatu
Demonz,

There was nothing wrong or incorrect about what you said, but I can understand why Obby would get frustrated with the discussion.

Refusing to get off the solipsism track forks any discussion into a dead end, and that's never productive (not that arguing online is productive anyway).

Compare the two following conversations:

A: I'm going to prove to you that God must exist.
B: I'd love to see you try.
A: First off, the universe exists. It is here now in its present state.
B: Actually, we can't know that for certain. The universe is only experienced through human sensation, and our human senses are imperfect. Even our thoughts aren't perfect, so even if our senses were objectively accurate, we could still be processing those senses incorrectly.
A: ...
B: What? It's true!
A: Alright, how about we look at it this way: you exist, even if I don't, and even if the rest of the universe doesn't. Not your body, not even necessarily your senses, but your consciousness exists.
B: The problem here is that this makes sense within my fallible human rationale, which by no means is perfect. So you could go on arguing something that sounds reasonable, but I am certainly prone to misunderstanding, being deceived, and plainly irrational thinking.
A: ...
B: It's true!
A: There is no point continuing this. You need to make the assumption that the way we perceive reality is faithful to what is real before we can gain any ground in this discussion.


A: I'm going to prove to you that 2 + 2 is equal to 4.
B: I'd love to see you try.
A: First off, we can see that 2 is really just twice the number 1, or two individual units.
B: Actually, we can't know that for certain. Mathematics is, after all, an invention of fallible humans, and there could easily be some glaring error in mathematics that we haven't discovered yet that makes even statements like 1 + 1 = 2 defunct.
A: ...
B: What? It's true!
A: Alright, how about we look at it this way: there is a dot, and then there is another dot. This is the total number of dots you have on one side. We're going to do this by counting.
B: The problem here is that you're going to be forced at one point to represent the situation with mathematical terms. Your entire argument is futile because it is based on something that is impossible to prove infallible - mathematics.
A: ...
B: It's true!
A: There is no point continuing this. You need to accept the fundamentals of mathematics as axioms before we can gain any ground in this discussion.

#305275 132 2007-03-14T23:37:32Z Tsukatu
Quote: bonzai, 2007-03-14T19:37:04Z
I think that purpose in this context means the reason for which something exists.
This is a legitimate definition of purpose, and is the same one I use.

Quote: bonzai, 2007-03-14T19:37:04Z
I feel like I've stated a reasonable hypothesis for a purpose but you keep telling me it's a good idea.
The hypothesis you made does not qualify as purpose under our definition of purpose.

If something is said to exist for a reason, it is put into existence by a creator in order to fulfill a particular task.
Let's use artificial intelligence as an example.
Humans create an artificially intelligent robot for construction work.
Is assisting in construction a good idea or a purpose for the robot? It is a purpose because humans have created the robot to achieve a particular goal, and the robot exists as a means of attaining that goal.
The robot, because it is artificially intelligent and has its own personality, takes a liking to training puppies.
Is training puppies a good idea or a purpose for the robot? It is a good idea because it has nothing to do with the robot's creators' intentions or the goal they wanted to work toward by building the robot as a means of attaining that goal; humans did not create the robot to train puppies, but to assist in construction.

Now let's take a society of these robots.
Humans have no plan for them other than constructing a skyscraper.
The robots, because they are artificially intelligent and have their own personalities, decide that they would like to be compassionate toward one another.
Constructing the skyscraper is the robots' purpose, because that is the reason they were built. Being compassionate toward one another has nothing to do with their creators' goals; being compassionate toward one another was an idea generated by the robots entirely; being compassionate toward one another is not the robots' purpose, but a good idea for the robots.
The robots also get the idea that, while they exist, they may as well pursue the full range of joyous and depressing experiences to enrich their existence. This is still not a purpose for the robots, but a good idea, because the robots' creators did not make the robots so they could enjoy the full range of joyous and depressing experiences, but to build a goddamned skyscraper. The robots' decision to pursue the full range of joyous and depressing experiences to enrich their existence is therefore not a purpose, but a good idea.

Now imagine this scenario:
Aliens with such an advanced understanding of the universe that we could not begin to fathom predict that their planet will collide with another planet far, far in the future. Rather than putting resources into avoiding the collision, they take advantage of the fact that a little planet, one we know as Earth, is directly along the collision course. So they send an expedition to Earth and create a destructive and arrogant but nevertheless clever creature called a human. They let humans develop for the most part, but occassionally help them along from the shadows, knowing that when the humans realize that another planet is going to hit them that the humans will collaborate on a means of destroying that planet, thereby also saving the aliens.
The humans on Earth, as they grow, decide that they should be compassionate toward one another and that they should make the most of their lives by experiencing the full range of life's joys and pitfalls. But neither their compassion toward one another nor their desire to fully experience life are purpose, but good ideas, because they have nothing to do with the reason humans exist. The humans' purpose is to save the aliens, knowingly or otherwise, from the planet rocketing toward them.

As you can see, there needs to be a goal in mind if we're talking about purpose, and if we have a purpose then we are the means of attaining that goal. Being nice to one another and experiencing the joys and pitfalls of life are ideas we've developed on our own.

I'm sick of typing.

In the same way that the statement, "he's not fat; he's diabetic," is not quite right (because diabetes tends to be the thing that makes diabetics fat), saying that "he's not a selfish coward; he's depressed" is also not quite right because it's the depression that makes him a selfish coward. A healthy person would care that he's being selfish and a coward, but someone heavily depressed tends to have a defeatist attitude and continues crashing and burning.

Suicide is a cowardly and selfish action to take. A healthy person, even if he sees reason to commit suicide, can be held back by his conscience. But someone who is depressed (which is unhealthy, clearly), even if he does think about it as being a selfish coward, will likely not give a rat's ass because he sees the world collapsing around him.
I'm pretty sure I've never been seriously depressed, but I've certainly been in that position where I stop caring about the morality of my actions and how I appear to people. I've had that defeatist attitude before. And I've always had it when I have been depressed. I don't think I'm incorrect to think that people who suffer from chronic depression tend to have this sort of defeatist attitude as well - letting themselves go in terms of what they eat, how much they spend, how many classes they attend, which test scores they're satisfied with...

You want to know the most wonderful thing about LaVeyan Satanism, Obby?
It doesn't actually introduce a new way of living your life that you need to internalize and work on upkeeping as much as it describes what humans do naturally. And one of the most amusing things to a Satanist who likes people-watching is noticing that people can claim to follow different moral codes but follow the most natural one (which Satanism describes) regardless.

In this case, we're talking about the Golden Rule.
Think about this carefully, Obby: how many times have you really turned the other cheek?
Here's an example that immediately comes to mind: I've seen you talk about how you beat up some punks who were tormenting a disadvantaged kid (and you got suspended for it). If you had treated those kids as you wanted to be treated, you would've approached them peacefully, or not approached them at all, because you don't want to be attacked. But you attacked them - you gave those bastards what they had coming to them. That was the most natural thing for you to want to do; it was psychologically satisfying, wasn't it? Much more so than it would have been had you followed Christ's teachings. Christ doesn't teach "an eye for an eye," does he?
But no, when you saw those bastards beating up on the disadvantaged kid, you weren't thinking about your Christian morals, but you acted on instinct. Turns out, you felt confident in retrospect that that was the right thing to do. So did I. I applauded you for it. Some ninnies started spouting their hippie peace nonsense, but you were satisfied in your un-Christian decision.

The Golden Rule as you know it allows people to tramp all over you. They can keep taking advantage of you, but if you adhere to the Golden Rule you will only be treating them with more undeserved kindness. And if you expect everyone around you to follow the Golden Rule, then you can't really hope that someone will come to your aid, either, could you? Bastards would rule the world (which I suppose is why Christianity was invented in the first place, right? Controlling the gullible? Making the people submissive?)
But the improved version goes hand in hand with another principle - instead of Christ's "turn the other cheek" nonsense: "if someone smites thee on one cheek, SMASH him on his other" - and lets you stand up for yourself and let an oppressor know that you aren't someone to mess with. Once you demonstrate that it's a bad idea to be on your bad side, they can see that it's a good idea to be on your good side.

The fact is that the world today follows this improved Golden Rule, even while they claim to adhere to the original and to Christ's "turn the other cheek" rubbish. But people are vengeful ("righteous," as you'd probably call it). People believe in justice. People are fined and incarcerated for being mean to each other.

Stop being so idealistic and take a look at how you actually act, and how that has worked out for you.
Think of the situations in which you gave people what they deserved, and think of how useless the common Golden Rule would have been, and how much more suffering to you and to those around you it would have brought.
Think about it.

Quote: apg, 2007-03-24T12:18:34Z
When do you use its'?
That word does not exist.
(It's technically a possessive of a possessive, so it makes about as much sense as "my's.")
The English language has the words "it's" and "its."
"It's" is used as a contraction of "it is." You would use "it's" any time you would normally say "it is."
(e.g. "it's raining" or "it's done.")
"Its" is used as a possessive pronoun. It shows that the noun following is owned by "it."
(e.g. "I crushed its puny skull.")
But there is no word "its'."

#307830 22 2007-03-26T04:34:45Z Tsukatu
I kind of want to split the topic, but I kind of don't want to dig through every post that involves the definition of atheism.
So for now:

I've fought the dictionary war before, macaddict. You can find an incorrect definition of atheism for every correct definition of atheism. Most dictionaries have multiple definitions, some that are right and some that aren't. Dictionaries are unreliable, and have made me consider starting an organization that contacts dictionary companies and informs them to use the proper definition.

Either way, this is a way I've recently come across that does well to explain the meaning of atheism (thanks to a man named XOmniverse):
Let's take a look at the word "moral."
"Moral" means "having a behavioral code that encourages good actions."
There's also the word "amoral," which is a- (not) moral (moral), or "not" + "having a behavioral code that encourages good actions" = "not having a behavioral code that encourages good actions."
BUT, there is also the word "immoral," which is im- (against) moral (moral), and it means "having a behavioral code to the opposite effect of morality," or "having a behavioral code that encourages bad actions."
So we have the a- prefix which tells us that something is not something else, and we have the im- prefix which tells us that something is against something else.
So let's look at "theism" again.
Where "moral" means "having a behavioral code that encourages good actions," "theism" means "having belief that the divine exists."
We attached the a- prefix to turn "moral" into "amoral" - "not having a behavioral code that encourages good actions," or "lacking in a behavioral code that encourages good actions." In the same way, we can attach the a- prefix to "theism" to make it "atheism," which means "not having the belief that the divine exists," or "lacking in the belief that the divine exists."
We attached the im- prefix to turn "moral" into "immoral," which means "having a behavioral code to the opposite of morality," or "having a behavioral code that encourages bad actions." In the same way, we can add the im- prefix to theism to get "imtheism" (if such a word exists), which would mean "having belief to the opposite of theism," or "having belief that the divine does not exist."

Your definition of atheism is the definition for the theoretical word "imtheism." If you know the distinction between "amoral" and "immoral," you should see the distinction between my definition of atheism and your definition of atheism pretty clearly.
"Antitheism" is slang, and I never claimed that it was anything more. I have in fact even taken the time to mention every so often that it is slang. Either way, its prefix, anti-, has the same meaning as the prefix im-, which means "against." So "antitheism" describes beautifully the same concept as the theoretical word "imtheism," and it means "having belief to the opposite of theism," or "having belief that the divine does not exist." This is what you are describing.
(Note also that you can be both immoral and amoral - if you have [a behavioral code that encourages bad actions], you clearly are [lacking a behavioral code that encourages good actions]. In the same way, antitheism can be called a flavor of atheism because having [belief that the divine does not exist] means that you are [lacking the belief that the divine exists]. But do keep in mind that just because someone is amoral (no behavioral code) that he is not necessarily immoral (behavioral code to the opposite of morality), and in the same way someone who is an atheist (no belief in the divine) is not necessarily an antitheist (belief that the divine does not exist).)

I don't think I can spell that out any more directly.
You have countered my explanations so far with "your post is long," "I cherry-picked the following definitions," and "I asked my friends if they were retards and they said no."
Let's put that behind us; let's say that you did even a semi-competent job at taking apart my argument for the definition of atheism.
Now - answer to this one.

I say that the meaning of the prefix "a-" is "without."

The site gives the following examples using the "a-" prefix, which means "without":
achromatic - "Not of color." Note that "achromatic" does not mean "draining of color" or "opposed to color," but merely the lack of color; the "a-" prefix is applied to the entire concept of color.
amoral - I used this one, and you called it stupid. Disagreeing with your own sources, are you?
atypical - "Not typical."
Let's take a look at some examples of the uses of "atypical":
You find water in a bucket. Is this an atypical thing to find in a bucket? No - it is a typical thing to find in a bucket, and therefore the water is not an atypical thing to find in a bucket.
You find a sofa in a bucket. Is this an atypical thing to find in a bucket? Yes - it is "not typical" to find a sofa in a bucket, and therefore the sofa is an atypical thing to find in a bucket.
You find the dream you had last night in a bucket. Is this an atypical thing to find in a bucket? Yes - it is "not typical" to find the dream you had last night in a bucket. The dream you had last night is an atypical thing to find in a bucket.
You find a lkzjxhchv in a bucket. Is this an atypical thing to find in a bucket? Yes - it is "not typical" to find a non-existing thing in a bucket. The lkzjxhchv is an atypical thing to find in a bucket.
Clearly, "atypical" can be used to describe anything, anything, including abstract nouns and non-existing things.
If we were to apply the "a-" prefix the same way you applied it to theism (that is, applying it to only a specific portion of the meaning as opposed to the whole thing like it's supposed to be), we would get a word that means "something typically not found in the given environment or circumstance." anaerobic - "Without oxygen." Let's examine how the "a-" prefix is applied to the word. "Aerobic" means "containing oxygen." Putting the "a-" prefix there makes it "not (containing oxygen)," or "without oxygen." anticrime - "Against crime." This word does not mean "without crime." The "anti-" prefix appears to be applied in the same way that you apply the prefix "a-", which is a different prefix altogether.
antipollution - "Against pollution." This word does not mean "without pollution." The "anti-" prefix appears to be applied the same way that you apply the prefix "a-", which is a different prefix altogether.
antacid - "Against acid." This word is the opposite of "acid," which means that an antacid is basic (pH > 7). "Antacid" cannot be used to describe a neutral solution because a neutral solution is not basic. To describe a neutral solution, we would need a word that is "without acid" as opposed to "against acid." They are two different things. Agnosticism has nothing to do with belief, and has everything to do with knowledge. It is a different perspective entirely, distinct from (a)theism.
In the same way that you can be both "blue" and "bouncy," you can be both an atheist and an agnostic.
(In the following examples, it is necessary to say "non-agnostic" instead of "gnostic" because some bastard Christian sect uses that name to describe itself. "Non-agnosticism" is that which an agnostic denies.)

If you're blue and bouncy, you are blue and you are bouncy.
If you're a non-agnostic theist, you believe that the divine is knowable and you believe that the divine exists.

If you're blue and non-bouncy, you are blue and non-bouncy.
If you're a non-agnostic atheist, you believe that the concept of the divine is understandable to humans and you do not believe in the divine

If you're non-blue and bouncy, you are not blue and you are bouncy.
If you're an agnostic theist, you do not believe that the divine is knowable and you believe in the divine.

If you're non-blue and non-bouncy, you are not blue and you are not bouncy.
If you're an agnostic atheist, you do not believe that the divine is knowable and you do not believe in the divine.

Just as "blue" and "bouncy" are not connected, "agnostic" and "atheist" are not connected. They describe two different properties.
The definition you gave for agnosticism, "the belief that the divine exists but that it is not knowable" is the definition of agnostic theism.

Atilla,

Meaning is not of necessity defined by common usage. For example, "weight" is commonly used to mean "mass". However, this does not mean physicists are incorrect when they define weight and mass as separate concepts. When using these terms in serious discussion, the correct usage is not determined by majority, but rather by the technical meaning which is required in those circumstances. If you say that you've lost 5kg (rather than 49N) since you started going to the gym in casual conversation, that's fine. If, however, you write on your physics exam that something "weighs" 50kg, you will lose marks, because that usage is incorrect for the context regardless of popularity.

OP makes me want to cry.

Infinite causation is nothing but speculation. Not only is there no shortage of ways that the universe could have spontaneously generated (for example, in this nifty concept called a quantum flux, there appears to be a result without a consequence), but it also can't be anything other than inconclusive. All our lack of knowledge shows is nothing beyond just that - we don't know enough. It is foolish to make conclusions when we know next to nothing.
You are making the "God of the Gaps" fallacy, even though you're not talking about God. The "God of the Gaps" fallacy is when you see something you don't understand and declare that it is caused by something supernatural. People did this all the time before humans knew much about science. They were convinced that things we can explain easily today, such as rain and nighttime, were the results of magic, or animal spirits, or angry gods. They made up an answer to a question they didn't have any means of figuring out, and that's exactly what you're doing - you're making up an answer because you don't know nearly enough to try any other approach.
In this instance, it's much, much more rational to remain content with your ignorance if you aren't willing to scientifically investigate the matter.
I, for one, don't give two shakes of a lamb's tail about the origin of the universe. I'm not concerned about it in the slightest.

Cho Seung-Hui's Perspective:

Firearms are illegal to own:
I'm depressed. I've decided that I want to kill myself, but I want to go out with a bang. I know, I'll walk into this building, chain the doors closed, enter a classroom, and kill everyone in it.
Result: 33 people dead

Firearms are legal to own and carry onto campus:

I'd better just pick a few people to surprise, and then kill myself immediately.
Result: no more than a handful of people dead


Sure, if you carry around a firearm, you'd be more tempted to use it in a confrontation, and all kinds of accidental disasters can come from carrying and using, but think about it this way:
As opposed to the way the world is now where you can pretty much assume that someone is not carrying a firearm, how likely are you to commit any sort of crime when you know that a meaningful percentage of people just walking around are armed. And you know how tempting it is to use that thing - just how much do you think they're itching to use that gun on someone like you? And what do you think is going to happen if you do something stupid and make people around you feel threatened? How desperate do you think you'll feel when you see the unarmed people fleeing in all directions, and the armed people running toward you and finding cover to shoot at you from?

With the exception of murder-suicide cases like the VTech (...just kicked in, yo) shooting, people commit crimes because they think they'll get away with it. What's the point of mugging someone if you expect to be arrested? And even if you're willing to take the risk, try weighing that against being shot by people nearby.

This makes sense to me:
let A = the number of people who lose their lives from accidents that happen because guns are more present and available + the number of people who lose their lives when people actually pull out their guns and do stupid things + the number of people who lose their lives by accidentally running in the way of a responsible gun-owner who is shooting at a rampaging psychopath + the number of people who are mugged, robbed, assaulted, and killed because guns are more present and available
...and let B = the number of people who get to keep their lives because someone was present to stop a murderer before he killed more people + the number of people who do not get mugged, robbed, assaulted, raped, killed, etc., because the person who would normally do that is heavily dissuaded by the fact that every other person is armed and willing to shoot him in the face if he does anything stupid

I think B is much, much greater than A, especially with the second part of B. Most crimes are committed with the intent to get away with it, and if there are people nearby willing to open fire on you, you're not going to risk your life for $12 in some guy's wallet. Well, maybe if you're a crack addict, but in that case you're going to do it whether or not people around you are carrying guns.

Another perspective to consider:
I fully admit that if I were to carry a gun around that I would be very tempted to use it. I'd be actively watching out for people to give me an excuse to pull that thing out.
Who do you think is going to carry guns around openly, other than people who think like I do? There are going to be people walking around on the street who are just itching, itching to find some idiot to threaten people around him so they can pull out their guns and destroy him. That's a libertarian equivalent of a fascist state under martial law, but with preserved freedoms. Are you going to commit a crime if there are squads of military police roving about and keeping a suspicious eye on everyone at all times? Why would your willingness to commit a crime be different if it would be your potential victims who are willing to shoot you in the face instead of military police?

A big part of how huge the second number in B, above, is is the fact that all crimes suddenly become very serious. If you're mugging someone you can assume to be unarmed, you're going to approach him as though you have complete control over the situation. But if he's carrying a gun, the only way to ensure that you don't end up dead is to shoot first. First off, how many people are willing to kill for the $20 in your wallet who wouldn't do it anyway, regardless of gun control laws? Second, how many people are willing to risk a homocide investigation instead of something pithy in comparison? How many people are just as willing to run from potential witnesses as they are from police sharp-shooters and the FBI?
Sure, crimes might be more lethal in general, but they'd happen so much less often that the net number of lives spared would be greater.

When I told my roommate this, he compared my proposition to the Wild, Wild West, but he quickly agreed that the only police enforcement there was a handful of guys with guns, and that today's day is much different when you toss in kevlar vests, sharp-shooters, SWAT teams, and riot police.

Anyway, I've rambled long enough.

The VTech shooting is an excellent example that this society needs more guns.

The premise is simple and easily understandable so long as you don't really think much about it. Just accept it and live your life according to it without thinking critically.
If you hadn't noticed, McP, I've been talking from our perspective, about what we actually can know.
Y'know, that's what I was talking about when I said this:
If someone is talking about an entity that exists outside of the natural universe, one not only has absolutely nothing to say about this entity (including that it exists), but you're also demonstrating that the being you're talking about couldn't exist because you possess understanding of it (which basically means that the entity you're talking about exists in your mind, and nowhere else).

You can't actually know, or even think that God exists. When I say "God," you're thinking of God. That conception of God that you have proves that it can be grasped by a human mind, which means that if God does indeed exist, He is nothing at all like what you currently think He is. If God does exist, then you won't ever be able to grasp anything about Him. You wouldn't even be able to come up with the idea, or understand the idea that He exists.

It's like this...
A child who has never heard of language or mathematics is sitting on one side of a brick wall. On the other side is a book about quantum physics. The child can invent all manner of silly things that exist beyond the wall, but they'll all be things that he can imagine - and since he flat-out cannot, ever, have anything even remotely close to language or mathematics enter his head, it is impossible for him to think that a book about quantum physics exists on the other side of the brick wall. And no matter what the book about quantum physics does, it cannot make itself known to the child, because it is permanently unintelligible to him.
The book on quantum physics plays absolutely no role in the development of that child, and the child is incapable of understanding that language and mathematics exist. Neither plays any role in the other's life.
This is the relationship between things within the natural universe and things outside of the natural universe (or "supernatural" things).

Is this really that hard to understand?

*uses his Force powers to move this thread into Off-Topic*

My personal stance is that Star Wars would destroy Star Trek on a personal (and maybe even larger) scale, but that Star Trek could probably out-technologize Star Wars.
I'm not nearly as big a sci-fi nerd as the people who are likely going to be in here, so I could be saying something pretty stupid, but I remember something about Darth Maul teleporting into a ship and pwning everyone in it.

My immediate feelings about both are as follows:
Star Wars: epic battles involving extremely skilled and dangerous combatants; all action is intense and fast-paced; there are some so skilled that they can take down small armies alone; when high powers get pissed, planets are slaughtered
Star Trek: all conflicts are resolved by methodically tracking the other ship's position and locking on with weapons that never seem to have enough energy to be fully operational; people fight in melee and in a firefight as clumsily and slowly as though they had never had any formal training in it; when high powers get pissed, the Prime Directive needs to be discussed for six years before action is taken, during which time the Romulons will get in everyone's way

If we're talking about who has more order, it's definitely Star Trek. But if we're talking about a fight, Star Wars would humiliate Star Trek.

For one thing, ships in Star Trek are much more scarce than they are in Star Wars, and they also have slow-firing weapons and puny shields compared to what you'd find on a Star Wars ship. Let's take, for example, the Enterprise against a fleet of TIE fighters - there is no chance the Enterprise is going to come out of that one alive. And that's not even nearly representative of what a Star Trek ship would be up against - imagine the Enterprise against a star destroyer... the star destroyer could literally ignore the Enterprise and accidentally ram into it, even as the Enterprise is emptying its phasers into it. The Enterprise's size is insignificant compared to the size of a star destroyer.

And let's take a look at a battle between heroes, while we're at it:
Captain Picard against General Grievous - who do you have your money on?
Do you seriously think that anyone in the Star Trek universe could take on one of these guys?
And the Borg are nothing compared to the number and power of Star Wars battledroids.

I can't believe I just wrote all that.
