But even if free will somehow existed as well, I just can't see how you think that anything you're saying addresses what I've been saying. Let me put this another way:
In the history of mankind, there has been at least one person who has died an atheist, and who was an atheist when he died because every influence around him convinced him that God couldn't possibly exist and that God was in fact a malevolent psychopath. At least one such person has existed since the dawn of time. That person is now in Hell because He rejected Jesus Christ. The problem here, if you haven't spotted it, is that God knew that this man's life would be like this. He knew that the man would make his own choices, but that the influences around him would turn him into an atheist. The man's faith never stood a chance, and it wasn't his fault. And now he's in Hell. Given that these are the circumstances, that the man will go to Hell (and it's not at all his fault), the only thing that can turn him back to the truth is God's direct intervention. But God didn't intervene. He let the man suffer in Hell, even though he was blameless.
If one such person has ever existed, your God is not omnibenevolent, and He does not love all of His children, because that innocent man that He let go to Hell was a child He clearly did not love.

Let me give you a parallel:
I know that a nuclear attack is imminent. I know the exact time it will come. I have a shelter that will protect anyone inside of it from the nuclear attack. In order to get into my shelter, you have to figure out a riddle that I make. Some people believe me and work together to figure out the riddle and then just tell everyone they know the answer so that they can get into my shelter. Other people don't know what to believe, and they half-assedly work on the riddle. They've been told the answer before, but they might not recall it correctly. And then there are people who deny my claim that there will be a nuclear attack and refuse to do the riddle or hear the answer.
There is one person who is surrounded by conspiracy theorists all of his life, and they constantly work to deny most any claim made by any source, including my claim that there will be a nuclear attack and that people should figure out that riddle. That person will grow up around people who reject my riddle, and even though he can think for himself he throws it back in my face as well. On the day specified, people flock to my shelter, and they're granted access. The skeptics, including the person who doesn't believe me through no fault of his own, stay outside. The nuclear attack comes, and he dies.
If I wanted everybody to be safe, I would be demonstrating proof that the nuclear attack is coming, not just sitting back and watching as people don't believe me and condemn themselves and others. If I saw that person who doesn't believe simply because his environment has done nothing but give him lies that make him think I'm wrong, I'd do my best to convince him. The only explanation for me leaving the man to die without exerting any effort whatsoever to help him would be that I don't in fact want everyone to be safe.
And the only reason that God didn't let the innocent skeptic know the truth is because God doesn't love everyone. (And that also makes God unjust.)

If you had perfect conditions, you'd see that prayer doesn't matter one bit. It's 50/50. Like the movie said. You'd do just as well praying to a horseshoe or a milk jug. Or Joe Pesci.

#315933 16 2007-04-26T03:31:16Z Tsukatu
I'm gonna have to contest the "im in ur ship, killin' ur crew" situation.
Anyone that would be sent to a ship alone (the "heroes" in Star Wars, such as any competent Sith or a Jedi Knight) can move frighteningly quickly, ignore ranged weapons, and kill with a single hit, and do it all very easily. If Darth Maul was suddenly in the Enterprise, half of the crew would be dead before they even knew he was in there, and he could easily trash any vital components of the ship before reinforcements (who would be useless anyway) got there.
And if you're talking about forcefields as walls blocking off corridors, then keep in mind that the force can be used through forcefields (flipping the switch back off, for example, or just plain ol' forcechoking someone until they turn the forcefield off).
And, more importantly, do keep in mind the strength of the ship's interior. On the Enterprise, walls and doors are sleek and thin, and there are only occassional walls that are much thicker (but these walls either wouldn't lead anywhere or there would be an easier way to get to the same place). If you're stuck somewhere because there's a forcefield in the corridor, then use your goddamned lightsaber to cut a hole into the next room. Whatever it is, you'll be able to kill anyone inside it. You don't see this kind of stuff happen in Star Wars because the ships tend to be preposterously large, with massive chasms and 100-foot high ceilings, and the walls that support the ship are as thick as you are tall. But going through the walls of the Enterprise if you have a lightsaber is like Homer Simpson walking through Japanese ricepaper walls.

And even if you got Darth Maul trapped somewhere with a forcefield...

(This is from memory, since I don't run Windows, but the path should be similar to this):
Start -> Accessories -> System -> Defragment Hard Drive
The process can take a while if your HD's in bad shape (the longest I've had to wait is three days), but if it's not spyware and it's not Norton, this is the next place to look.

After all of that, if your computer is still choppy, double check to make sure you don't have any spyware (Spybot Search & Destroy and Ad-Aware will help you with this), and then Ctrl-Alt-Del to get to the Task Manager and sort your processes by their CPU usage and their virtual memory usage. If something is out of place, end that process, and if you don't need it do Start -> Run -> msconfig, and disable that process from running at startup.

It makes sense to me that the apostrophe would follow the period, yes.
I'm not convinced of that, though.
Either way, you could just use "pages'" to eliminate chance of error.

skyline:
The apostrophe is there to show that the worth is possessed by the pages.
Here's another example:
"I'd like a dollar's worth of cabbage."
It would be incorrect to say "a dollar worth of cabbage," because we need to show that the worth is a property of the dollar, and the best way to do just that is to use the possessive form - "dollar's."
The possessive form of a plural that ends in 's' includes the apostrophe after the final 's', as in the following example:
"I'd like two dollars' worth of cabbage."
This is saying that there are two dollars, and that the worth is possessed by the two of them collectively.

I used to call myself a Satanist.
I don't really anymore.

The main reason I called myself a Satanist was because LaVey's views as he explained them in the Satanic Bible (9th edition) were extraordinarily similar to my own. I already held those very same beliefs and opinions, but I didn't know they had a name. Satanism gave me a way to concisely explain what I think, even if it ultimately confused more people than it helped get the message.
("I'm a Satanist" is a shorter way of saying "I'm an antitheist with a particular dislike of Christianity who also believes that basic human impulse, coupled with mild indulgence to characteristic human selfishness and adherence to a slightly modified Golden Rule, is the sanest, healthiest, and happiest way to live your life, for both yourself and most everyone around you," but only to those who know what Satanism is.)

I left for reasons that include:
-The second half of the Satanic Bible (the part about magic) is hugely hypocritical. It spells out in the first half that the universe is more or less free of supernatural elements and that we should focus on the human being... and then comes out of left field with instructions on how to cast a fireball. What the fuck? The first half mocks everything about a holy ceremony, including the idea that saying some cool-sounding stuff methodically will actually produce any effect, but the second half tells you to do just that. It's ridiculous.
-I'm sick of explaining what a Satanist is. I kind of liked the shock value of it at first, and it was interesting to see some reactions, but overall it's not worth it, especially if you list that on an online profile and a potential employer sees it. Hardly anyone knows what a Satanist actually is, and of those who do, very few give a shit. There are even people (such as my mother) who can't get past the name and will continue to think that it is the actual belief in and worship of the Satan of Christianity no matter how much you explain.
-"Satanism" is also the name of what is basically assbackwards Christianity. These guys, whom I call "Moronic Satanists" as opposed to "LaVeyan Satanists," think that Satan is the true creator being who loves us all and that God is the banished angel, and that God made the Bible to trick humans. At its core, it's Christianity with some names swapped. Moronic Satanists give LaVeyan Satanists a bad rep (not that it could get much worse).
-Satanism attracts the usual pagan/goth/emo crowd who only claim belief because of its shock value, and are not interested in the slightest with LaVey's thoughts.
-Many Satanists are in it for the "free love." Sometimes I think that Satanism is more of a way for all manner of ugly, obese, and generally repulsive people with no saving graces to readily identify themselves, band together out of realization of their permanently lonely condition, and engage in depressing and pathetic sexual practices. I mean, if you're an ugly, repulsive little idiot with no personaity, instead of just cutting yourself and weeping silently while masturbating in the dark like you usually do, why not do it with someone just as digusting and despicable as you are? Both of you know that you would never get any on your own, so why not do each other? It's not with any sort of person you'd like to be around by any means, but something is better than nothing, right?
-The Church of Satan is overrun with Moronic Satanists, and has one as its leader. Even though Dr. LaVey's grandson, Stanton "I shrugged off an anthrax attack like it was a common fuckin' cold" LaVey, is working hard to fix this problem, I don't think it can be easily prevented. Moronic Satanists are too abundant, and I want as little association with them as possible.
-By declaring your Satanism, you should expect the rate of death threats from theists to increase dramatically, as many Christians and Muslims feel that it is their God-given duty to slay demons like you where e'er they're found.
-(For me, anyway) the title "atheist" is far more liberating and independent than "Satanist." When I called myself a Satanist, I felt that I was more an extension of someone else's ideals and that I was just a meager follower.

Those are the reasons I can come up with off the top of my head. There were probably more, but I just don't concern myself with Satanism that much anymore. I do have the benefit of knowing what someone is talking about, and I did find a portion of my own worldview in writing that I can now use as a reference, but I won't associate myself with Satanism unless it is in some unusual circumstance socially beneficial for me to do so.

For one thing, there are plenty of evolutionarily disadvantageous traits humans can have and still be able to survive because the trait is largely inconsequential. Homosexuality is sort of a good example, actually.

I used to think that this is how I act.

Knowing that you have a single future that you're forced to live does not mean you are forced into inaction.
I'm typing up this response right now, and it has just occurred to me that I could choose to not type up this response. But it occurred to me immediately afterwards that I wasn't thinking about it as a choice when I started doing it. For the most part, I don't think of my life as a series of choices. Maybe that's a sign of some personality flaw or something, but I just don't think about it that way. The way I act is the natural consequence of my brain carrying out so many processes as background processes that my life is pretty much entirely subconscious with my consciousness observing, often amused by what it sees.
And when I am presented with a choice, I of course fully realize that I couldn't have made any other choice. I see it as more of a deliberation process, with my brain performing a subconscious weighing of benefits until it understands that one option is superior.

Two programs:
Program A receives input from the environment, twice, and turns each into a single idea, then passes both to Program B.
Program B assesses carefully the differences between the two ideas and by comparing the two determines the superior idea, which it then uses in a way appropriate to that idea to influence its environment before calling Program A.
Program B does not have a moment of "free choice," but instead is a process with only one correct answer. Program B can be imperfect in many ways, such as failing to take into consideration all aspects of either or both ideas and screwing up somewhere in the comparing process.

This is how my mind works.
No, this is how the mind works, in general.

This is just silly - how does anyone who knows that all thinking, conscious or subconscious, is a massive series of chemical reactions not see how this leaves out this magical notion of free choice? What reaction, what particle, represents your consciousness, somehow as a separate system from the neurochemical system that actually makes it possible, determining how the unshakeable natural laws of the universe are applied to the chemical reactions that determine your actions?

The controls for 2-dimensional games are two-dimensional; Metroid has directional keys that take you up/down and left/right. There are no other directional controls. There are controls for actions, such as "shoot," but there are no other directional controls.

#325028 23 2007-05-28T19:04:18Z Tsukatu
I read a review for this movie with which I agreed 100%. I wanted to grab a copy of the newspaper it was in before I left work, but I forgot to. I can probably grab it tomorrow.

Actually, let me see if I can find it online...
Quote
Nearly 45 minutes into Pirates of the Caribbean: At Worlds End, Capt. Jack Sparrow (Johnny Depp) still hasnt shown his face on screen. But because screenwriters Ted Elliott and Terry Rossio and director Gore Verbinski can basically do whatever they want with the franchise at this point, they attempt to make up for this inexplicable oversight in a way that ultimately summarizes everything thats wrong with the movie: They populate the scene in which Sparrow finally does appear with approximately two dozen hallucinatory duplicates of him. This is because apparently theres nothing that cant be solved by more, more and, oh yes, still yet more in this film.

Pirates of the Caribbean: Dead Mans Chest sailed into last summer as a rousing, phenomenally successful follow-up to the 2003 original. Plenty of critics blasted it as bloated, but it seemed to me a fine mix of energetically choreographed adventure and Depps enthusiastic reprisal of Sparrow. At Worlds End, however, turns out to be everything Chests fiercest detractors claimed it was over-stuffed, over-plotted and, most surprisingly, just plain dull.

It is possible to stay awake by trying to keep track of the several hundred plot threads drifting through this thing. Will Turner (Orlando Bloom) and Elizabeth Swan (Keira Knightley)along with their returned one-time adversary Barbossa (Geoffrey Rush)are seeking Sparrow as the film opens, since we last saw Sparrow dragged to a watery grave at the end of Dead Mans Chest. But Will still has a mission to free his father Bootstrap Bill (Stellan Skarsgrd) from the curse of Davy Jones (Bill Nighy). Barbossa has his own secret mission involving a promise to the mysterious Tia Dalma (Naomie Harris). Elizabeths one-time beau Norrington (Jack Davenport) is controlling Davy Jones and the crew of the Flying Dutchman. And there are more pirate captains, including another old adversary of Sparrows, Sao Feng (Chow Yun-Fat). If it werent set in a world before indoor plumbing, Im sure the kitchen sink would have made an appearance.

None of the previous films could exactly be called textbook examples of streamlined storytelling, but at least they were buoyed by an understanding of where the focus needed to be. For one, it needed to be on Depp, who provided that rare example of a franchise built not on a premise, but on a performance. Yet Sparrow not only takes forever to appearthough, admittedly, 45 minutes here only amounts to about a quarter of the running timebut he disappears for other chunks of the film as well. Sparrow gets too few of the kind of scenes that made him such an engaging creation, while ample time is given to the now-pouty romance between Will and Elizabeth.

Meanwhile, Verbinski cant even provide action set pieces with enough zip to counteract the narrative fat; theres nothing here remotely comparable to the moonlight skeleton swordfight in Curse of the Black Pearl or the runaway water wheel in Dead Mans Chest. At Worlds End back-loads all the action into a climactic sea battle between the Black Pearl and Davy Jones Flying Dutchman on the rim of a swirling vortex, and by that point the film seems so desperate to leave viewers energized that it practically pummels them insensible. A few of the individual elementsincluding an impromptu wedding in the middle of a grand meleeactually achieve a little sizzle, only to be overwhelmed by whatever Verbinski decides to throw at us next.

The real shame of it is that for all their bombast, the Pirates films at their best will be remembered not for all the CGI-abetted sequences, but for the small comedic showcases for Depp. Every once in a while, At Worlds End will stumble upon such a low-key bit of businesslike the rivalry between Sparrow and Barbossa manifesting itself in the size of their spyglasses. But for every one of those bits, theres a decision as ridiculous as giving Elizabeth a rousing speech to the pirate army, and actually playing it with a straight face. No one seemed able to tell Verbinski and company when to stop puffing the film full of grandeuror that 20 Johnny Depps in one scene isnt the same as one Johnny Depp used correctly.
Source: Monterey Coast Weekly

I've been thinking about a movie I've been wanting to make for a very long time now, and I recently settled down to write the cinematic trailer for it. After this, I don't actually think I have it in me to write an entire script, but here's what I have for the trailer so far:

(Fade in to a shot with the camera looking up from the ground to the top of a catholic cathedral. The environment is very dreary and somewhat gothic: the steps leading into the chapel are in very poor repair, the stone ground is cracked and covered in grime, the sky is filled with dark clouds with occassional lightning strikes in the background, and the dark facade of the cathedral stands domineering like the iron fortress of a tyrant. A crowd of miserable, wretched figures in simple dark, hooded robes are hunching their way slowly up the steps to the cathedral.)

NARRATOR: In a world...

(Cut to a shot of the altar inside the cathedral at a dramatic upward angle. The inside of the cathedral is as dark and tyrannical as the outside, only more fanciful, and behind the altar stands an ornate, menacing crucifix. The priest of the cathedral is wearing fancy robes that are black as charcoal with silver embroidery and a massive cross around his neck. He stands with his back turned to the camera, facing the altar, and turns around dramatically with his hands raised. The camera zooms in on his face as he turns around, and we can see that his ghostly pale face has a sinister, almost demonic, evil scowl.)

NARRATOR: ...where religion rules...

(Cut to a horizontal pan from the altar's point of view at the hundreds of wretched dark-robed figures sitting humbly in pews, praying. The figures are all bent, dirty, and miserable, and all are wearing wooden crosses on simple white string around their necks, on top of their robes. These are the CHRISTIANS. The inside of the cathedral is very majestic, though thoroughly demonic. As the camera pans across the pews filled with CHRISTIANS, very brief clips of violent scenes flash intermittently: gunfire and screaming in a chemical laboratory; men and women in white lab coats being shoved forcefully into line by CHRISTIANS with submachine guns; an enormous pile of books in flames surrounded by the CHRISTIANS, who are watching, limping about, and driving wheelbarrows full of books into the burning pile.)

NARRATOR: ...and science is punishable by death...

(Cut to a shot of a man in rags manacled to a wall by all four limbs, several meters above the ground, wrestling uselessly against his bonds and screaming. The camera flies back quickly to show an enormous, dank, underground torture chamber that features a stupendously large assortment of torture devices and rag-wearing people strapped to them. The devices are being operated by the CHRISTIANS, who are limping about all over. Some of the CHRISTIANS are standing guard at doorways and holding machine guns. Fade out when the camera backs out through the wooden double-doors leading into the torture complex, which slam shut in front of the camera. There is a CHRISTIAN on either side of the double-doors with a machine gun in hand. This shot shows us a glimpse of the face of a CHRISTIAN underneath the hood, which reveals a long, hooked nose, drooping flesh, and a permanent scowl, covered in warts. Like Emperor Palpatine from Star Wars, but uglier.
Fade back in to a shot of the inside of a tavern, which is dimly lit by oil lanterns and has simple wooden tables, and is generally very medieval-looking. The shot is focused on a group of three CHRISTIANS sitting at a wooden table, all sipping out of crudely-fashioned wooden mugs. Their hoods are pulled low so that none of their faces are visible.)

NARRATOR: The only hope for mankind...

(A CHRISTIAN hobbles quickly over to the table where the three are sitting. He slams his hands down on the table dramatically and then slowly raises an accusing finger at the CHRISTIAN sitting in the middle.)

CHRISTIAN (hissing): I know who you are... scientists!

NARRATOR: ...is applied reason.

(The three accused CHRISTIANS (#'s 1, 2, and 3) sitting at the table leap to their feet. CHRISTIAN #2 (middle) quickly pulls something out of her robe and tosses it at the CHRISTIAN (#4) who approached them. CHRISTIAN #4 catches it and looks at what it is - it's a bar of soap. CHRISTIAN #4 is confused.)

CHRISTIAN #2 (female): That bar of soap is made out of a base.

(CHRISTIAN #4 is still confused. CHRISTIAN #2 holds up her cup.)

CHRISTIAN #2: And this is lemonade, which contains citric acid.

(CHRISTIAN #4 is confused and worried. CHRISTIAN #2 pulls off her hood, revealing herself to be CHEMIST, a stunningly attractive woman in her late 20's. She stands confident.)

CHEMIST: Have you ever heard of "heat of neutralization?"

(CHEMIST splashes the lemonade onto CHRISTIAN #4. Upon contact with the lemonade, the bar of soap explodes like an incendiary grenade, completely engulfing CHRISTIAN #4 in flames. CHRISTIANS #1 and #3 pull off their hoods, revealing themselves to be PHYSICIST and BIOLOGIST. PHYSICIST looks like a stereotypical male engineer in his early 40's, complete with glasses, plaid shirt, and pocket protector. BIOLOGIST is a more or less bland asian woman in her 30's. CHEMIST, PHYSICIST, and BIOLOGIST all sprint for the door of the tavern, but the surrounding CHRISTIANS rush to block the way.)

NARRATOR: Three ex-professors of science...

(The three scientists stop suddenly, as they are facing a few dozen angry CHRISTIANS. The three are in an open area in the middle of the tavern, and a few dozen more CHRISTIANS are surrounding them in a wide circle. Cut to the three to show the worried but determined look on their faces. Fade out.)

NARRATOR: An evolutionary biologist...

(Cut to the three scientists standing at a simple pier at dusk, overlooking a lake. BIOLOGIST is explaining what she is about to do.)

BIOLOGIST: According to Darwin's Theory of Evolution, all organisms keep mutations that help them survive in the environment.

(BIOLOGIST squats down on the pier, leans toward the water, and fills her cupped hands with some of the lake water. She stands back up, turns around to face PHYSICIST and CHEMIST, and raises her cupped hands above her head and drinks dramatically. Because she is looking upward, the camera has a clear shot of her neck, which grows gills as she drinks. She then smiles at CHEMIST and PHYSICIST, and dives backwards off of the pier. Fade out.)

NARRATOR: A chemist...

(The three scientists, dressed in their modern clothes instead of the dark CHRISTIAN robes, have just stopped walking on a trail through a forest because they've spotted a half dozen CHRISTIANS charging at them farther on down the trail. CHEMIST steps forward and pushes the other two scientists back.)

CHEMIST: I got this, you guys. A gas' pressure, volume, and temperature are all related to each other. Down here on the surface, the pressure is going to be constant. (The charging CHRISTIANS are getting close.) So in order to increase the temperature, you have to increase the volume. (The charging CHRISTIANS are almost upon them.) And the best way to increase the volume of gas...

(CHEMIST inhales deeply and, just as the CHRISTIANS are closing in, breathes fire on the lot of them. All of the CHRISTIANS are disintegrated instantly by the heat. Fade out.)

NARRATOR: And a physicist...

(The three scientists are standing on a post-apocalyptic metropolitan street. The three were sneaking through the city and were spotted by a CHRISTIAN, who is screaming and charging at them from a distance. PHYSICIST pushes CHEMIST and BIOLOGIST behind him and explains what he is about to do aloud to them.)

PHYSICIST: According to the right hand rule... (he does a thumbs-up with the base of his palm on his stomach and his thumb pointing out of his stomach, straight in front of him) ...when you make a rotation... (he curls and uncurls his fingers to show that the rotation is clockwise) ...the direction of the torque is along the axis of rotation. In this case...

(The charging CHRISTIAN is now upon them. The scene goes into bullet-time as the PHYSICIST does a Matrix-like sideways cartwheel clockwise, supporting himself on one hand. His other hand punches the CHRISTIAN in the stomach when PHYSICIST is upside-down. The resulting punch tears the CHRISTIAN into ribbons: in slow motion, the rest of the CHRISTIAN's body folds inward as he is sent flying backward by his stomach, and his spine visibly snaps almost immediately. As he flies back, his flesh, muscle, and bone are twisted and torn in an excessively bloody manner that is entirely too gruesome even for a movie intended for mature audiences. The body of the CHRISTIAN is so mangled and mutilated after flying two meters through the air that he is no longer recognizable as something that was once human, but he continues flying across the street until the clump of flesh and sinew slams into a ruined building, splattering blood, shards of bone, and unidentifiable organic bits all over its wall. Fade out.)

NARRATOR: ...meet a student...

(Brief shot zooming in toward STUDENT's face. He is in his early 20's and has a clean punk/biker look: cleanshaven, short spiked hair, stylish leather jacket. Fade out.)

NARRATOR: ...of thermodynamics...

(Close-up shot looking over STUDENT's shoulder as he explains to whoever is behind him (he is looking through the camera) what he's going to do to the pack of CHRISTIANS charging at him like a horde of trolls in the distance.)

STUDENT: You know what entropy is? It's disorder, chaos. And it's proportional to heat. So if you increase the heat, you increase the chaos.

(STUDENT pulls out a zippo lighter, lights it, and holds it out in front of him. The camera pans as he moves his hand to show what he's looking at through the flame. Every CHRISTIAN he looks at through the flame as he sweeps his gaze over them is vaporized. Fade out.)

NARRATOR: ...and embark on a journey...

(Shot of the four dramatically coming to the top of a steep hill. Fade out slowly.)

NARRATOR: ...to find the ultimate weapon...

(STUDENT is sitting in front of a campfire and looking into it. Close-up on a portrait view of his face - he turns to his left and looks at the camera dramatically.)

STUDENT: ...the Logician!

(Brief shot of the inside of a humble log cabin. A gentle old man wearing a hooded pale gray robe (with the hood on) looks up mystically at the camera.)

NARRATOR: ...to fight their greatest foe.

(Very fast zoom in to the face of the POPE. POPE is sitting in an immense cathedral in the same style as the first cathedral shown, but much more ornate. Most everything about POPE and the cathedral he's in is pitch black with ash-grey and silver designs. POPE is wearing very ornate robes, as a Catholic Pope would wear, complete with ridiculous hat, but completely black and diabolical. His face is contorted in such a drippingly evil, ghoulish scowl that he hardly seems human. Zoom back out very quickly, out of the cathedral doors and over several miles of land to show that POPE is in the middle of a completely ruined, post-apocalyptic city, with streets completely filled with CHRISTIANS. Cut to a close-up of PHYSICIST.)

PHYSICIST: One does not simply walk into the Vatican.

(Cut to a shot of PHYSICIST standing on the roof of one skyscraper in the city and looking at a pack of CHRISTIANS standing on the top of another skyscraper about fifty or sixty meters away. PHYSICIST sprints and jumps off the edge of the skyscraper. Cut to a view of the front of the CHRISTIANS on the other skyscraper, who are unaware of PHYSICIST. PHYSICIST is visible leaping in the distant background. His jump takes him into the air out of view of the camera, but he definitely soars at least thirty meters high with his jump. After several seconds of uneventful silence, the PHYSICIST lands directly on the CHRISTIAN who is just in front of the camera, crushing him out of view. PHYSICIST lands as evenly as though he just performed a simple hop.

Rock music starts playing to accompany the following scenes:

BIOLOGIST, with the gills she grew earlier still visible, jumps off of a sea-side cliff and starts flapping her arms desperately. As she flaps, her arms morph into large feathery wings, and she is able to fly with them like a bird.

CHEMIST is holding her ground from the CHRISTIANS surrounding her in an abandoned old shack in the dead of night. She is spraying any CHRISTIAN who comes near with a supersoaker filled with a bluish fluid. Every CHRISTIAN who is hit by the spray is petrified instantly into a chalky white stone.

PHYSICIST is wielding an enormous industrial spring as a weapon. He is on the ruined city streets at night surrounded by CHRISTIANS, and he's doing clockwise hands-free cartwheels and hitting CHRISTIANS with the spring whenever he's upside-down. Every CHRISTIAN he hits explodes very messily.

BIOLOGIST, surrounded on an open field by CHRISTIANS, still with gills and the wings she grew earlier, now has two enormous mammoth tusks sticking out of her face that she is using to attack the CHRISTIANS coming at her.

An epic battle on a field leading into the city - the three scientists, STUDENT, and LOGICIAN are attacking an army of CHRISTIANS. The CHEMIST is doing flame-related nonsense to destroy the CHRISTIANS who come at her; the PHYSICIST is bopping CHRISTIANS with the spring (no cartwheels) and sending them flying; BIOLOGIST has gills, wings, mammoth tusks, and now has a pair of human-sized spider legs behind her own legs as well as a scorpion tail, and is attacking CHRISTIANS with her tusks, wings, and tail; STUDENT is using his vaporizing lighter trick, and the LOGICIAN is standing in the middle of the group not really doing anything.

End rock music montage.

Cut to a dramatic shot of POPE coming down the steps from the altar of the cathedral he was in. Cut to a shot behind him, showing that LOGICIAN is at the base of the steps. The POPE raises his arms mystically.)

POPE: Intelligent Design!

(Swirling violet light fills the space between POPE and LOGICIAN, and a very demonic-looking and over-muscled unicorn is assembled out of thin air, facing LOGICIAN and snarling. LOGICIAN raises a hand to it.)

LOGICIAN: God of the Gaps.

(The earth shakes and an enormous crack is opened in the ground directly underneath the unicorn, which fails to scramble out of it in time. The crack is wide enough to separate LOGICIAN and POPE by a few more meters with a gaping pit, and it splits the cathedral in two. POPE is concerned about the falling debris while LOGICIAN stands ominously. Fade out. The title of the movie fades in, then fades out. Fade in quickly to a shot of the three scientists traveling over land:
PHYSICIST, on the left, is in an enormous contraption made entirely of springs. He is very high above the ground, standing on the legs of whatever the hell the thing is he's in, which are a few dozen meters tall.
CHEMIST, in the middle, has a box of table salt and a jug of water. She is pouring the two in front of her, which is enabling her to somehow ride on top of the flames that are resulting in the water meeting the salt. If this movie trailer has so far had its desired effect, the audience should not even want to know the ridiculous excuse used to justify her riding flames through the air.
BIOLOGIST, on the right, is now a horrifying amalgamation of at least 15 different animals, and is completely asymmetrical and dilapidated. She's as big a beast as PHYSICIST's "vehicle," and features random body parts from different animals, including four spider legs (which are as big as she is), that enormous scorpion tail in addition to a whale fin, and enormous insectoid mandibles. Her torso and the right half of her head look like those of a seal, her left arm is a penguin flipper, her fifth leg is some kind of bird leg, her right arm is a pair of enormous octpus tentacles, and her left eye is an enormous compound eye (as from a housefly) that takes up the entirety of that side of her head. Her enormous lizard tongue is flicking in and out of her mouth as she's gimping along like the disgusting mutant that she is, and her second pair of honeybee wings (oh, did I not mention she has enormous honeybee wings?) is twitching uncontrollably.
The three race past the camera "heroically." Fade out.
Fade in on the release date of the movie, and fade out again.
END.)

The Technological Singularity is nigh!

There is no flippin' way that a single human could create what we have now from rocks and sand. Our technological accomplishments are the result of continually mounting effort.
The time it takes to figure out a novel concept is far, far longer than the time it takes to explain it to someone after it has been discovered and perfected; it could take Og years to figure out that you can sharpen a stick with rocks, but it will take only moments for Og to teach this to his son.
That, combined with the fact that kids are knowledge sponges, means that the next generation can pick up where the previous one left off!

There's also some relevant quote about standing on the shoulders of giants that I'm too lazy to Google.

#15627 1 2007-06-11T07:08:30Z Tsukatu
"Jesus Christ, [Tsukatu], just let the poor thing die already!" -my brother

Never, I say!

To start off, here is a brief summary of my laptop's specs:
Name: JEBUS
Price: $1500 in 2003, close to $400 today
Model: Toshiba Satellite Pro
Screen Size: 17" WSXGA
Weight: 10.0 lbs
Processor: Pentium 4 @ 3.4 GHz
RAM: 512 MB DDR
Video Card: Radeon 9600/9700 Series (64 MB; Integrated)
HDD: 80 GB @ 5400 rpm (30 GB NTFS for WinXP Pro SP2, 49 GB ext3 for Slackware 11.0, 1 GB linux-swap)

My laptop has issues. I've taken it apart about 8 times now to perform random maintenance.
At its worst, back before the fifth repair or so, the touchpad didn't work, the wireless card didn't work, the cd drive didn't work, the monitor wouldn't turn on, the hard drive had bad sectors, no operating system was detected, and the internal temperature was hot enough to fry eggs after half a minute. After the seventh repair, I had fixed the overheating issues, fixed the wireless card, fixed the hard drive, fixed the operating system detection issue, and had the monitor working again, albeit with some irreperable damage, and the problems with the cd drive and touchpad remained unresolved.
Most recently, the monitor stopped working. I decided to chronicle my repair this time around because I realized recently that I own a digital camera that I may as well put to use.

Here we go!

My monitor without the front casing: [Picture - 32.9 KB]

After a whole lot of poking around, I more or less accidentally stumbled upon the location of the problem.
The doodad responsible was on that bit of board below the monitor.

Closeup: [Picture - 37.8 KB]

The last time I had monitor trouble, it was with that connection on the right being loose. This time the problem wasn't so straight-forward. I found out that the monitor turned on again after I applied pressure directly to the plastic. To investigate why the hell that was, I had to take off the plastic:

Plastic removed: [Picture - 54.4 KB]

The problem piece: [Picture - 45.1 KB]

It turned out that for some reason those connectors on the left were ever so slightly suspended above the contact points. Applying pressure forced them into contact.

Connectors not touching: [Picture - 101.5 KB]
(Wow, that picture came out 80 times better than I thought it would.)

Connectors being forced together: [Picture - 84.3 KB]
(That's not a piece of smoked salmon - that's my finger.)

Demonstration: [Video - 1.04 MB]

After trying to tape the plastic back around very tightly (and failing), I got a bit more creative. I needed something to sit on the inside of the monitor frame and press into that doodad to make sure the contacts are in contact. The nearest thing to me happened to be the cover of a USB flash memory drive.

My dirty little hack: [Picture - 58.0 KB]

Closing up the casing: [Video - 669 KB]

The test: [Video - 1.95 MB]

Success!

This is what makes Tsukatu different from the average consumer - where most people would just give up and get a new computer, I make sure that I Jew every ounce of functionality out of my expensive purchases. I only hope that I can keep patching JEBUS together with such crude fixes until I can save up enough to get a new laptop... and we'll see how long I can make that baby last me.

#332090 3 2007-06-17T08:32:03Z Tsukatu
Strictly speaking, water, air, and space aren't dimensions, but physical mediums; they're physical things that fill the distance between us and the places we want to go. When traveling through water, we physically push off of the water we're moving on top of or through. When traveling through air, we use properties of the air itself (air pressure / Bernoulli's Principle) to physically push ourselves through the air. When traveling through space, we expel mass to give us a momentum in the opposite direction.

Time is not quite so physical, so it's not really a good idea to think about traveling through time as we travel through water, air, and space. The way we interact with water, air, and space is not the same way we interact with time. Namely, because time isn't physical, we can't play around with it and figure out a way to control it.

I don't believe time travel is possible other than at the velocity vector we are traveling through it right now, with some insignificant modulation thanks to Relativity.

#15842 1 2007-06-23T04:15:05Z Tsukatu
(Assume that you are guaranteed to receive the money and that you will be unable to retrieve your eye.)

So I was mindlessly surfing earlier today when I came across this questionnaire that was supposed to determine whether or not I would go to Heaven or Hell. It said some pretty silly things like, "the Bible says that all of mankind has broken the first commandment, and by claiming that you didn't, you're also lying" (even though you could truthfully believe that you hadn't broken the first commandment).
But anyway, it ended the questionnaire with questions like "based on this, do you think you're Innocent or Guilty?" The "Innocent" led to a page that said "INCORRECT," and the "Guilty" was the right answer. The next question was "so are you going to Heaven or Hell," and of course the only right answer was "Hell." The final question, which prompted this thread, was "are you concerned that you're going to Hell?"
I of course answered "no," and I got this page: [link]

All along, I was reading the explanations it gave for each question and was answering honestly. I found that most of their real-world parallels involving judges and Jesus paying my bail kind of silly, but I was still answering many of their simple questions to myself honestly.
Now read the first sentence in the link I just gave - "would you sell one of your eyes for a million dollars?"
My answer was "probably, depending upon how it's removed."
Then it said I wasn't in my right mind. ;_;

So now I extend the question to you (and this is completely unrelated to Christianity):
Would you sell one of your eyes for one million dollars?

Bonus question:
Would you sell both of your eyes for ten million dollars?

Please do not discuss religion in this thread, unless you worship a beholder or something.

---

My answer:

Hell yeah, I'd sell one of my eyes for $1 million. So long as it's properly, surgically removed (in an American hospital by American doctors) and I can receive full hospital care until I recover, I wouldn't even care which eye they took.

The way I see it, the cons are:
No depth perception: This is the biggest problem, obviously, but much of what I want to do in my life doesn't require depth perception. I really don't need to see how far away my computer screen is if I can still read the code I'm writing. It might be a little frustrating if I'm trying to assemble something, but I don't think it would be frustrating enough to matter. Precise depth perception really doesn't matter in the majority of tasks you will perform in your lifetime.
Otherwise, failing to throw things accurately won't really affect me because I already suck at throwing things accurately, and using a firearm won't really be affected negatively because of its point-and-click interface (not to mention my second eye won't skew my aim - I'll be forced to use the sights without complications).
No driving: Ouch. That actually would suck. Then again, $1 million gives you a chauffeur, right? Otherwise, I usually walk or take the subway anyway. And if I continue to live in Boston or any other populous metropolis, I'll probably continue to do so.
Social suckage: I really don't think this is enough of a drawback to matter. Sure, every now and then my glass eye may wander or my eyepatch will fail to impress, but that's trivial for me.
Blindness on the appropriate side: That would also kind of suck, but it'd still be natural to turn your head farther toward the blind side when, for example, looking both ways before crossing the street. Things will be able to sneak up on me easier on that side, too, but that really doesn't happen often in life.

The pros, however:
A legitimate excuse to wear an eyepatch: Hell yes.
A glass eye: ...can be thrown at people and gives me a few more party tricks, as well as distinguishing me from other people.
$1,000,000: This in and of itself greatly outweighs the cons. Having this money will, among lots of other things, allow me to quit my day job and live without having to work, which would not only ease the whole "living at an inconvenience" thing, but exceed it in its emotional benefit.

But about those cons:
Bionic eye: My generation will live to see it (punny!), and my $1 mil will let me buy it. I can totally survive with an eyepatch and/or glass eye until something actually functional is developed, and by then my panel of personal accountants will have turned my $1 million into a far larger fortune.

End result: After a substantial amount of time being at a minor inconvenience, I'll have a fortune and will be able to see better than you can.


And as for the bonus question - would I sell both of my eyes for ten million dollars?
HELL NO.
Having one eye is a slight inconvenience, but being blind would suck. $1 million is good enough of a launchpad to get a larger fortune; the $9 million difference wouldn't matter in the long run.

Quote: Kablizzy, June 25, 2007 01:23 pm
Yes, let's argue semantics and opine. Bottom Line? They're the biggest-selling band ever. As The Juggler said, they inspired *everything* you hear now. To claim that any band that came after the Beatles is "better" than the Beatles on some arbitrary condition is rather silly.
The Beatles were the best at rock because they invented rock. There is no one who will ever be better at rock than The Beatles.
Newton was the best at calculus because he invented calculus. There is no one who will ever be better at calculus than Newton.
Hippocrates was the best at medicine because he invented medicine. There is no one who will ever be better at medicine than Hippocrates.

Starting or inspiring something doesn't make you the best at it, or even half-way decent at it.
In the case of the Beatles, they made an assload off of their music - whether that's because they were the only rock band when they became a hit or because they actually had talent is arguable, but starting or inspiring anything is not an argument for anything.

Quote: 321southpaw, June 27, 2007 12:06 am
I figure this:

If you get an iPhone and you are out in the middle of the forest using your GPS to find out where you are, when all of a sudden you iPhone runs out of battery, how are you supposed to CALL someone for HELP? Not only does it remove the many features it has once it runs out of battery, I can see the guy or girl walking down the street, saying, "nonononono, pleeease don't die!!! AWWW GOd it died!!! Why?!? Now I can't find my way to the Starbucks!!!" *then they whimper silently while lying down on the street, completely in shock*

^I know people just like that. It is scary.

So yeah, if I were trapped in the woods with my iPhone, I would be sure to bring along my iPod too, just so I can listen to "Crazy" by Gnarles Barkley as I slowly go insane.
Why get a cell phone? I mean, let's say you're hiking and you fall down a steep slope, knocking yourself unconscious for a few days. When you wake up, your cell phone will be dead - what use then?
And why get a laptop? I mean, let's say you're paratrooping into North Korea, your parachute doesn't open, and you barely get your spare open before you hit the ground, so you're alive but with broken legs. You have your laptop so you have a way of getting help, but there are no wireless networks around! Useless! Why would someone ever get a laptop? What possible use could it be?
And why wear pants? I mean, let's say you're running from a serial killer through an unchartered jungle in the Congo when you're captured by indigenous cannibals. You might be able to use your pants to strangle one of them, but the tribe took them away from you - what possible use are pants if they just get taken away when you need them? That's why I don't buy pants.

In fewer words:
There is a set of objects you should bring on excursions into the forest, and an iPhone is not one of them.
Taking your iPhone camping is like bringing your bagpipes to the movies.

Don't make decisions about buying something based on what functions it doesn't have or what dumb circumstances it can't help you avoid.
"I'm not going to buy an iPhone because it can't deflect bullets or control people's minds." -321southpaw

(Referring to OP:)

One of my random random tabletop gaming ideas was to have five girls born in random places in the world who each had dominance over one element, and that power would grow exponentially with age (so that they'd be more or less gods by the time they hit 20-ish). (The fifth "element" was more of an internal harmony / perfection.)
But my biggest issue was balancing their power. Air could fly and make strong wind and Fire could burn things... but Water is crazy powerful because humidity exists, and Earth was insane because that's what the ground happened to be made of. I really couldn't think of a good way to keep Earth in check - if you piss her off, you're suddenly in the center of the planet, or in a meteor freshly flung from the planet, or she used the adamantium in the nearby adamantium mine to blender your insides through your contact to the ground. If you wanted to hit her, she could put the planet between you and her, etc.
Just so the fifth sister (who was supposed to be better than the elemental four) wasn't outdone by Earth, I gave her the option to remove herself from reality temporarily and to change her past actions.

But yeah, I don't think those four elements are very balanced.

#16083 1 2007-07-06T08:14:21Z Tsukatu
You know what I'm sick of?
I'm sick of this pretentious invasion of language by other languages.
You know, when some asshole insists on writing his name in English with characters from a foreign alphabet, or demands you use the pronounciation of his language for a character in your language that looks similar to a character in his.

I said that as generally as I could, so I'm sorry if it's confusing.

But here are some examples:
"Jose"
Question: How many letters are there in the English language that make the sound we normally start off "Jose" with? I can count one - 'h'.
Question: How 'bout 'j'? Does 'j' make the same sound as 'h' in any English word? No, I don't believe it does. 'J' only makes the 'h' sound when it's in another goddamned language. But we're speaking English, so no, Jose, unless you write your name "Hosay," I'm calling you the plural of 'Joe'. You're Joes, bitch.
But "Jose" is sneaky - what about this flagrant "Garon" shit? Does '' look like an English goddamned character to you? When do you say '' in your A-B-C's? I'm rhyming your ass with "archon" unless you write it Garson. And don't use your silly little accents; English words have all kinds of wacky pronounciation rules, so you're free to tell me to put stress on a different syllable, but don't spell it "Garon".

Here's the deal, folks:
If you have a name from a culture that uses a different language, it is your responsibility to intelligibly represent your name phonetically in English when you're writing your name in English. It is not polite to sporadically switch to French or Spanish in the middle of an English sentence, so keep your shit consistent. When writing English, you use English characters, and don't think you can get away with using similar-looking characters that have different pronounciations, Juanito (or should I say "Hwanito?").

My name is not Constantine - my name is Константин, which is actually pronounced noticeably differently from "Constantine," but I have taken the effort to represent my name in English characters using English pronounciation to make a sound that is as faithful to the original phonetically as I care to make it. I do this whenever I'm writing in English. Notice that I do not use Russian pronounciation rules - I do not write my name Konctantine, Koнctaнtiнe, or use characters that aren't identical to English characters at all like и - Koнctaнtин. I don't sporadically switch to Russian when I'm speaking in English.
When some Chinese dude writes his name, he writes in phonetic English, using English characters and their English pronounciations - you don't see Chinese names in English spelled with random Chinese characters.

But "Jose" is ridiculous. If you believe that the best phonetic English representation of your name is "Jose," then your name is pronounced "Joes." There is little more to it than that. "Juan" is "Jew-on." When I ask for your name in English, I am asking for a reply in English, bitch. Don't you switch up languages on me in the middle of a sentence, because then you're just being a twat. Our George changes his name to Jorge for your ungrateful asses, but you need to meet us halfway. Otherwise, you're calling your language better than ours by refusing to use our barbaric, unenlightened tongue to represent your precious name.

Moving beyond names, even, I don't go to "ballets" because that's a nonsense word in English. It sure does mean something in French, but we're not speaking French. My sister does "balley," but I have no idea what "ballet" is referring to. Similarly, I enjoy "buffeys," but don't rightly think I've ever been to a buffet. Ever been to Illinois? I haven't, but there's a state in the US with a similar name - Illinoy. Have some Merlow while you're there, and maybe some kesadias.
"Oh, but it's a Spanish food, so we use the Spanish spelling - quesadillas." Yeah, well we call it borscht, not борщ, and we say chai, not чай.

Enforce logical language!
Half of you probably think I'm an ignoramus - you guys can go split the bill for a bag of dicks!

#341221 14 2007-07-10T04:46:32Z Tsukatu
I'm a registered member of The Brights community, which is composed of (or should be composed of) people who don't believe in anything outside of this natural universe, which generally rules out God, ghosts, psychics, etc.

First off, I think it's absolutely ridiculous that people should think what they were raised to think. It is my firm belief that people should find out about things for themselves, and to not form opinions about things if they don't know enough about them.
Don't hold a particular religious or political stance just because your parents are. That's just dumb.

I believe whatever it is that I find most rational at any point. In terms of religion, this means that I cycle between agnostic atheism and antitheism (gnostic atheism) a few times a year. I know that none of the Abrahamic faiths could be true because they are ridiculously inconsistent, and I can't see how someone could fail to see that after critical examination.
Because I know far less about social and political issues, I'm all over the board, and every new piece of information that I get will probably have some impact on my stance on any given issue. I don't believe in anything unless I become convinced that it is probably correct (I've said that I don't know enough about a subject to have an opinion more times than you'd think), and I will argue for my point of view only so long as I continue to think I'm correct after seeing the opponent's argument, but there have been plenty of times in which I've surprised the guy arguing for the other side by declaring that I was wrong and apologizing. I can easily see why someone could hang on to a losing argument because they don't want to be incorrect, but I also think that's ridiculous; I know that if I have the correct position that I won't be proven wrong, and that I shouldn't argue for something that I no longer believe is correct. I usually stop arguing when I lose the conviction for my own position, long before I actually start considering that the other guy is right.
(You don't see this when I argue about religion because I've put more thought into religion than anything else in my life. My atheism is very strongly grounded, and it would take a long series of feats that I think are impossible to break that position.)

In summary, I believe things because I am convinced that they are correct, and otherwise don't have a solid opinion one way or the other. I am more than happy to change my views about a subject if I see compelling evidence for it, because I just want to know what is correct.
As I find out more and more about things, I'm less likely to change my position because my beliefs are based on the full domain of knowledge I've gained about the subject.

#344255 4 2007-07-17T22:50:54Z Tsukatu
I don't really like to use the word "choice" when talking about Free Will for precisely this reason (though I usually end up doing so because it's the best I can think of).
There is a meaningful difference between Free Will and Free Choice. I'm a Hard Determinist by your definition in the OP, but I firmly believe that humans face choices every day, so I'll readily tell you that there is such thing as "Free Choice," though that term is somewhat awkward. However, I will deny (until convinced otherwise, if that happens) that there is some magical intending force that guides you to make any given choice, completely free of your natural tendencies (which reduces to experiences, which reduces to brain chemistry, which reduces to the deterministic laws of the universe).

Imagine such a robot:
The robot is designed to dig a hole in the ground. The robot receives sensory input and assesses the plot of land it has been told to dig up. The robot then considers the means by which it could accomplish this task - after some processing, it determines that the functional methods of digging up the dirt are with its hands and with a nearby shovel.
The robot is clearly presented with a choice.
The robot then considers both options and decides which method is most effective. After weighing both options, the robot has determined that the shovel is most effective, and chooses the shovel.
If you were to put the robot in the same circumstance multiple times, he would pick the shovel every time. He can't make any choice other than to use the shovel, and this is why he can't be said to have Free Will; his decision-making is all determined by a process that only has one possible outcome.

So, again, I will happily admit that we have "Free Choice," though that particular phrasing is a little awkward, but I am also convinced that we do not have "Free Will."

Your OP pretty much relies on the existence of choice to prove Free Will, when in fact they have little correlation. You have proven that we are presented with choices, not that we are free from deterministic forces that will lead us to make any specific choice. If you believe in a deterministic universe, you'd have to believe that some part of us is supernatural in order to believe in Free Will.
#344266 20 2007-07-17T23:13:29Z Tsukatu
Quote: AMomentLikeThis, July 17, 2007 04:55 pm
I could never imagine falling 'in love' with one of the characters. Falling 'in love' with a cartoon character is lust more than anything.
I really don't think so.

Humans fall in love because they want to be in a certain person's company, including in her romantic company. Meeting in person is not actually a requirement. In many cases, that can be an unhealthy sort of love, but it could just as easily be extended to someone you meet through business in which neither of you physically appear before one another. It's also easily possible to fall in love with someone whom you've not only ever met but probably never will meet, such as a celebrity. As long as you know enough about the person's life, behavior, character, etc., you can't really call that love unhealthy.
When you're talking about anime characters, you're simply guaranteed to never personally interact with her. But an anime can show you a great deal about that fictional character's personality, and so falling in love with an anime character is little different from falling in love with someone you'll never meet - it's still love in the truest sense of the word.

Hell, you don't even have to see someone to fall in love. Many people don't care in the slightest about looks, or are satisfied with a description. I bet you plenty of people have fallen in love with characters they've read about in a book, of whom any sort of illustrations have never been made.

But what bothers me a little more is that you say that anime characters can't present any traits other than their appearance. Unless you're looking at static images and not seeing that character interact with her world in the slightest, then yeah, it'd be lust (yet also in the truest sense of the word). But when you're looking at, as you say it, a "cartoon character," you actually get less from the appearance, and your knowledge of that character's behavior and personality is much larger in proportion, compared to what you would know if the character's appearance was more realistic. It is far more shallow to be in lust with an anime character than it is to be in lust with a human, because you know even less.

Then again, that doesn't make falling in love with an anime character very functional. If you are in love with a fictional character, or broader still, someone you'll never meet, that could very well impact your realistic romantic life. You could subconsciously turn down romantic prospects, for example, because you subconsciously compared her to an object of your love whom you'll never meet and found the more realistically feasible prospect inferior.

Being in love with an anime character, just like being in love with any fictional character, and just like being in love with someone you will never interact with (such as a celebrity), is just as much love as love for someone you could know in person, albeit guaranteed to be unrequited.

That said, I'd totally sex Haruhi any day of the week.

You say that free will must be the kind of thing that encompasses those two incompatible elements. I don't see why it must be. As I said, that sort of free will is logically impossible under any scenario.
Logical inconsistency in the meaning of a phrase is never an argument to change the meaning of that phrase. When we talk about a "square circle," we really are talking about something that's supposed to be both a square and a circle; it's an impossible thing, but we don't use that as a reason to change the meaning of the phrase to refer to something more practical.

I meant what I said about the intellectual dishonesty.
"If you are presented with choices, you have Free Will" is narrowing your scope strictly to events that happen to you, and becomes a term that has nothing to do with your inherent ability to choose your own outcomes. Free Will should be about some ability of yours.

I'm standing in line at Starbucks and I have an option to choose a mocha or a latte - therefore I have Free Will? What if some external circumstances force me to choose one over the other, like someone threatening to kill my family if I don't choose a mocha? By your definition, that doesn't matter because I'm still presented with a choice, and therefore, by your definition, I still have Free Will.

Everyday usage of philosophical terms tends to be inaccurate and inconsistent. Atilla can tell you about weight vs mass in everyday vs academic contexts.
I firmly believe that Free Will has the technical definition that I'm arguing for. cal me crazy, but I swear to the goddess that I see the future in the dreams I actually remember.

For example, I dreamed I met this girl with a bunch of my friends after a long hard day. #345625 14 2007-07-20T23:42:50Z Tsukatu
CounterStrike is always a classic, as is Half-Life Deathmatch.
If your group is 4-6 people big, you could try out the Splinter Cell 3 multiplayer, which is designed specifically for that number of players (one group is 2 or 3 spies, the other is 2 or 3 soldiers).

If you're playing with one other person, I highly, highly recommend Splinter Cell 3 cooperative mode. I'm really into that concept, though, so I may be kind of biased.
Actually, so much am I in love with that idea that I'll hijack the topic slightly - does anyone know of any excellent games you can play cooperatively (preferrably 2-3 people)?

As for turn-based strategy...
Any 'Total War' game is excellent if you want to play a relaxed multiplayer game, since any given turn can last a bit (especially if you want to command the battles yourself). One of the best LAN parties I've had with a group of friends was spread out across a few rooms playing Shogun: Total War. We had a movie going on in one room, music in another, and on any given person's turn, the rest of us were just chilling out and talking. Our idea for future games (which we sadly didn't have) was to set up two additional monitors so that the rest of us could watch personally-commanded battles from the perspectives of both people involved. I started playing a game of chess with someone else on the side, too.
Anyway, the point is that it was very good times. I don't know if you'd enjoy that sort of an evening or whether you're more focused on an action-packed shooter, but I found it most excellent.

For Conservatives who think that life is sacred:

What'd you have for breakfast today?
I had a bean and cheese burrito. It was pretty tasty.
Unfortunately, all the products that went into it had at one point been alive. Some farmer took the time to grow the plants, just so they'd grow up to be slaughtered, treated, and stuffed in our mouths. How is that unlike raising a cow just so it can be slaughtered, scorching its flesh, and then stuffing their damaged and torn corpses down our gullets?
I didn't have any bacon, at least. If you believe that life is sacred, you should most definitely stay away from bacon. Can you believe those pigs are raised in horrible conditions, and that the only purpose of life - sacred, sacred life - is to be murdered, have its wonder of a natural phenomenon that is it's body mutilated, torn, and distributed to such ghoulish people who feel no remorse about treating another living thing this way? How can you expect these people to have any morals? What's to stop them from eating another human being? Or a relative? If life is sacred, eating bacon is just as bad as eating your grandmother. If you believe in the sanctity of life, you probably shouldn't be eating bean and cheese burritos, and you definitely shouldn't be eating bacon.
So let's say you stayed away from the bacon, and you just had some pancakes with syrup with scrambled eggs and orange juice. That pretty much minimizes the murder you'd have to commit to get those on your plate. Rather, the murder you commit isn't against anything that has emotions or can think about its circumstances.

And here's where we get to abortions.
Murder is wrong, absolutely. But y'know what makes murder the worst? When something can't defend itself, or doesn't have a say whether it lives or dies. A baby fetus, for example, can't defend itself. And a baby fetus, you say, is alive, and so it's sacred. For those of you Conservatives who say that life begins on conception and that life is sacred, you should definitely be against abortion.
I know this is in Serious Discussion, but let me tell you a quick joke:
What do you call a murdered human fetus? An abortion. But what do you call a murdered bird fetus? An omlette.
Cooking and eating a bird fetus is frighteningly close in its moral implications to killing, cooking, and eating a human fetus. Would you kill, cook, and eat a human fetus? No, of course not! And if life is sacred, you should feel the same way about whale fetuses, elephant fetuses, and bird fetuses.
Y'know what else is alive, just as much as we are? The bacteria you sneezed a few days ago. You didn't give a damn about it's survival, or its happiness and well-being, did you? A life is a life, and if you believe that all life is sacred, you should be torn up about throwing out another life into the cold - just as bad as you'd feel about tossing your children out of the house for good, right out into the snow on Christmas morning.

If you are against abortion because you think that life is sacred, and you eat eggs, even if it's every now and again, you are a hypocrite.

Would you kick a pregnant woman in the uterus? Of course you wouldn't - but you have no problem cracking an egg on the edge of a frying pan?

If you believe in the sanctity of life, you should not be alive. You should've either starved to death long ago, or you should've been living with crippling depression about how utterly vile and disgusting your need to murder just to continue your own existence, that you probably should've killed yourself by now.

So who do we have left, the Conservatives who are against abortion for reasons other than some "sanctity of life" nonsense?

Okay, you could believe that animal life is inferior and is for the most part unworthy of being treated like a human life. In other words, you can believe in the sanctity of human life. That's perfectly fine. It's somewhat arrogant, but it's certainly a solid position.
But if you're like most Conservatives, you're also against all of these hippie liberal programs that take your well-earned income and give it directly to government programs that take care of poor people and/or children. So in other words, if you're a Conservative who claims to believe in the sanctity of human life - why aren't you a pacifist? Why do you support the Conservative agenda that typically involves going to other countries and shooting people? Why don't you support a child's development after birth? You realize that without your contribution, plenty of children will be dead, right? If you believe in the sanctity of human life, you should believe that money is less important than a human life. But by supporting a Conservative agenda, you're saying that you couldn't care less about human life. You only care about the baby until it's born, after which it can grow up to be starving, uneducated, and homeless, and you don't care - this is not consistent with the belief that human life is sacred. This isn't even consistent with the narrow-minded belief that American human life is sacred.

No, you don't believe that life is sacred. You don't think that at all. If you do, you should think you're a terrible human being, and should damned well be ashamed of yourself. The fact that you're still sane despite the fact that you know what a callous monster you are is evidence that you're most likely psychotic.

So what other reasons are there to oppose abortion?
Well, it's still murder, right? Even though you may not place inherent value upon a human life, you can still feel that directly taking away a life is wrong (whereas not supporting it is simply leaving it to its own devices - you made sure it has a fighting chance in the world, and now it has to work hard to succeed). Again, another perfectly valid opinion - if you actually held it.
You've probably guessed this by now, but yeah, you don't have that opinion. You couldn't. I mean, if you're that serious about the fair chance a life should receive to succeed in this world, you must really think that that fetus is a human being. But then why does this belief extend only to abortion, and nothing else? I mean, you don't speak up about fetuses being counted as humans in the census polls, do you? If you have two kids and your wife is pregnant, you say that you have "two kids, and one on the way," instead of "three kids," don't you?

What else is there? You think teenagers ought to be denied this opportunity to get away with careless sexual practice?
How 'bout you own up on the responsibility of raising your kids properly, instead? Abortions are very necessary procedures for victims of rape and for mothers who will die if they have to go through labor - you want to deny these people otherwise happy, healthy lives simply because you can't be bothered to raise your kid properly? My parents never had to demand that TV stations stop showing violent shows - I knew what I could watch and what I couldn't, because my parents were (for the most part) good parents. If you can't raise your child well enough that you're concerned that she'll become a prostitute, don't have children.

Conservatives are morally inconsistent and don't think their ideas through to any meaningful extent, with regards to issues regarding right to life.


What do I think? When do I think life starts?
I don't think life starts at conception, and I don't think life starts at birth. I think life started 3.7 billion years ago and is a process that continues through today. From a purely analytical standpoint, I don't see how a developing fetus is much different from a parasitic, malignant tumor that will probably not require an operation to detach from the patient. When you toss human emotion into the mix, then of course I relate to a human child much more readily than to a chicken egg, but I'm perfectly fine with terminating a pregnancy for the same reason that I'm perfectly fine with cracking open a chicken egg - it's a natural part of life; organisms will dominate other organisms naturally, and there's nothing wrong with that.

But, again, that's from as objectively analytical a standpoint as I can have. If you toss in my human nature and emotions, then I would have far much harder a time terminating an abortion than I would cooking an omlette, but I still believe that net benefit is maximized if abortions are legalized and widely available to the public.

Re: Death

In California, I'm a registered voter of the Human Death Party. It's a party that my friend and I made up to explain many of our views on human life.
Basically, we advocate as much consensual /necessary death as possible. Euthanasia, abortion, and suicide should all be fully legal and readily available to the public. The same goes for contraceptives and comprehensive sex education. We support capital punishment, and we also support programs that encourage adoption as an alternative to birthing a child, as well as cutting funding for insane asylums and the Special Olympics. There are a few other policies about healthcare and welfare, as well. The main focus of this party is to minimize the damage done by overpopulation and old people living too long, because both can wreak havoc socially and economically. (We disagree about cloning.)

This world requires more death. We're above our natural limits as a species, and we desperately need to cut back on the population growth.
My idea for a motto was, "Stop living so much, you selfish bastards," but that conversation never went very far.

But no, I'm otherwise highly against other people deciding when my life ends. If I want to life a long life, it should be my responsibility to make sure that I can handle that. If I can't, then it ought to be my decision alone that I should stop living (unless I deny myself that right by denying someone else the same), and I should be able to easily arrange for some quick and painless euthanasia.

i deeply resent the fact, and wish i dont. I loath the idea of being individually responsible for my actions
"I don't wanna live life, cuz life has paaaaaaiiiin. Waaaaaaaah."
The way I see it, at some point I'm not going to exist anymore. Rather than switching over now (chainsaw to the face - I'll YouTube it), on the chance that existing might actually be more enjoyable than not existing, I don't want to leave the party before I have to and be disappointed.

In other words, Tsukatu's Wager:

-If existing is more enjoyable and I exist for as long as I can, afterward failing to exist for the rest of time: enjoyment is maximized
-If existing isn't more enjoyable and I exist for as long as I can, afterward succeeding to not exist for the rest of time: enjoyment is maximized (infinite enjoyment outweighs finite, lesser enjoyment)
-If existing is more enjoyable and I choose to stop making myself exist as fast as possible: enjoyment is minimized
-If existing isn't more enjoyable and I choose to stop making myself exist as fast as possibe: enjoyment is maximized

This means that if I choose to stop existing as quickly as possible, I have one failure mode. But if I try to continue existing for as long as I can, then I have zero failure modes.

Here's a parallel with fewer words:
You have a square and a circle in your hand, and you can put on of those onto either a square table or a circular table. The rules are:
If you put the square on the square table, you get $50.
If you put the square on the circular table, you die a horrible death.
If you put the circle on either table, you get $50.
...why wouldn't you put the circle down? It doesn't matter what table you put it on - you benefit the same. Only a dumbo dumby-head would choose to put the square on either table.
...and why wouldn't you continue to exist? It doesn't matter whether it turns out that not existing is more enjoyable or not - you benefit the same. Only a dumbo dumby-head would choose to cut his existence short.

southpaw:

Haha, my mom's currently getting ahead of herself on her doctorate thesis in that very field. She already has a Master's in it.
...and I do Natural Language Processing research for the US Navy as my summer job.
Oh, man, how coincidental is this?

But yeah, no, I'm not very partial to the idea that any given culture has a better inherent understanding of any given subject simply because of language.
What I mean, using that eskimo/snow example, is that any human will be able to know just as much as any eskimo about snow, even if they have completely different languages. Every minute difference in snow that would mark a different word for the eskimos can easily be reduced to an observable property. The fact that they've been around snow long enough to care about such minute differences doesn't mean they have a greater potential for understanding all that is snow - it just means they're more knowledgeable about it for the same reason that Americans are more knowledgeable than eskimos about CPU architectures.

I fully agree, though, that most people think in a language. I say "most" because I agree with one of Jung's discoveries, which is that a small proportion of the population thinks mostly in ineffable, abstract terms (and I'm one of them, which has meant for me that I'm a quicker thinker but can have serious difficulty explaining my more brilliant ideas).
