Quote: Mosh, July 30, 2007 11:25 am
Quote: Tsukatu, July 29, 2007 08:46 pm
Unless you're willing to show me some studies in which stimulation of the very same regions produce the very same results in a wide variety of brains, it makes sense to me that different people will store their memories in different parts of any given gyrus.
This study on one individual demonstrates that even without the depicted temporal lobe of the human brain, memories can be evoked by electrode stimulation. A well-cited article, and a six-year old article at that, too. I'm surprised it hasn't been brought up more recently.
This study also shows a much more cited, well-written demonstration of electrode-stimulation through slow-oscillation (increasing and decreasing electrode stimuli above and below a certain median). While it doesn't pertain to the actual remembrance of memories, it does pertain to boosted memory on a trial-tested basis.

Also stated in the second article is a very valuable piece of information regarding the citing of past studies. It simply says they weren't very well documented in the past, and were near-random in their application. Inconvenient to anyone writing a neurostimulation thesis, but just a simple speed-bump for our discussion.

By looking at these two articles, you can come to a number of assumptions. Two of the most prominent are:
-That there is a relation between electrode stimulation of the cortical regions and memories.
or
-That there is a relation between electrode stimulation of the cortical regions and the brain thinking that it remembers something.

I also stumbled upon an article in which a similar experiment was performed on cats, but I felt it irrelevant to cite.

Unfortunately, neither of those studies were of the sort I asked.

They both provide evidence for the assumptions we've been making, so I suppose it's relevant, but those studies have nothing to do with any general statement about the function of all human brains.

#353067 44 2007-08-09T15:47:30Z Tsukatu
Obby:

The problem with increasing the size of insects (*cough*ascoveredbyanymiddleschoolbiologyclass*cough*) is that expanding something by some linear dimension means that its volume will go up by the cube of that amount, and two-dimensional things like surface area only expand by the square of that amount. Surface area is very, very important to know if you're going to figure, say, whether or not the skin will be able to contain the bloody meats of the organism inside of it.
Imagine a cube that's 1 arbitrary unit on each side. Its volume is 1 au, and its surface area is 6 au - that ratio is 1:6, which is pretty safe.
Let's double its dimensions. Now it's 2 au's on each side. Its volume is now 8 au, and its surface area is 24 au - that ratio is also 1:3. The surface of the cube has to work harder to contain that volume.
Let's keep going.
4 au's on a side: volume is 64 au and surface area is 96 au; a 2:3 ratio.
8 au's on a side: volume is 512 au and surface area is 384; a 4:3 ratio.
...and if we get to 10 au's so we can apply this directly to the ant thing: volume is 1000 au and surface area is 600 au; a 5:3 ratio.
Basically, as size increases, the skin has to work much harder to contain the volume.
That's a factor of 10 different than the skin's used to - it now has to work 10 times as hard to contain the ant's bloody meats. And that doesn't apply to just the exoskeleton. The ant's lungs will tear as soon as it takes a breath, its stomach will rip open the first time it eats, and the heart will explode when the ant takes its first step. This doesn't even bring into consideration the fact that it would require dangerously low blood pressure so as not to tear its veins when (and if) its heart makes its first pulse, and we're of course assuming that this ant won't be trying to actually move anywhere.
So how do we help this thing live? Well, we can start by increasing the thickness of every surface area it has tenfold. This doesn't come close to solving the problem, however, since an increase in stomach lining, vein thickness, etc., is even more of an increase in volume, which ends up requiring the exoskeleton to be up to 100 times as thick (1000x thicker than its original size) just to contain the bare minimum required for the ant to continue a fragile, sedentary existence.
If we were to set this thing into motion right now, with its massively increased weight, it wouldn't be strong enough to expand its carapace enough to draw in a single breath. Let's fix that. To move, things need muscle, right? Aww, hell, that sounds like an awful lot more volume, and dense volume, at that. Already this ant's exoskeleton is 100 times thicker than it should be, meaning that it's basically something of an organic rock that, deep down inside, has some barely functioning organ system, and now we want to put more stuff in it?
Well, more volume means more exoskeleton thickness. If, as you said, this ant turned out to be about as bit as your hand, its exoskeleton would have to be the entirety of that volume with the exception of some internal, organic stuff about as big as your thumb.
I'm just going to skip the fact that its organs will need even more thickness to 'em to resist multiple organ failure due to the weight of the rest of the body on them.

There are plenty of other disadvantages the ant now has, assuming it can actually function. For one thing, producing offspring would require significantly more resources and effort, it would require far more resources, itself, it would require much longer periods of rest, etc.

And that's why ants aren't bigger than they are.

To make a larger organism, you have to ditch the "exoskeleton" design entirely and go with an internal skeleton, meaning that the ant would become something like a mouse or a lizard or something.
Other than fish, the only animal I can think of that's that size and that focuses on producing lots and lots of offspring is a bunny. Bunnies are also like ants in that they dig complex homes in the ground.
Do bunnies rule the world, Obby?

So no, I don't think that ants 10 times their size would rule the world. I think ants 10 times their size would be bunnies.

As I understand it, the proportion of the measured material remains at a more or less fixed percentage while whatever it is being measured is alive, and that's the standard we use. Regarding your "school uniform" problem... I think you need to understand something:
Private schools are private institutions. They often ask their students to wear uniforms.

When you apply to a private school and the private school accepts you, it is its right, just as it's the right of any private institution, to deny you business for any or no reason whatsoever. One of the things they ask you to do is wear a uniform. You are not legally bound to wear a uniform, but do keep in mind that they're not legally bound to continue educating you.
Let's say I am a private institution who is willing to perform a service for you, such as baking you a cookie. Let's say I bake a mean cookie, enough that parents are willing to pay ridiculously high prices for their children to receive my cookies. I happen to have the philosophy that cookies are best baked when the person who ordered it is standing on one leg throughout the entire baking process. So your parents come to me and say, "we'd like a four years' supply of cookies for our son." I say, "sure, but your son has to stand on one foot for the time it takes to bake those cookies." If you hand me any bullshit letter saying that asking someone to stand on one foot is a human rights issue, I'll just laugh in your face and up the price, if I don't deny you service.

#356399 11 2007-08-17T15:40:41Z Tsukatu
*groan*
Are you serious, southpaw?
"Awareness of transfer of energy?"

While the definition of consciousness is hotly debated, the definition of "awareness" really isn't. "Awareness" only comes about when something has the right amount of cortical matter, which plants don't. Plants are an excellent example of an organism that is completely mechanical - the plant has absolutely no decision-making abilities or thoughts, consciousness, or awareness of any kind; all of its structure is devoted entirely to growing physically.
(For example, here's how vision is processed by your brain:
1) Your occipital lobe receives the input from your optic nerves, and sends it (mostly) in two different directions: the ventral pathway (toward the parietal lobe) and the dorsal pathway (toward the temporal lobe).
2) The ventral pathway identifies the object and the dorsal pathway determines its context. They both forward the information to your prefrontal lobe so you can actually make use of these identifications.
3) Your prefrontal lobe receives that information, decides its importance, and shifts it higher on your priority list based on how unlike the object is from what you were expecting. The entire process has so far been entirely unconscious.
4) AWARENESS: Information is sent back to your occipital lobe, specifically to your V1 area, which is in the extrastriate cortex. If this information does not get back to the occipital lobe, you are not aware of the visual stimulus.
...and that's how visual awareness comes about. People who can perform all of steps 1-3, but not 4, exhibit the "blindsight" phenomenon: they think they are completely blind (which makes sense because they have no awareness of any visual stimula), and yet if asked to guess about what they're looking at they'll get it right with a very, very high accuracy, as though they were able to see the stimulus normally, but they still insist that they're just "blindly" guessing.)
In short, "awareness" is achieved through a specific pattern of neural activity. Since plants don't really have any meaningful amount of nerves, it's really not very reasonable to say that they have any sort of "awareness" whatsoever. They are purely mechanical; they have as much "awareness of energy transfer" as a clock does.

"Awareness of energy transfer."
So, for example, if I were to stare blankly at a wall while I thought intensely about something, I'd be unconscious by your definition. I actually do this quite a lot at work - I stare at the wall behind my computer monitor while I think about a better way to write something, or while I think about the theory behind the research I do. My mind isn't paying attention to much of anything else.
Yet I say I'm deep in thought, and that I'm still quite conscious.

"Awareness of energy transfer."
You should write sci-fi. Y'know, the cheap kind they find in drug stores. There's an art to writing that stuff, and I think you have it down.

#357669 54 2007-08-20T23:49:20Z Tsukatu
Dave didn't say it, but I sure as hell will.
*ahem*
Science and religion conflict.

Science is based on application of reason and copious quantities of evidence before anything is believed.
Religion demands that you make several obnoxiously pervasive assumptions about the function of the universe that you should never ever question.

You may have noticed that throughout all of history religion has been openly, directly, and in many cases violently opposed to scientific progress.

And how is it exactly that theists use science? They distort it with theories like Intelligent Design.
Here's how theists use science:
1) Develop arbitrary conclusion about the universe.
2) Use science to find evidence for this conclusion.
This is not how science works.
Here is how science works:
1) Notice a pattern.
2) See if you can make a generalization about it.
3) Request that the scientific community finds proof that you're wrong.
4) If the scientific community proves you wrong, go back to step 1 or 2. Otherwise, proceed to step 5.
5) Well damn, it's a scientific principle now. Go back to step 1, but specific to what you've just discovered.

In other words, science does not begin with one conclusion in mind, but it builds on basic knowledge in an undetermined direction.

I really don't mean to condescend, but there's the right way to interpret statistical data and the wrong way to interpret statistical data.
In this case, we're looking at the difference in proportion of atheist scientists versus religious scientists, so the wrong way to interpret that 15% vs 30% is "most of Australia's scientists are still theists," and the right way to interpret that is "the proportion of scientists who are atheists is fully twice the percentage of atheist population."
Here's another example::
In America (2002), roughly 16% of the population was atheistic, and 0.4% of the American (2002) prison population was atheistic. The wrong interpretation is "atheists are the minority," because that doesn't address the difference in the rate, but only states the amount in one of the relevant places. The correct way to interpret this information is, "the proportion of atheists in prison is one-fortieth the proportion of atheists in the population."
We can therefore conclude that either "atheists are more likely to stay out of prison" or "people are less likely to be atheists in prison."
Similarly, we can conclude that either "atheists are more likely to become scientists" or "scientists are more likely to be atheists."
Either way, my point stands.

We're all forced as humans to use logic as a standard, and I wouldn't be able to function if I refused to acknowledge the legitimacy of anything that I conclude logically (which would be everything, including the fact that I conclude things logically, which would just make me plain ol' insane).
Even so, when we use logic, we see that it can be applied consistently, and this makes us very, very happy, because we can then make progress. If the logic we used did not produce consistent results (i.e., if the logic we used does not lead to consistent conclusions), then a computer wouldn't exist and I wouldn't be typing on one. That and we'd be chimps with severe cases of schizophrenia.
I have far fewer problems accepting logic as an axiom over the foundational claims of most religions because the application of logic has been fantabulously successful, 100% of the time. We have such stupendous quantities of case histories in which the application of our logic was successful (the sum of pretty much all logical conclusions ever made, such as "today is Thursday because yesterday was Wednesday") that abandoning logic appears to be an extremely poor idea.
I define science as applying logic in order to understand the universe. The logical way to do this is to only make conclusions when the probability of truth is extremely high and when there has been no evidence to the contrary.
It gets a little circular because acceptance of logic is being a good scientist, and being a good scientist is a logical thing to do, but as I've said I have few problems accepting this because it is a requirement for me to be functional, and my cortical pleasure centers are active when I compare my current capacity for function versus inability to function.
Religion says, "hey, I have this idea, but you'll need to abandon scientific thought momentarily - is that cool with you?" The reason scientific thought needs to be abandoned momentarily when accepting a religion is because the claim you accept is not based on any sort of high probability or evidence; it could just as easily be the case that it's not right. As a matter of fact, there is a high probability that it's wrong, since religion describes a single case that is essentially a guess about the nature of reality, and it's no more likely than the infinite possible natures reality could hold. I feel a story about a cookie coming on...
There's a box on the ground. For the purposes of this comparison, it should be assumed that the box is impossible to open or examine, and the only thing known about the box is that it's a box. If you were to think scientifically, you would end up ignoring the box after you discovered that there is no way the box can be examined. Religion comes along and tells you there's a cookie in the box. How does it know? It doesn't. What are the reasons it thinks there is a cookie in the box? There aren't any. Is there a reason Religion chose a cookie over any other object? Nope.
So how likely is it that there's a cookie in the box? Well, for one thing, consider every object you have ever seen in your life - how many of them are cookies? Now add to that every object you've never seen in your life. The percentage of those things that are a cookie is infinitely small; religion has an infinitely small chance of being right.
But that doesn't mean that it is wrong, only that it's probably wrong.
Rejecting religion is akin to pointing out that the chance that it's correct is probably wrong and therefore refusing to believe it because it wouldn't be a scientific thing to do. Accepting religion, on the other hand, goes flagrantly against this scientific rule that you should only believe things that are probably true.
...and that also helps to explain why I think religion is unscientific.

Um... believing in things you know aren't true.
Taking the scientific approach to things, the definition of which I'll use in this explanation I've stated at the end of my response to Atilla, is the most reasonable thing to do. It has worked extremely well for us. It generally benefits everyone.
Believing something you know isn't true does not follow this approach, and is therefore not effectively guaranteed to be as awesome as a scientific sort of view. I suppose it could be beneficial, or maybe even better, for yourself and the world as a whole, but there are a number of problems with this:
1) you have no assurance that it is the case that it will be at least as beneficial for parties involved as a scientific approach
2) this notion is hostile to scientific thought, and you can very well be encouraged to go even farther in your deviance from scientific thinking (wow, that almost sounded like an uptight moral authority - "you deviant")
3) you are lying to yourself, and you know it; this is not healthy
4) what's wrong with adopting those views as part of your personality / general behavior without forcing yourself to believe in something you know is wrong?
Let's say you're thinking scientifically and realize that you should be a more moral person. You believe you have good reason to think that Christianity is wrong - not that it's unlikely, but that it's false. Let's say you also draw the mistaken conclusion that Christianity turns its adherents into more moral people because of the looming threat of eternal agony. If you were to become a Christian, you would still know that the looming threat of eternal agony is a farce, and it wouldn't really discourage you from acting much differently. But even if it does turn you into a more moral person, what's wrong with simply adopting (what you think is) Christian morality without becoming a Christian? You know that Christianity is false, which means that you basically became a more moral person purely through your own efforts, so why is Christianity involved at all? In addition to taking the choice that is more logically beneficial to yourself and others, you're also avoiding problems 1 through 3, above.
And now that I've said all that, I can deduce, using logic, that believing something you know is wrong is a bad idea, because it comes down to these choices:
1) do what you know will work
2) do what may work, with risk involved, where the thing that might work can just as easily be accomplished in #1
And that basically reduces to:
1) profit
2) profit, maybe
...where "profit" is to the same magnitude.

No, I got that far. My problem isn't with omnipotence (in this thread, anyway).
We have Free Will. When we say "we," we're referring to something that does exist in this universe, and so much be logically consistent.
One of the parts of omnipotence that we puny humans can comprehend is that omnipotence entails the ability to do anything, completely without limits that we can comprehend.
I don't know about you, but I can comprehend the concept of prediction.
Free Will can't exist if our actions can be predicted, either by something within this universe or outside of it - it doesn't matter.
Prediction falls within the scope of "anything" when we're talking about doing things, and so predicting things is something an omnipotent being can do. Maybe omnipotence means more than being able to do anything, and we wouldn't know, but what we can comprehend about omnipotence is that the omnipotent thing can do anything. If we come across something that can't do anything, then we wouldn't call it omnipotent, even though it may have a lot in common with omnipotence other than this inability to do anything in the natural universe, but from what we understand we would not call it omnipotent. God, we are calling omnipotent. God can do anything.
*gives the horse a few more solid kicks*
Once events can be predicted, Free Will as we comprehend it (the ability of your consciousness to directly influence the unfolding of future events) crumbles, because Free Will as we comprehend it cannot exist if there is a single, true future that we can't help but live through.

#361011 33 2007-08-30T22:39:09Z Tsukatu
So why is it that I can say "God is illogical" and have people yelling at me, but Obby can freely say "logic doesn't apply to God," and it's okay?

Obby:
Even though we can't know anything about God and therefore can't talk about anything from His perspective, we can still damned well talk from ours. We happen to have a universe that abides by logic, and we've studied that to death. If God was to perform some kind of action that would be inconsistent with the logic by which we know the universe operates, we would suddenly get some extremely inconsistent results. 'Course, I suppose God could be a filthy liar, hide the fact that he made a massive change to the universe, and make us think that that was the way it was the whole time, but in this case we're talking about something that, if it exists, will be logically inconsistent, period. An ordinary person can recognize that Free Will + Omniscience is inconsistent, so clearly this big change hasn't happened.

The point is, we've only been talking from our perspective, and we can draw the conclusions we've drawn just fine from it. We may not know God's motives, but we can obviously witness and understand such significant properties of the universe that He effected (allegedly).

Let's say there's a big box, and we all live inside of it. We can't escape the box, and we can't observe or draw any conclusions about the outside of the box. There is a cookie inside the box.
Who put the cookie there? Was it one of us? Was it someone, or something, from outside the box? These questions are irrelevant to our observation that there is, in fact, a cookie inside the box.
When did the cookie begin to exist inside the box? Was it always inside the box? Did it recently appear inside the box? Were our memories changed to think that the cookie has been in the box for as long as we can remember? These questions are irrelevant to our observations that there is, in fact, a cookie inside the box.
How did the cookie get there? Did an outside being knock us all unconscious, slip inside, place the cookie, and escape? Was it teleported inside? Has the cookie always been there? These questions are irrelevant to our observations that there is, in fact, a cookie inside the box.
Why is the cookie there? Did something from outside the box want to see what would happen? Are we meant to fight over the cookie? Is the cookie there due to an accident? Is there no reason at all for the cookie being inside the box? These questions are irrelevant to our observations that there is, in fact, a cookie inside the box.

Quote: blue_tetris, 2007-08-31T00:45:08Z
For example, let's take these values: 6, 5, 4, 3, 2, 1. We'll call these "gene powers". Six is prime cut breeding stud material. One is lowest common denominator Wyoming stock. Assuming that the superior genes win out, then breeding with those like yourself would yield:

6 and 6; offspring 6.
5 and 5; offspring 5.
4 and 4; offspring 4.
3 and 3; offspring 3.
2 and 2; offspring 2.
1 and 1; offspring 1.

Ultimately, this has done nothing to assist the gene pool. The sum of all components of the newer generation still add to 21. Now, if we were to breed unmatched pairs of quite different people and assume that the superior genes win out, we get:

6 and 1; offspring 6.
5 and 2; offspring 5.
4 and 3; offspring 4.
3 and 4; offspring 4.
2 and 5; offspring 5.
1 and 6; offspring 6.

A much higher array. And this is assuming that there is only a single trait which determines how "good" genes are. In actuality, humans have many traits with many degrees of potence. Assuming that different gene pools have different strengths and weaknesses, humans composed of stock from different gene pools would take on the superior gene in a variety of different facets.

[6,1,3,8,2,4,9] and [1,7,6,2,5,5,3] would make a nice healthy [6,7,6,8,5,5,9]; assuming that the system you used to discuss the heredity of traits was absolutely sound.

That video was actually inspired by a discussion I was having with my supervisor during my summer internship, and he mentioned an experiment I wish I could find, and I realize that this isn't hard evidence because I don't have an actual case study to show you, so consider it a musing if you want to be a lawyer and remove it from consideration entirely.
The experiment involved two groups of ducks. The general idea was that there were two kinds of duck, black and white, and they were all mothers attending to a nest. The researchers took pairs of one white duck and one black duck, hatched their eggs away from their mothers, and colored half of the white ducks black and half of the black ducks white. Then they put those hatchlings in a room with the two parents, and the first thing the parents did was gather the ducks of the same color, regardless of what the natural color was. When the coloring was taken away, the ducks abandoned the ones who were a different color (and the other duck would adopt them).

Quote: Gforce20, September 02, 2007 11:05 pm
The ability to enter or exit dimensions as I choose.

Why?

Because the universe we live in has 3.5 dimensions: 3 matter dimensions and half a time dimension (we can only go forward). When you think about it, if there were a 2d person, he/she could only see in those two dimensions. If you're in three dimensions, you wouldn't have to be in the same plane as the 2d person. Hence you could turn totally invisible and re-enter the world at any place. You could also go backwards in time, or even look down at time and choose where to go based upon what you see from a 2nd time dimension.
I'd be scared to death to involve a fourth dimension, cuz I could just walk off, or trip, and never be able to find that exact fourth-dimensional depth to be back in the world I know and love.

I'd pick invisibility, for reasons I've already explained in two threads on the topic.
Less fancifully, though, I'd go with some kind of super slow-motion in which I could have excessive amounts of time to plan out and perfectly coordinate things... basically speeding up my brain power drastically. It'd be useful for last-minute cramming before a test, socializing in general, and doing crazy stunts and stuff, not to mention extremely helpful for getting myself out of sticky situations (take all the time in the world to line up a shot with a gun, perfectly coordinate every block and punch, have generally insane reflexes, etc.). If I could somehow cram a full night's rest into, like, eleven minutes, that'd also be pretty dandy.

I don't know, though. I think just about any remotely useful power would greatly help you in life, even in ways you may not realize. Something like not needing to eat or drink could save you loads of time and money in the long run. Not needing to sleep could give you an extra eight hours in the day of productivity, so you could get bored off your ass of video games and actually learn something, and you won't have periods of reduced productivity because you wouldn't ever be groggy. Not needing to breathe, even, would keep you from snoring and waking up your wife, not to mention that it's an excellent precaution against drowning. You could be the guy on the block who has this nifty trick of wearing diving weights into the swimming pool and staying at the bottom for hours.

Let's say, for example, that you're walking down the street, when suddenly a group of four gangbangers pop out of the alleyway and start firing at you with semiautomatic handguns. The first thing that happens is the guy driving the car behind you is nodding off at the wheel and accidentally swerves to hit one of those guys, the second guy realizes that he forgot to actually fill his magazine, and the third and fourth smash into each other in an attempt to jump at you at the same time, knocking one unconscious and sending both of their guns flying - the first one goes off upon contact with the asphalt and shoots the conscious one in the braincase, and the other gun flies neatly into your hand, ending up aimed at the guy who has an empty mag. Over a table of imagined tea and plastic china, she declares that it would be a very naughty thing for one of the dollies to spill the tea. She then reaches over, grabs the hand of one of the dollies, and knocks over one of the cups with the dolly's hand, because she has decided that that's what that particular dolly will be like, and that that's what that particular dolly will do because of the way she has decided the dolly will be. She then proceeds to punish the dolly for something for which she deserves the blame for entirely. And if we're talking about a Christian God (who punishes people with Hell), the punishment involves cutting open the dolly with a pair of scissors, gleefully tearing out the stuffing, and methodically coloring the exposed stuffing with a red marker.

If I may...
When I was about 9 or 10, my friends and I stumbled across a very small cave by the beach. In the process of exploring that cave, we stumbled onto a stack of what must have been a dozen issues of Playboy. We all got excited that we were doing something we shouldn't have been, obviously, but we got bored of the magazines very quickly, because we were 10 goddamned years old. I remember picking up a magazine and flipping through it, but feeling completely disappointed. I didn't really understand what the hell I was looking at or why adults were all so serious about it, and it all seemed like no big deal to me. It was just... wierd. None of us really had any inclination to continue looking at them. We just re-buried them and continued on our merry way.
In retrospect, I think I would've been confused and terrified if I had seen any hardcore pornography at that age. So I agree with you that hardcore pornography can seriously mess a kid up.
If I may continue...
My parents never said a thing to me about my Special Purpose or sexuality in general. Not one thing. I got to discover all of that for myself. Thing is, though, I was very resourceful, and so I sort of eased into looking at softcore pornography. At first, I was completely filled with shame and guilt, and felt totally wierd about it, but I gradually got much more comfortable with it. It certainly never led me to anything sexually perverse - I didn't try to sneak into the girls' locker room or anything, and I remain to this day disgusted with the thought of stumbling in on my parents, and I think that's all good and healthy. I had some friends at school who I knew came from very strict households, and to my surprise those were the kids who couldn't stop talking about sex, and said the most awkward and retarded things about girls and sex. I always stayed as far from the subject as possible, because I knew that those retards would start saying stupid things again. It was also those kids who didn't have a clue who tried hiding in the girls' locker room and such. All in all, I was far more mature about the subject than most kids my age - and I credit that entirely to my decision to explore the subject on my own terms and at my own pace several years before society would deem it acceptable for me to begin responsibly having sex. To this day, I'm annoyed at people who talk about girls purely in sexual terms, and I leave the conversation if I can't change the subject. My mind is pretty much always far from that. I'm more of a lovey-dovey sort of person than a "ya man lets get hammered and do all the vag this side of the river" kind of person, the latter of which I look down upon considerably, as a matter of fact. When someone says something like "you need some pussy," that officially marks the end of my willingness to listen to any advice they give me.
So, what's the point of all that? Well, I think the way I learned about sexuality was an excellent way of doing so, and I can't help but think that the very people you're talking about, the ones who can't help but think of women as sex objects and who talk about having sex in very lewd terms, are the sorts of people who weren't properly introduced to the subject. #17182 1 2007-09-12T01:49:24Z Tsukatu
Sentience is normally thought of as having consciousness; thinking.
I don't believe in the existence of anything supernatural like a soul or spirit, so I think that we should be able to narrow down sentience and define it in terms of organization of matter and energy states.

Here's how thinking works:
Your brain is made up of billions of neural cells, which have a very simple "processing" center and a long tube called an axon that sends a charge when activated. At the end of the axon is a large number of dendrites, each of which connect to other neural cells. That way, when one neural cell fires, the ones in contact with it are affected. A neuron will fire (which means it will release a charge) when it receives enough of what is called an action potential, which basically means that a neural cell has to reach a certain higher energy state. Some of the other neural cells attached to our neural cell, when they fire, will increase our neural cell's activation energy. The others, though, will decrease our activation energy. When the activation energy of our neural cell reaches a certain threshold, it will fire, which will in turn increase the activation energies of some of the neural cells it's attached to and decrease the activation energies of the other neural cells it's attached to.
This happens at an extremely high frequency, in extremely large amounts, constantly. This is how cortical thinking works.

So what we call our sentience is really just a royal mess of biochemical interactions and electrical impulses. That's really ALL it is. It's just interactions between matter. Unless you believe in something like a soul, thinking doesn't have any kind of "magic, special rainbow power," in the words someone called Lucidium. At least I think so, because I don't believe in a soul, or similar.

So, knowing this, why do we call ourselves sentient? If we're just a mess of chemicals acting as chemicals act, and a rock is a mess of chemicals acting as chemicals act, what makes us different from a rock?

Here's how a rock will act:
A rock will lie in place, unmoving. If it receives any stimulation from the outside world, if it's poked, if it's yelled at, or if the sky turns to fire, it has no way of knowing or even processing this, and it will continue to lie there.

Here's how a human will act:
A human constantly receives sensory input from his environment, and his behavior is based in part on the stimulation he recevies from the outside world. A human being takes in sights, sounds, smells, tastes, and tactile sensations and responds to them, and he can respond in a relatively short time frame.

If you were to isolate a rock in a sterile, featureless room, and then put a bouncy red ball with stars on it into the room, you can observe that the rock has absolutely no mechanism for identifying the fact that the ball is even there at all. The rock can't perceive the ball, and the ball's presence does not change the behavior of the rock in the slightest.

If you were to isolate a human in a sterile, featureless room, and then put a bouncy red ball with stars on it into the room, the human would respond immediately. The human would respond to the ball's presence at the very least by tracking it with his eyes. The sound of the ball bouncing could frighten him and he could leap to his feet and give the ball its space. The color of the ball and its motion could anger the human, leading him to attack the ball. If the human tries to taste the ball and finds the taste pleasing, he could continue consuming the ball.

The point is that the human has:
-a mechanism to perceive the ball
-a mechanism to comprehend the ball
-a mechanism that directly adjusts his behavior based on his comprehension of the ball

The rock has none of these. These things, in my opinion, are the criteria we can use to determine if something is sentient.

NOTE: I am NOT saying that reacting to a change in the environment, in general, constitutes sentience. If this was true, it would mean that lighting a piece of paper on fire and seeing it burn is grounds to call the piece of paper sentient. I am saying that a reaction must be produced which is caused by an internal mechanism based on that mechanism's comprehension of an outside stimulus. The change in behavior MUST come from an internal mechanism that directly sends the signal to act differently to whatever portion of the system is to change in response. It is the difference between retracting your hand from a white-hot stove and letting it sit and sizzle.

We've already seen how we can test that something has the first mechanism experimentally, but we can also just take that something apart to make sure that it actually has the appropriate mechanisms if we want to be sure. For example, we know that the human eye does, in fact, send signals to the brain that are different based on the wavelengths of the photons that hit the rods and cones in the retina, that this signal becomes any number of things based on different combinations of signals sent through the optic nerve (e.g. to the 'chair' comprehension center if the pattern of signals resembles the pattern that would result from viewing a chair), and that the brain will then have active signals in regions responsible for thinking about sitting, which may be forwarded to the motor cortex on the frontal edge of the parietal lobe if the human's somatosensory cortex has signals associated with muscle fatigue, resulting in the human's movement toward the chair and sitting upon it. The human would not have acted in this way if the object was, say, a water faucet, because the photons that would bounce off of the water faucet would not be turned into a pattern of electrical impulses that resembles the pattern of electrical impulses resulting from the collection of photons bounced off of a chair.
Anyway, the brain is the human's mechanism to perceive stimulation, his mechanism to comprehend that stimulation, and his mechanism to adjust his behavior based on his comprehension of that stimulus. The human is therefore sentient.

So let's start applying these criteria to things we normally think of as sentient and non-sentient, and see if we run into any problems.

The obvious test case: a rock
The way a rock acts is not actually based on any kind of chemical interaction inside the rock. The rock doesn't have a processing center that directly commands any other part of the rock to act in a manner any different from a normal behavior (which it is lacking). The closest thing a rock has to a mechanism to perceive a stimulus is the shockwave created on a molecular level when the rock is poked, but that signal dies very rapidly and doesn't actually reach any carefully-arranged portion of the rock in which that shockwave can go different routes based on an internal arrangement of matter and energy states inside of the rock, so pressing on the rock with any intensity and with any object will never make the rock do anything other than act like an inert clump of matter. There are no complicated sequences of events that can result based on any special internal arrangements inside the rock to produce any change in behavior for the rock.
The rock is therefore non-sentient.

I'd move on to a human at this point, but I just did that two paragraphs up.

Test case: a bug
A bug usually, like a human, has eyes. That statement establishes that the bug has a mechanism to perceive its surroundings, that the photon-receiving cells in its eyes send a signal to a mass of nerves inside the bug, and that the signal then goes in a unique route based on the properties of the object viewed. But that's really no big deal, because a video camera does that, too, and we don't normally consider a video camera to be sentient. The difference is that the bug has a mechanism that then works with this information and develops a set of signals that it will send to its limbs to produce a unique reaction to a visual stimulus. That's what makes the bug sentient.
However, there is still an argument in the fact that more modern video cameras will work with the information they take in and automatically adjust how it handles, for example, automatic lighting or focus. These sorts of features make video cameras essentially computers, which I'll get to in a second. But a video camera without these features is clearly non-sentient because it doesn't have any internal mechanism for changing what it is doing or changing its behavior based on the information taken in.

Test case: a cat
Just like a bug and a human, a cat has many different senses that can produce a variety of different results based on an internal mechanism that the cat uses to "comprehend" the stimulus. The cat will send the appropriate signal to its limbs from an internal arrangement of matter and energy states, where that signal depends on how the stimulus was perceived by the mechanism whose job it was to carry out that perception. The cat is most definitely sentient.

Test case: a computer
A computer has a mechanism for perceiving stimulation: a mouse and a keyboard. A computer has a mechanism for comprehending that input: the CPU, not to mention any running programs that are looking to interpret keyboard or mouse input. A computer has a mechanism for making a change in its behavior as adjusted through an internal mechanism as the result of an interpretation of stimulus. I would therefore call a computer sentient. Well, provided that it was actually running a program that took in input, did something with it, and responded in a unique way specifically because of a decision to do so made by the internal mechanism that comprehends the input. A computer is not sentient when it's more or less a space heater or turned off.
However, consider that a computer, much unlike an organism, is entirely subject to the whim of whoever controls it. It does not grow or improve itself, it doesn't learn, it doesn't innovate, it is only active when we decide that it should be active, and it has an extremely limited capacity for "sensation" (keyboard and mouse input). The closest organic equivalent to a computer would be an extremely submissive, blind, numb, handcrank-operated autistic who is incapable of learning (though his capacity for factual memory is astounding) and can become inert matter for an indefinite amount of time upon request. Because I don't think that the ability to learn or to innovate are requirements of sentience (as many smaller insects or simpler organisms who are otherwise normally considered sentient do neither of these things), I have few problems calling computers sentient. It is a very, very limited form of sentience, limited more than even a bug in many ways, but is still sentience. Computers are most definitely not LIFE, and some people may not take too well to the idea that a computer is sentient because it is not organic, but I think a computer, even one produced today, has the potential to be just as sentient as a simpler creature that we would call sentient.

Test case: a tree
See "How Trees Work."


How Trees Work:

There is no internal, central mechanism that decides the behavior of a tree. A tree is actually an excellent example of an organic automaton whose only purpose is to propagate itself and generate copies of itself.

Let's compare a growing tree to a supercomputer whose goal it is to maximize its ability to produce mobile agents of its will. The supercomputer is constantly churning out new robots and sending them radially outward toward land that doesn't have robot factories built on it already. This sort of robot civilization doesn't really have any central hub because each robot constructed has the computing power of the supercomputer. Its procedure is essentially to find land that doesn't have a factory on it and build a robot factory there, one that produces robots who will do exactly the same. Let's say that the supercomputer starts off on land that has mineral-rich land to the North, very hostile land to the West, land with very scarce resources to the East, and an ocean to the South (the robots are only built to survive on land, and don't actually know what an ocean is or what to do if they find one).
North: The robots who voyage north will find that minerals are very easy to come by, and so the factories are completed in short order and have a very high output. The spread of the robots to the north is very rapid and successful.
East: The robots arrive at land that doesn't have a factory, but they spend too long of a time searching for materials out of which to construct a factory. When it is finally built, there are hardly anymore resources to start producing more robots. Expansion toward the east is very, very cripplingly slow, but the central plot of land is still happily churning out robots in all directions, so resources continue to be devoted to the East, even though production there is almost non-existent. The robots who walk around searching for materials eventually run out of battery power and die.
West: Resources are not as plentiful as to the north, but a factory can still be built at a reasonable pace. The only trouble is that that land happens to get hit from orbit by eleven thermonuclear warheads every two weeks. Every time the robots begin building a factory, it is annihilated, as are all robots in that area. The central plot still churns out robots and sends them in that direction though, so it's still expending resources on them even though there's zero progress.
South: The robots find the ocean and find that they can't proceed. They either stand at the shore until they run out of battery life and die, or wander in another direction.

The end result is that the robots have grown north, and not much of anywhere else. There's a little stub on their eastern side, but it's really not worth mention.
How can the expansion of these robots be helped? The answer is simple: introduce a mechanism that allows the robots to report back to some central database of the success of the expansion by region, and then have that central database determine how many robots are sent where so that expansion is more efficient (i.e. cuts down on the wasted resources). In other words, we can give the robots sentience. Unless we do that, if we were to look at the robots progress after some time and see that they've only expanded north, it would be a very silly thing to say that the robots "avoided" the east and west, or that they "chose" to grow in a particular direction. The fact is that they were trying to expand EVERYWHERE, and simply failed in many places.

A tree grows in much the same way. It devotes resources to growing everywhere. Based on its DNA, different proportions of it can grow at different rates (redwoods, for example, grow faster upward than they do outward), but it's still more or less growing every which way. Even so, the point of this is to show that trees don't "avoid" objects or "choose" to grow toward the Sun - they in fact grow full speed ahead completely regardless of obstacles, and the portions of it that grow toward the Sun are the portions that actually end up surviving the best, which is why we see those portions and not the ones that couldn't possibly have survived.
Let's put a growing plant in a similar situation as the supercomputer we were talking about earlier. North of the plant is an open patch of mineral-rich soil with full exposure to sunlight and rain. The land to the West of the plant is Mr. Perepelitsa's property, and he hires a gardener to keep the plant we're talking about out of his petunias. The land to the East of the plant is a sandbox, and it's also completely blocked from the Sun by another, larger plant. To the South of the plant is a concrete wall. To make things interesting, let's also stretch a thick lead tube, one meter in diameter, about two meters above the plant.
Let's see what happens when the plant devotes resources to growing in every direction. When it tries to grow into the sandbox to the West, it gets absolutely no resources and its growth in that direction is a complete failure... but that doesn't stop the plant from continuously trying (if the sandbox were to be removed and the tree blocking the Sun were to be cut down, our plant will become successful in growing to the east). If the plant tries to grow to the west, Mr. Perepelitsa's gardener is just going to weed-whack that portion of it out of existence... but the plant won't stop growing into Mr. Perepelitsa's petunias, and will just have to be cut next week. The plant can try growing to the south, but will fail miserably because it can't grow through a solid wall... but it will still devote resources to trying just that, and its trunk will end up flush against the wall. The plant can really only successfully grow to the north. It TRIES to grow in every direction, but after some time we will see that it only succeeded in growing north. It would be a silly thing to say that the plant "avoided" getting weed-whacked (because it never stopped trying to grow into that area), or that it "chose" not to grow into the sandbox or through the wall (why, otherwise, is the trunk of our plant flush against the wall?), because we're only seeing the parts of it that survived. And for the diehard, what about the lead pipe above it? When the tree grows tall enough, it'll just split itself down the middle to accomodate the pipe, no matter how thick it is. How is the plant "avoiding" that pipe, then? How is our plant sensing the pipe, relaying that information to some internal mechanism, and having that mechanism reach the decision that allocating resources toward the portion of the tree that would grow into the pipe is a bad idea? Otherwise, trees have been know to grow right through rocks and other obstacles. It's not an uncommon sight to see a tree integrating itself with a chain-linked fence. For an organism that some say has sentience, it does a pretty terrible job at making decisions and avoiding obstacles.

That leads into a more direct approach: the cellular structure of a tree.
Biologists have long, long ago identified the kinds of cells you can see in a tree, and none of them have any capacity that remotely resembles passing information about external stimuli, any capacity to actually interpret this information (i.e. some internal arrangement of matter and energy states that becomes a unique configuration of matter at varying energy states based on the information passed to it through a mechanism that handles external stimulation), or any capacity to send to different portions of the tree any command to adjust its normal operation. None of these cells exist in a tree. Senses, brains, and muscular nerves sure do exist in humans, but not in trees. A tree is incapable of comprehending external stimulus or adjusting its behavior based on external stimulus. It lacks the three essential mechanisms that I believe sentience must have, and so I do not consider a tree to be sentient.


Whew.

They just won't ever be able to argue with you about Machiavellian ethics. And they are therefore non-sentient?
Let me make this clear - if you say that something is non-sentient, you are effectively saying that it is an unthinking, unfeeling construct, akin to a little clockwork toy. Quote: southpaw, 2007-09-12T05:08:47Z

Quote: southpaw, 2007-09-12T05:08:47Z
The idea of sentient being to me is the being who can gain knowledge and ponder the use and application of the knowledge, to understand what something is like just from the explanation of it. Being able to think about gravity, something whose only visual clue is when an object falls to the ground, is a good example of abstract thought.
And I call that something that requires sentience but that is not required for sentience. I call that something beyond sentience. I don't see why we can't call, say, a mouse sentient, even though it can clearly think for itself, make its own decisions, and act with judgment based on past experience. Just because a mouse can't innovate like we can or ponder its place in the universe, at least in my opinion, is no reason to call it non-sentient. It's reason to say that the mouse isn't as clever as we are, but I'd still say it's well within what we consider sentience.

Either way, my definition of sentience was supposed to be a model based on physical properties. Tossing in "logical thought," which is entirely abstract and can probably be reproduced in any number of ways that doesn't involve nerve cells, introduces horribly convoluted addendums to the definition. You can only really comment on such abstract capabilities in terms of the way a human would do it. Even though, say, we could build a computer far in the future that could replicate logical human thinking, a part of me tells me that you'd say it's just a mockery, even though it's a fully functional system that performs just as well as us - so what's the difference? But that's getting off-topic.
Point is, this is a very, very low-level, physical model. I don't think such abstract notions (that I think are also obnoxiously laden with pretention and assumptions) like "it must be able to think abstractly" actually belong in this definition.

Suicidal intentions are the result of serious depression, which is a mental disorder. Such an extreme is caused by a catastrophic failure to maintain a healthy emotional state and the thought itself comes from panic and desperation, so it is essentially by definition an unreasonable thing to do.

Still, any idiot can determine, even without me having to tell him this, that suicide is a subject that should be handled with utmost caution and, in situations as these where the suicidal thoughts stem from depression, should be unconditionally discouraged.
But you are an ignorant child. If you are as ambivalent as you claim to be on people thinking about suicide, you are an ignorant fucking child. You seem to think it's as easy a choice as picking out a cereal at the grocery store. It's not like that at all - it's accompanied by weeks to months to even years of mental anguish: severe disappointment with oneself, strong feelings of failure, guilt, humiliation, shame, worthlessness... the feeling doesn't come about if anything significant in one's life is going well, if any part of the person's life makes him happy, or if he's in anything more than a shattered emotional state. What you're saying would be completely valid if considering suicide was something people considered as frequently as they consider vanilla vs chocolate, but that's far from the case.

Many of us have been through shitty enough times to have lived through this, myself included, and I'm quite certain I can say for all of us that we're really fucking glad we didn't go through with what would've been the biggest mistake of our lives - unconditionally the biggest mistake of our lives.

#474104 8 2008-09-29T01:02:04Z Tsukatu
I'm an atheist. I also don't believe life has any purpose whatsoever. I don't live for a god, and I freely accept that my life has no meaning whatsoever. I understand my place in the universe - none of my actions will have any meaningful consequences, and everyone I affect is just going to die anyway.

But given that, making a logical conclusion to suicide is just plain stupid.

For one thing, why exert the effort to end something that doesn't matter? You'll have to think of a means, you'll have to prepare it all, find a place to do it, ponder whether or not you want to leave a note, and finally, at the moment itself, it's not going to matter how callous you can pretend to be on an online forum - the event itself will be extremely emotionally traumatic. If life is meaningless, it certainly isn't worth all that effort to end it. If you really don't care, then just shrug and leave it alone, and let it play out.

On top of that, I don't even see why you're being so hasty. From what you've said about your life, it seems like it's going pretty well. That's pretty much my story at this point, also - I'm succeeding in life, and I'm having fun doing it. I don't derive any holy affirmation of purpose from life, because as far as I'm concerned that's completely inapplicable, but I am having fun.
Think about what else is fun but pointless - video games. Video games are completely frickin' pointless, but they're fun! I play video games, completely with the understanding that they will do absolutely nothing for me except entertain me. It's the same reason I watch sitcoms, or porn. None of it is meaningful, but it's obviously enjoyable.
If you were to apply the same logic you're using about life to these things, I should hope it's obvious why it would be absurd to declare that a huge avenue of entertainment is pointless and therefore must be destroyed; if it's pointless, then don't frickin' worry about it. Life, like so many other things, is pointless, but that doesn't mean it's not fun as all hell, and it's irrational beyond all else to conclude that it should be ended because it's pointless.

From my perspective, this life is what I have and it's enjoyable, so there's no reason to exert the effort to end it. In fact, there's all the more incentive to let it keep going, and even to make it a point to improve myself more so that I can maximize the enjoyment I can derive out of life.

If nothing else, I've always been curious as to how my perceptions of the world will change as I get older. When I was 13, I was fairly certain I pretty much knew it all. A few years later, I could only laugh as I looked back at myself and remembered how secure I was in my convictions, what I thought about the world, my place in the world, and my general outlook on life. Then I aged a few more years, and repeated the process.
I'm 20 now, and so far it's been one long amusement park ride. Even the things that weren't fun are at the very least interesting, and my mind only ever wandered into the same place your mind is now when I wasn't rational enough to realize how silly it is.

I, for one, can't wait to see where my life takes me. I enjoy watching movies and I enjoy playing games, and to me, my life is like some amalgamation of the most interesting movie and the most enjoyable game I've ever played, and the fact that it's pointless doesn't slow me down one bit.

I'm similarly confused about why religious people ask me why I simply don't kill myself if I believe life is pointless, because they - just as you, apparently - don't realize that that knowledge is empowering, and gives me all the more incentive to live my life and love every second of it, and not because it's some happy-go-lucky mindset I've tried to enforce on myself (vis most religions today) but because it's genuinely entertaining to me.

So stop being a retard and get back in the game.
